The power of single cell analysis has been increasingly proven within the scientific community, particularly in studying the complex immune system by identifying cell types and their expressions via single cell RNA sequencing. However, the process of converting tissue sections into single cells for sequencing is full of uncertainties due to the inherent characteristics of sample preparation. To address these challenges, a new method has been developed to extract lymphocytes from breast cancer samples on a cellular level, which is represented by a probabilistic model that uses H\"{o}lder exponential convexity to maintain the consistency and accuracy of images. By applying this model, the shape and location of lymphocytes can be distinctly identified within whole slide images without being affected by tissue deformation, and the area of interest for Lymphocytes can be isolated for further analysis. To establish a benchmark for cancer-related research, a new database called CELLS of BREAST CANCER has been created which includes binary images of lymphocytes, the surrounding cancerous tissue, and a quantity representing the density of cancerous cells. To test the effectiveness of the proposed method, a study has been conducted using the proposed database in order to study the characteristics of whole slide images of breast cancer tissue, which led to a 90\% accuracy rate of lymphocyte detection and 85\% accuracy in distinguishing cancerous cells from healthy tissue using shape and size features. The study shows the potential of advanced image analysis methods in understanding tumor microenvironments through single cell based image analysis. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to combine convex optimization and image analysis techniques in understanding breast cancer through a new lens of image-based single cell analysis. To verify the effectiveness of our method, a new approach has been introduced to compare our method with existing techniques used in image analysis. The study demonstrates that a more comprehensive and accurate representation of tumor microenvironments can be achieved by using a probabilistic model based shape and size features of lymphocytes over traditional image analysis techniques. To ensure the robustness of our study, a new concept of $k$-Nearest Neighbor Based Shape Consistency Metric has been introduced which measures the performance of our method against $k$-Nearest Neighbor and Support Vector Machine algorithms based on features extracted from CELLS of BREAST CANCER database. The study shows that our method outperforms existing techniques used in image analysis by achieving a high accuracy rate of 92\% in detecting lymphocytes and 88\% in distinguishing cancerous cells from healthy tissue when the features are based on the density of cancerous cells. A groundbreaking technology known as cavity magnomechanics has the potential to synchronize two distinct types of quantum systems - mechanical and magnetic - for the development of advanced quantum devices. Previous experiments relied on traditional magnetic materials that were heated by light used in measurements, limiting the technology's applications. Researchers have now overcome this challenge with the help of two-dimensional magnetic materials, like atomic layers of antiferromagnetic manganese heptazine (Mn7Tz), to create a new type of device that can manipulate magnetic fields without the issue of heating. This breakthrough was demonstrated by building an optical cavity with a Mn7Tz magnetic mirror and a silicon nitride cantilever, which was used to develop advanced quantum effects, like mechanical quantum immunity to thermal fluctuations. This achievement paves the way for developing robust quantum devices that can operate near the limits of quantum theory. Additionally, the technique opens up new applications for studying two-dimensional magnetic materials, including the investigation of magnons - collective excitations within the magnetic material - and the development of new magnetic field sources. The authors' work presents a new direction in the study of magnomechanics, which will contribute significantly to the growing field of topological quantum computing. Satellite images often exhibit irregular shapes and numerous compact regions with shared characteristics. Conversely, abnormal areas are typically scattered and concentrated in specific, compact regions. Current methods rely on evenly divided areas for feature extraction but fail to account for the irregular shapes of compact regions. To resolve this issue, we propose an innovative area partition technique that dynamically adjusts the partition based on the shape of compact regions. Our approach significantly enhances the detection and mapping of abnormal areas by utilizing a shape-based partition, which facilitates effective feature extraction and identification of abnormally shaped compact regions. Experimental results validate the superiority of our method over traditional grid-based techniques. For example, when applied to the detection of abnormal urban areas at night, our technique outperformed the grid-based method by 15.6%. Following the partition adjustment, we calculated key features for each region. The images were then combined into a feature space, where we utilized an Unscented Model Subset Simultaneous Approach based on latent variables to identify and map abnormal areas. This multi-scale method effectively detects areas of abnormally shaped compact regions at various scales. Experimental results across multiple datasets consistently demonstrated the high accuracy of our technique in detecting abnormal areas of compact regions at different scales. For instance, when applied to the detection of abnormal urban areas at night, our technique achieved an accuracy of 93.1%, surpassing the grid-based method by 15.6%. Furthermore, when applied to the detection of abnormal agricultural areas, our technique reached an accuracy of 94.6%, outperforming the grid-based method by 14.3%. Lastly, when applied to the detection of abnormal rainstorm areas, our technique reached an accuracy of 92.6%, surpassing the grid-based method by 14.9%. These experimental outcomes confirm the superior performance of our dynamic region partition technique in detecting abnormal areas of compact regions at different scales. Our method may be adapted for various applications on compact regions with distinct characteristics. Its scalability makes it suitable for various dimensions of compact regions. This approach may also be utilized in the detection and identification of compact regions with distinct shapes and features. Potential applications include the detection of compact regions with distinct agricultural patterns, the identification of compact regions during natural events, and the detection of compact regions with distinct urban features. To evaluate the effectiveness of our method, we conducted experiments on detecting compact regions with distinct features such as abnormal areas at night, compact regions at irregular angles, and compact regions with distinct features. These experiments demonstrated the high accuracy of our dynamic region partition technique in detecting compact regions with distinct features

Our findings indicate that pre-trained models can be effectively utilized in downstream applications through the application of a special purpose task, called the code-specific mask language modeling objective, which can enhance the performance of these models on technical papers coding challenges. Moreover, we observe that a pre-trained model trained on a extensive code base with the goal of improving next-token predictions in a sequence-to-sequence framework can serve as a robust feature extractor for a variety of technical code-related tasks. This represents a significant shift away from the prevailing paradigm in programming where features are traditionally computed through complex algorithms or by sampling code from a database. This study builds upon the BERT-SWE model, which was initially proposed in the paper "Exploring the Boundaries of Search in Programming with BERT-SWE". The simple classification of galaxies into discs and spheroids hides a complex reality of diverse galaxy morphologies and multiple formation mechanisms. The distinct origins of discs and spheroids are rooted in their unique formation processes, which are influenced by factors like the availability of angular momentum, gas supply, and whether stars are initially formed rapidly or slowly. These mechanisms are intertwined and interact dynamically, leading to the development of galaxy families that defy straightforward classification. To address this, we propose a new approach that takes into account the varying mass of the dark matter halo, angular momentum, and gas supply as a function of time, and uses a combination of numerical simulations and observational data to classify galaxies. This approach allows us to track the temporal evolution of galaxy mass, angular momentum, and gas supply, and provides new insights into the disc-spheroid formation process. Additionally, we perform multiple component photometric and spectrographic analyses on mock galaxy observations, and find that a significant fraction of galaxies (40%) cannot be classified using traditional disc-spheroid criteria due to the complex nature of their formation. These results have significant implications for ongoing and future galaxy surveys, and highlight the need for a more detailed and time-dependent classification of galaxy evolution.

Utilizing calibrated photometry from the ATLASx wide-field photometer enables the determination of sky brightness at 0.5 deg angular resolution without the need for absolute calibration. Subsequently, applying a model relating photometry to spectroscopy yields the vertical aerosol optical depth at that resolution. This method was validated during daytime observations at the La Silla Observatory utilizing ATLASx and using IAU-63A spectrographic data as a reference. Comparing the results with individual spectral aerosol optical depth measurements revealed a 0.03 correlation coefficient and a standard deviation of 0.04 between the two techniques. This innovative method offers a versatile, portable, and low-maintenance technique for monitoring aerosol optical depth over large areas and may contribute to future satellite mission ground truthing efforts. with performance has been a long-standing goal. Previous studies discovered
synergies between architecture and performance attributes. However, there's been
no comprehensive exploration of how different program properties contribute to
performance improvements. We developed a novel method to address this by
identifying distinct program configurations that yield superior performance. 
Overall, our results demonstrated that simpler program properties can achieve
better results than more complex ones, and there are multiple efficient
configurations possible, all resulting in similar performance outcomes. 
Notably, our findings also uncovered a transition phase between search-based
training and evaluation, where the impact of program properties is misrepresented. 
We believe our analysis will foster new research directions in program
attribute optimization. Additionally, the efficient configuations identified can
be used to inform the design of next-generation search spaces. We have made
the code and search space available on https://github.com/uchastroup/NAS-PC.

In molecular communication, simplified models of an expensive-to-operations channel can be useful for research purposes. Conversely, in wireless communication systems, the cost can be justified by significant gains in system performance. This difference in perspective leads to investigating three strategies for enhancing the capacity in multicasting a message to multiple antennas at the receiver in millimeter-wave communication. The methods considered involve channel pre-distortion, amplitude/phase modulation, and combined strategies. Performance evaluation is conducted using a 60 GHz mmWave channel model and simulations demonstrate that multiple antenna reception can substantially improve system performance, particularly with combined amplitude/phase modulation being the most effective approach when the phase noise has little impact, and a well-designed distortion strategy outperforming modulation-based strategies in systems with phase noise. Additionally, it is observed that when there is no phase noise, modulation-based strategies offer better performance than the distortion-based strategies seen earlier. The findings suggest that while higher cost may be associated with additional antennas, they can yield substantial performance benefits in mmWave multicasting systems. Specifically, when the phase noise is high, a combination strategy with phase noise mitigation is desired, and when the phase noise is low, a distortion-based strategy is preferred. These results can serve as guidance for system design. The study also proposes a new metric for evaluating multicasting performance in mmWave communication systems with phase noise. A novel framework, Compressed Federated Distillation, has been developed to enhance the performance of learning techniques, specifically Federated Averaging and Federated Distillation, used in decentralized deep learning processes. CFD capitalizes on the findings from our in-depth analysis of data compression methods and the integration of distillation with quantization. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that Compressed Federated Distillation successfully combines the benefits of both technologies, resulting in significant communication efficiencies while maintaining equivalent accuracy levels. The proposed method achieves a 5.3 times improvement in communication requirements over Federated Averaging and a 1.5 times improvement over Federated Distillation, making it a promising innovation for the development of communication-efficient decentralized deep learning algorithms. The source code is publicly accessible via the URL https://github.com/ones4wa/CFD. Additionally, our research is part of an NTT research project publicly available at https://researchmap.org-jp/800000390/. Further details can be found in the document number NTT-04-2022.

In complex networks, delivering services efficiently is crucial for a satisfactory user experience, but discovering and integrating relevant services appropriately is a difficult task. An innovative service discovery-assisted dynamic orchestration algorithm, SDADO, is proposed to tackle this challenge, which optimizes service delivery by selecting the suitable service route based on the instant network conditions and resource availability. SDADO integrates with a dynamic orchestration module to prioritize the service delivery route and ensure seamless QoS through network resource reservation. An experimental demonstration highlights the advantages of SDADO in terms of improved service delivery time, increased throughput, and reduced service delivery time. Additionally, the results illustrate the convenience and interpretability offered by SDADO in adapting to various traffic patterns and network conditions. Furthermore, the feasibility of SDADO is showcased by successfully delivering services over multiple routes in a real-world communication system. Finally, the comparative performance of SDADO with respect to other leading algorithms in the industry is presented. This study examines the exponential stability of a star-shaped metric graph with non-uniformly weighted edges, lacking in elasticity at the edges. We develop novel generalizations of the Poincare and Phillips inequalities for functions defined on such graphs. We define a weighted tracking distance and prove that it is complete with respect to a suitable norm. We derive an evolution equation corresponding to the graph's non-uniformly weighted exponential stabilizability issue and establish its exponential stability via the energy method. We provide specific conditions for the positive definite matrix $Q$ and the negative semi-definite matrix $P$ that ensure the exponential stability of the system. We present numerical examples to verify the validity of the derived exponential stability criteria. Furthermore, we investigate the conditions for the stability of the corresponding equilibrium position of the graph. Finally, we discuss the applicability of the obtained results to certain classes of simple graphs. Moreover, we provide an application of the obtained results to the study of a nonlinear model describing a coupled pendulum with discrete time delays. Optimization problems often necessitate determining the optimal solution among a multitude of alternatives. Typically, this is achieved by defining a utility function, which enables the identification of the best option through maximization. Utilizing expert knowledge is an effective approach to constructing a utility function offline. This knowledge can be expressed as result preferences, which can be satisfied by defining a utility function. The proposed method, KUPL, learns a utility function offline by leveraging expert-provided result preferences. Contrary to traditional approaches that rely solely on pairwise result preferences, KUPL takes advantage of the increased information, while also accounting for their relative importance. The technique involves initially mapping the result preferences to a utility function space, which is subsequently refined through kernel-based support vector regression. Experiments on diverse datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of KUPL. This study's findings show that KUPL can satisfactorily accommodate the increased information from result preferences and their relative importance without a negative impact on its offline performance. Moreover, a comparison with an approach that relies solely on pairwise result preferences in a black-box setting confirms KUPL's superior performance. The proposed method, KUPL, contributes to two key research areas: the offline learning of utility functions and result preference-based optimization methods. This study bridges these two fields and shows that constructing a utility function offline by leveraging result preferences can outperform alternatives that rely solely on pairwise result preferences. extraction problem in domain adaptation for reinforcement learning can be tackled.
While previous methods primarily focused on using pre-trained models to guide
policy extraction, our proposed approach instead uses them to forecast future
action sequences and then employs an extractor to process and generate abstract
features based on this forecast, resulting in superior sample efficiency and
performance compared to the state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, we've developed
an efficient abstract feature extractor using a pre-trained model, which
significantly outperforms previous techniques on multiple complex continuous
domain adaptation scenarios. Experimental results show the exceptional value of
pre-trained sequence-to-sequence models in predicting the future actions of
trained reinforcement learning agents and the effectiveness of our feature extractor
in generating abstract features based on such predictions. As a result, we've
achieved notable gains in sample efficiency and performance, surpassing the
current state-of-the-art methods in domain adaptation for reinforcement learning. 
The source code for our approach can be found at https://github.com/agrija/FeatureExtraction-for-RLL.

The integration of a metasurface with tightly coupled resonances into an atomic trap offers a highly sensitive technique for detecting the weak electromagnetic fields emitted by single atoms. By positioning the atomic trap near a surface mode antenna, the device can efficiently couple to 50 $\Omega$ and enhance the transmission of the atomic emission over a broad frequency band. This setup enables the direct conversion of atomic spin states into electrical signals, potentially integrating quantum technology using single atoms with advanced electronic devices. The design presented here consists of an atomic trap made up of two gold patches and an array of gold-dielectric resonators, both Gold and dielectric materials being optimized to facilitate atomic interaction. The structure's electromagnetic behavior is governed by a loop antenna mode and an array of magnetic dipole resonances, both optimized to facilitate atomic interaction. The distance between the gold patches is critical and affects the efficiency of the atomic transmission, the optimal spacing being approximately $20\frac{d}{\lambda}$ in the given frequency range. The integrated device was found to increase the efficiency of the atomic transmission by at least $20$ times compared to a non-integrated atomic trap. This notable enhancement demonstrates the value of tightly coupled resonances in enhancing the efficiency of single atom-based devices. Furthermore, the device's simplicity and effectiveness make it a suitable model for the development of new devices utilizing single atoms, such as logical elements, quantum interfaces, and measuring instruments. Lastly, the device was found to be robust against variations in the dielectric constant of the surrounding environment, allowing for potential applications in environments with variable dielectric properties. The integration of the metasurface with the atomic trap yields a superior single atom-based device, offering a 20 times improvement in efficiency over a non-integrated trap. The newly developed device exhibits exceptional performance as a single atom detector, quantum interface, and measuring instrument, demonstrating its potential in the field of single atom technology. The device's effectiveness is showcased through the simulation of electromagnetic interactions with the atomic trap, the emission of atoms in the frequency range of 500-600 THz, and the optimization of the dielectric materials used. The design presented is a novel single atom detector, and its integration with the atomic trap enables the direct conversion of atomic spin states into electrical signals, and thus has the potential to be used as a quantum interface and measuring instrument. Furthermore, the device exhibits robustness against variations in the dielectric properties of its surroundings, and its simplicity and effectiveness make it a model for the development of other single atom technology devices. We have developed a novel method for inferring complex polymers composed of thousands of subunits called monomers. Our technique frames the polymer inference problem as a structural prediction challenge, where a polymer is represented by connecting its monomers in a specific sequence. To test the efficacy of our method, we created extensive datasets of real polymers composed of various proteins and studied the effects of different sequence representations on inference accuracy. Our approach uses learning-based techniques to determine the optimal connection strategy between monomers and has demonstrated superior performance on predicting the 3D structures of proteins, proteins with modified properties, and random sequences of amino acids. Furthermore, we have discovered that simplifying complex polymers into smaller structural components called proto-polymers enables accurate reconstruction of the original polymer structure. This new understanding provides a framework for inferring complex polymers composed of diverse subunits and demonstrates the potential of machine learning-based methods in polymer structure inference. The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic severely strained healthcare systems' ability to procure and allocate medical equipment, notably ventilators, which have become scarce in some areas. Unfortunately, a single ventilator must often be shared among multiple patients, a practice known as ventilator sharing, which presents several challenges. Primarily, ensuring that each patient receives their desired tidal volume (VT) is a significant concern. To tackle this issue, we have developed a new approach, the Intelligent Ventilator Sharing system (IVS), which is a fully automated, multichannel ventilation care plan creator that optimizes respiratory flow rate (Vt) to meet individual patient needs for bilateral spontaneous breathing, assisted breathing, and pressure support. By leveraging a custom-designed solver based on the Broyden–Fletcher–Shannon algorithm, IVS accurately calculates the optimal respiratory flow rate for each patient in shared-ventilator care plans. Furthermore, we validated the accuracy of IVS in an in-vitro setting with two patients, demonstrating that it effectively meets the respiratory needs of both subjects with a single ventilator. X-ray images are also analyzed to determine the ratio of functional lung tissue, which informs the care plan creation process. Our work is the first to address ventilator sharing with a computerized solution, and IVS has the potential to improve patient outcomes across various areas of respiratory care. Further research is needed to validate the system's efficacy in diverse clinical settings and through collaborative ventilation. Our source code is publicly available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/IndigoLane/IVS. Additionally, a related video can be accessed at https://youtube.cmmunity/covid19ventilators. Both patients were ventilated using the shared ventilator with tidal volumes of 350ml, which is in line with the recommended standard. Furthermore, the system calculated the optimal respiratory flow rate for each patient, which were 24L/min and 15L/min for patient 1 and patient 2, respectively. These values confirm that the system is functional and can create accurate care plans for shared-ventilator patients. Future work will focus on testing the system in a fully functional ventilator environment and expanding its capabilities to cover various respiratory care scenarios. As a first-to-market computerized solution for ventilator sharing, IVS shows great potential in this area. Nonetheless, further research is needed to validate its efficacy in diverse clinical settings and through collaborative ventilation. The effectiveness of live signature forgery detection in biometric systems depends on various factors including the quality of the user's own signature, the level of skill and copying ability of the would-be forger, and the ability of the algorithm to identify unique features in the signature. Since these factors can vary significantly across different cultures and age groups, the choice of algorithm and parameters becomes a crucial decision for the system designer. In this study, different methods of calculating the distinctiveness, complexity, and repeatability of signature templates were evaluated using a large dataset containing signatures from signers with varying levels of skill and experience. The results showed that using a specific approach that takes into account the unique features of each signature produced the best outcomes for live signature detection, while also demonstrating the importance of considering the characteristics of the target population when designing the algorithm. Furthermore, the benefits of this approach were confirmed through tests on a larger dataset of genuine and forged signatures. The research highlights the potential of this method to improve live signature detection and suggests areas for further exploration in the field. The project also evaluated an alternative method previously used to assess the quality of signature templates, which did not yield the same level of performance as the new approach. The study ultimately recommends the new method as the preferred approach for calculating the distinctiveness, complexity, and repeatability of signature templates. The output of the study can be utilized by biometric system designers to make informed decisions about algorithm and parameter selection that are adapted to the unique needs of their target users. We examine how supersymmetry constraints impact low energy effective interactions in string theory, with a focus on four-dimensional models featuring a single gauge field. Our investigation involves calculating low energy effective interactions using two methods: first, by applying the supersymmetry on the worldsheet through a Green-Schwarz formulation, and second, by deriving low energy effective interactions off-shell using a off-shell background field method. We demonstrate the validity of the off-shell background field method and reveal that supersymmetry constraints generate non-trivial low energy effective interactions, specifically a three-gauge-boson coupling, in the massless limit. Furthermore, our results show that the three-gauge-boson coupling in the massless limit is comparable in magnitude to the Yukawa coupling in supergravity. Advancements in graph neural networks have significantly enhanced image classification tasks by converting complex images into interpretable graph structures. Nevertheless, graph-based models still suffer from inherent vulnerabilities in their prediction capabilities due to their reliance on these graph structures, which can be manipulated to deceive them. In response, we introduce the Graph Privacy Advisor - an innovative tool that addresses these weaknesses by providing a predictive confidence score indicative of the risk of predictive deception resulting from graph manipulation. In our testing against the most advanced graph-based models, the Graph Privacy Advisor demonstrated remarkable performance, yielding remarkable outcomes with accuracies above 90% across various datasets including ImageNet, CUB-200-2011, and Flowery, in addition to remarkable outcomes with accuracies above 90% across multiple datasets. Furthermore, we found that integrating the Graph Privacy Advisor into graph-based models significantly boosted their robustness and overall predictive capabilities. In a notable instance, the Graph Privacy Advisor improved the overall predictive performance of the advanced graph-based models in the CUB-200-2011 bird dataset by 0.04 and 0.06 points, respectively. This marks a pioneering breakthrough, as we have achieved the first instance of graph-based models being trained to predict and mitigate deceptive graph-based attacks. Our proposed approach offers limitless potential for the development of predictive strategies that proactively anticipate and counter potential attacks on predictive systems. FOXSI is a solar observatory with a high-energy resolution of 100 eV and sensitivity in the 5-60 keV range, allowing for the detection of rare ionization events on the Sun. Launched on the International Space Station in 2018, FOXSI features a 12.5 cm x 12.5 cm aperture and employs a stack of three silicon detectors. Its capability to distinguish charge particles from Sun-generated X-rays makes it essential in understanding the Sun's quiet periods. However, the instrument's observations were hampered by a space debris incident in 2019, causing significant damage. Qualitative testing prior to the incident confirmed FOXSI's sensitivity in detecting charge particles, which can provide valuable data on solar plasma conditions. The instrument is designed to run three 30-second on-board experiments per day, with each experiment consisting of two observation modes - high and low energy ranges - to enhance its sensitivity and distinguish between particles and solar X-rays. Despite operational limitations following the incident, FOXSI continues to contribute to our understanding of the Sun's quiet periods and the detection of particles emanating from the Earth's atmosphere. Its 2020 findings established a statistical connection between terrestrial particles and Sun-oriented events, which require further confirmation. Long-term observations combined with three years of data on heavy ions and the detection of rare events less than 1% sensitive in the high energy range will allow scientists to explore the Sun's quiet periods more precisely. The findings presented in this paper provide a comprehensive overview of the FOXSI's capabilities and its potential in understanding the Sun's behavior and unusual occurrences on Earth. This research offers a novel error model for estimating pose using inertial sensors and external vision, which is able to account for a broad range of error correlation types. It's demonstrated that incorporating more general correlation types leads to more precise sensor data, which in turn yields enhanced estimation outcomes. A specific sequence of operations is proposed for accurately calculating the optimal error model in a timely manner, and the proposed method is empirically verified on actual flight data from a quadcopter. The outcome is a substantial improvement in estimated position and orientation accuracy, achieving reduced error rates of 50% and 30%, respectively. Utilizing this advanced error model, a calibrated visual-inertial algorithm is developed to achieve a notable decrease in overall loss of just under 20%, as well as a notable decrease in mean squared error of roughly 15%. Experimental findings indicate that the proposed method performs superiorly to mainstream alternatives in pose estimation tasks. In particular, it outperforms and surpasses the performance of popular vision-based localization and pose estimation tools, which rely on inaccurate error models, achieving roughly eight to ten times more accurate results. Consequently, this advanced error model is recommended for demanding applications such as autonomous aviation, which often encounter challenging environmental conditions and system malfunctions. Moreover, the technique also offers potential applications in fields such as robotics and medicine, where accurate 3D pose estimation is crucial for safe and successful navigation. Additionally, the technique shows great potential for extension to other sensor modalities in need of 3D pose estimation, as seen in the use of stereo or multi-view imaging technologies. It's worth noting that the proposed method has a computational complexity of O(N^3.5), which makes it efficiently applicable to complex systems involving numerous sensors with high dimensionality. Nonetheless, the efficiency of the method could be enhanced through the application of specialized hardware or alternative optimization techniques. Lastly, the technique is remarkably versatile and can be safely applied to a broad range of systems without any concerns of instabilities or unsafe behavior, as has been observed in testing thus far. Ultimately, the technique offers a safe and efficient solution for various challenging pose estimation problems in diverse domains. The task of colorizing grayscale images through prediction has gained significant interest within the computer vision community, and several techniques have been introduced to achieve this goal. While the methods developed previously rely on specific types of training data or utilize predictions made by a pre-trained model, our proposed technique breaks the color-image synthesis challenge down into two manageable tasks: color prediction and image synthesis, and addresses these challenges separately with novel approaches. The color prediction aspect leverages an attention-based neural network that utilizes prior image learning in an unsupervised manner to create higher-level features, resulting in more flexible color predictions, and the image synthesis aspect utilizes an autoencoder to fill in the grayscale areas of an image, and the incorporation of multi-scale color predictions enables better outcomes than previous techniques. The integration of these new approaches enables the innovative solution of color-image synthesis, and our experimental results demonstrate significant improvements over the established methods in terms of accuracy and flexibility. BD~And, a binary star system in the constellation Andromeda, has an unusually large and changing orbital period of 72.91 days.  Although it was initially interpreted as a binary system with equal components, more recent research has revealed that there are hints of a possible third body within the system, which may be responsible for the observed fluctuations in the orbital period.  To investigate this further, we carried out a comprehensive photometric and high-resolution spectroscopic study of BD~And during October 2020 - June 2021.  Our spectroscopic data covered 23 epochs while our photometry, using the TESS spacecraft, and our spectroscopy yielded a sample of 42 points, resulted in several significant discoveries.  Firstly, we detected noticeable changes in the measured orbital period, which confirmed previous findings and revealed new ones: an evident minimum in the O-C diagram at phase 0.82 and a possible one at 0.15 with an uncertainty of 0.07.  Our high-resolution spectra from November 2020 to June 2021 enabled us to identify three distinct sub-spectra in the measured data, which further confirmed that there are indeed three components to the system.  Our findings also established that the binary system's mass ratio lies between 0.69 and 0.99, while analysis of the system's light curve using the Wilson-Devinney code suggested a mass ratio of 0.83.  Our research also made several contributions to understanding binary systems generally, among them the most significant being the detection of variability in the measured activity indices, which further confirmed that there are indeed three components to the system.  Ultimately, our research established that BD~And system is an interesting binary system that warrants further study. Researchers increasingly post preprints before traditional publication to gain early visibility, but the effectiveness of this approach is still debated. This study examined the effects of preprint deployment on research output metrics using extensive data from arXiv and Nature Physics articles. Various factors influenced the analysis, including the timing and spread of preprints, peer review processes, and the impact of journal publication. Data showed that papers based on preprints are cited sooner and receive more citations overall compared to uncirculated research. To better understand the preprint phenomenon's causality, researchers were able to isolate a group of papers that were shared publicly but not subject to external review, revealing similar benefits. This study suggests that making research accessible earlier can boost its output, potentially by reducing delays between completion and publication. Although the optimal preprint usage remains uncertain, these findings indicate that widespread preprint deployment can accelerate scientific progress without compromising quality. Nonetheless, carefully controlling the preprint cycle and ensuring rigorous review remains crucial for maintaining scientific integrity. Collaborative efforts between research groups, institutions, and publishers can foster an open scientific environment where early exposure to research ideas drives faster discovery. Given the growing influence of preprints, it is essential for the scientific community continues to reevaluate the traditional publication pipeline and explore alternative pathways to accelerate research. In this research, we address the completeness problem of Sidon sets within the finite affine plane of order n, focusing on hyperbolas and ellipses. We find that completing a Sidon set in an hyperbola or ellipse is not possible. We support this conclusion by demonstrating that in an affine plane of order n, no ellipse can encompass three distinct Sidon sets with a maximum element count of n^2. We also reveal that the maximum number of Sidon sets that can be supported by a hyperbola is three when n is odd and two when n is even. We achieve this by constructing Sidon sets in planes of order four and six, and establishing a maximum of three Sidon sets for planes of order five and six. We further prove that the maximum number of Sidon sets supported by an ellipse in a plane of order four is two, and determine the maximum number of Sidon sets supported by an ellipse in a plane of order five as three. We establish the complete spectrum of Sidon sets within a plane of order three. We also derive upper limits on the number of Sidon sets within a plane of order four, and a plane of order five, as well as the number of Sidon sets within a plane of order six. We achieve this by using a computer to analyze all possible configurations. We also present a method for generating Sidon sets in a plane of order n by iteratively increasing n, beginning from n=4, and provide supporting examples for our conclusions. To facilitate our research, we developed a computer program for identifying Sidon sets in a finite affine plane, and an accompanying package for the calculation of elliptic curves. We also explored a more general concept of Sidon sets within a finite grid of size n x m that is not a square, but our findings are more inconclusive in this case. We discuss this in the concluding sections of the study. We chose the title 'The Completeness Problem of Sidon Sets in the Finite Affine Plane' for this research as the core focus. We also utilized a simplified abbreviation 'CSPSidon' to refer to this problem. We then examined an expanded concept of the completeness problem, dubbed CSPSidon+, which involves identifying a maximum number of Sidon sets within a given structure. We were unable to determine the status of this problem for planes of order four and six. However, we were able to determine the maximum number of Sidon sets in a plane of order five. We concluded our research by outlining potential avenues for further investigation

In the context of PDF fitting, understanding how to transition from one PDF at a particular scale to another at a different scale is crucial and can be achieved through the DGLAP evolution process. However, when using the fractionation or kernel representation of PDFs, the corresponding evolution equations become complex and involve the product of an auxiliary matrix and the PDF kernel, requiring computation of one-loop matrix elements. A new method to simplify this process is presented, based on the extraction of evolution operators from the DGLAP equations at next-to-leading-order (NLO). The results for the gluon evolution operator are compared with an all-order derivation and verified to be correct within the relevant context. Additionally, we outline how to apply this method at the next leading-order (NLO) level and propose an approach at the third-order level. The method here proposed allows for a straightforward integration of PDFs with higher-order corrections in the DGLAP evolution, thereby eliminating computational hurdles and facilitating the development of third-order parton showers or other matching schemes where the fractionation representation is employed. Furthermore, we introduce an innovative method within this work, which allows for the integration of PDF evolution with small-x modifications at the NLO level with minimal additional computational requirements. The method presented can be applied at different scales, making it a valuable tool for numerous tasks in the context of PDFs, including the generation of input PDFs, computation of PDF extraction from data at different scales, and matching schemes between different orders. The method is also compatible with other corrections, like vertex corrections and flavor breaking. The code to reproduce the results presented has been made available online. The code is part of the SharesRe tool, an interactive Python library that facilitates the computation of high-energy cross-sections, also including other useful functions to interact with PDFs. Quantum field theory hypotheses involving information geometric concepts like entanglement entropy, described by the surface area of a region in spacetime, are examined in order to accommodate a broader set of quantum gravity proposals than previously thought possible. Researchers initially assumed that each region in a quantum system has a single, unique entropy associated with it, which would restrict the set of possible quantum gravity proposals they could explain. However, recent developments have shown that this assumption can be avoided. This new understanding is based on two key points. Firstly, it has been observed that system boundaries do not necessarily correspond to regions from which information can be extracted in the context of holographic reconstruction. Secondly, it has been demonstrated that the requirement for monogamy of mutual information in bulk entropies comes at the cost of possibly allowing multiple boundary entropies associated with the same region. This new understanding has been used to construct entanglement entropy proposals that would be inconsistent according to traditional monogamy of mutual information requirements but are consistent when considering the more permissive guidelines set forth in [7]. Advanced observational campaigns like the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope often deal with vast numbers of images that need to be processed. To tackle this task, researchers have applied nonlinear coaddition methods like median and clipped-mean, which circumvent the requirement for accurate weight information. Although these algorithms are efficient, they have a significant drawback: they can't guarantee a consistent point spread function (PSF) profile across all coadded images. This weakness becomes a major issue when analyzing images from campaigns with steadily changing telescopes, such as the Hubble Space Telescope. In this research, we address this issue by developing a new nonlinear coaddition technique that maintains a consistent PSF profile and accurately accounts for image signal strengths. This innovative approach yields comparable results to the traditional maximum-likelihood technique and performs well even in scenarios where images have diverse sensitivity limits. We demonstrate the efficacy of this technique using real data from the HST, showcasing its ability to coadd images and produce reliable photometric results. This breakthrough offers promising possibilities for the future LSST project.

Research has shown that combining quantum computing and artificial intelligence holds great promise for driving breakthroughs in various fields. Yet, due to the limitations of current quantum computers, which are prone to errors, making reliable predictions with the help of quantum AI on local devices is a significant challenge. To address this, our team has created an innovative protocol that enables remote servers to verify that a client has correctly executed an AI model running on a quantum computer without requiring a perfect quantum computer for the server. Specifically, our CVQC protocol securely computes the classification result of a convolutional neural network, resulting in significant verification speedups over existing protocols while supporting a wide range of input sizes. The performance gains come from accurately estimating the quantum computer's error rate and utilizing the quantum approximation operator technique to translate quantum states into classical signatures, thus reducing the computational requirements of the quantum computer. Building on this foundation, our work lays the groundwork for a broader range of quantum AI protocols in the future. The implementation details of CVQC are available at https://github.com/QuABLA/qvlasim.git, and the performance evaluation can be accessed via https://github.com/QuABLA/qvlresearch/tree/main/CVQC. Additionally, isometric embeddings for specific quantum error correcting codes, as suggested in Section VI, are provided at https://github.com/QuABLA/qvlCodeCorrCCEC. Lastly, the quantum computing simulations for CVQC, as described in Section VII, can be found at https://github.com/QuABLA/qvlCodeCCEC. Our code is open to collaboration; feel free to contact [jxu22@umd.edu](mailto:jxu22@umd.edu) or [yli277@umd.edu](mailto:yli277@umd.edu) to join the effort. As a fundamental aspect of various biological processes, cell behavior has significant implications for analyzing phenomena like tumor progression, drug response, and microbial motion. Common methods for examining cell behavior include tracking cells within images and manually labeling cells within specific regions. Recent advancements in deep learning have improved image analysis, but generating a vast number of artificial cells through sampling from latent spaces often remains limited by the absence of a synthetic cell template. Lacking such a template hinders learning from combined real and artificial data for tasks like segmentation, as it restricts the possible shapes and forms that can be learned during training. To address this, we introduce a new method where a generative adversarial network trains both a cell synthesis model and a learning model in an unsupervised setting. The cell synthesis model, trained to map labels to latent spaces, and the learning model, which is trained to perform segmentation by using real and synthetic data, outperform existing methods on multiple datasets. This new approach allows for efficient synthesis of novel cell shapes and enables learning from combined real and artificial data for tracking cells within images, resulting in improved accuracy and faster identification of cell movements. Reinforcement learning research over the past decade has shown that certain geometric properties, such as a task's dimension or a feature's persistence, significantly impact performance and learning rate. Studies have often utilized a simplified framework, the linear bandit problem, to explore the effect of persistence, but applied persistence is typically defined by the features' projection onto the target space, a restrictive condition that often leads to overestimation. We overcome this limitation by introducing a new measure of persistence that quantifies feature properties and demonstrates its significant impact on performance, even surpassing previous persistence thresholds in some instances. We also reveal a novel scale that influences feature persistence and observe that features at a larger scale often exhibit different characteristics and behaviors compared to those at a smaller scale. To test the applicability of our persistence concept, we successfully applied it to a more complex task, nonlinear geodesic pursuit, and observed corresponding performance outcomes. Our research thus establishes persistence as a crucial attribute relevant to a broader range of tasks within the reinforcement learning domain. We have made our source code publicly available at https://github.com/laurLp/LpPERSISTENCE. We consider the task of identifying the number of synchronized groups in a network comprised of coupled chaotic systems, where their collective behavior over time is observed through a set of time-series data. Our proposed method, though simple, is effective in solving this problem, and we demonstrate its accuracy by applying it to previously unresolved challenges in the field of complex systems. Moreover, we successfully modify it to accurately determine the size of each synchronized cluster. Our approach is then compared to another method that estimates synchronized clusters by condensing the time-series data into a form that preserves its structural and sequential characteristics, and we show that it outperforms this method in certain scenarios. Our research showcases the value of integrating different techniques to solve complex problems in the field of complex systems. 

However, the approach faces obstacles when dealing with a scenario where the system switches between different synchronized clusters over time. It successfully determines the number of synchronized clusters in such cases once the time-series data is divided into distinct segments. 

One variation of this problem is to identify the instant when the system switches from one synchronized cluster to another. Our approach is ineffective in this scenario as it treats all synchronized clusters within a time segment as a single entity. 

Another potential issue with this method is that it may incorrectly split a synchronized cluster into multiple groups or combine several clusters into one, which can be resolved by further refining the time-series data and applying a more sophisticated technique to identify synchronized clusters. 

It's worth noting that this method can be applied both automatically and with human involvement. Our proposed method of determining synchronized clusters, along with its modifications and applications, is summarized in the flow chart included with this research. 

This approach was inspired by a 2010 paper by Ywazola et al., "Synchronization in complex networks via minor components," in which they developed an automated method for determining synchronized clusters by condensing the time-series data into a form that preserves its structural and sequential characteristics. Our proposed method outperforms this method in certain scenarios. 

To evaluate the performance of these methods, we used two measures: accuracy and computational speed. Our proposed method successfully determined the number of synchronized clusters in all tested scenarios, while Ywazola's method failed in a few scenarios. Both methods were successful in determining the size of each synchronized cluster. 

In terms of computational speed, our proposed method was significantly faster than Ywazola's method. Our results suggest that these methods can be used in combination to determine the number and size of synchronized clusters with a high level of accuracy.

The fundamental measurement process in quantum systems has long been understood, but a new phenomenon, continuous quantum measurement, offers a previously unexplored means to drive information-driven processes, including thermal machines, which can now operate under conditions of strong coupling between the system and a measuring environment. This environment not only disables standard quantum measurement theory but also introduces notable effects not seen before. Due to the high scraping rate caused by continuous measurement, the system's energy balance is severely disrupted, limiting its ability to operate efficiently. Therefore, to create an information engine powered by continuous quantum measurement, it is essential to manage and minimize the measurement-induced energy imbalance, making traditional designs no longer applicable. We demonstrate a newly developed method to turn the negative effects into beneficial factors in the optimal operation of the information engine and show that continuous quantum measurement can be a viable way to achieve optimal information-driven work extraction. We further establish that the Brownian Hathway-Linder model provides a reliable environmental model for weak coupling and explore the possibility of achieving maximum information-driven work in this scenario. Additionally, we develop a theoretical framework for studying the speed of information-driven processes and identify known paradigms within the established model. We also investigate the impact of quantum entanglement within the environment on information-driven work extraction and demonstrate the emergence of novel effects not seen before in standard models. LBS users' geographic position and time stamps make their data particularly vulnerable to privacy breaches. Current approaches to privacy preservation for spatio-temporal data often rely on synthetic or annotated data, but these methods have significant drawbacks: synthetic data can fail to replicate real-world precision, and annotated data requires costly and often impractical human input. Furthermore, these methods do not address another key issue - the loss of conditionally dependent data, which can lead to decreased model accuracy. To address these challenges, we propose a novel framework for privacy-enhanced spatio-temporal data processing and analysis based on differential privacy and Bayesian graphical models. This framework includes two key components. Ultimately, our study's findings suggest that inter-site effects play a significant role in detecting both individual and group differences in brain networks and probably contribute to the observed test-retest differences in fMRI data. This research introduces a novel positional encoding technique designed for code-mixed text, which enhances the performance of language models in zero-shot settings. The proposed encoding method exploits the linguistic characteristics of code-mixed language by spatially distorting word positions, resulting in improved model outcomes. We demonstrate the efficacy of this encoding technique across multiple zero-shot scenarios, surpassing existing methods and showcasing its adaptability across various task types, such as sentiment classification and question answering, using datasets like Ind vs. Eng and Hind vs. Eng. Additionally, we successfully integrate the encoding method into pre-trained language models, enhancing their performance in multi-lingual settings. The source code for this technique is publicly available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/amanbasu/SPE. Our results indicate that the SPE model outperforms current positional encoding methods, which we have integrated into models like RoBERTa and BERT. The trained models, along with the source code, can be accessed at https://github.com/amanbasu/SPE. To facilitate replicability, we have released the pre-trained models, datasets, and experiment results at https://github.com/amanbasu/SPE-reproducibility. Our study indicates that SPE offers a 1.5% improvement in accuracy over the best existing method and a 3.1% improvement with BERT and 2.4% with RoBERTa. Additionally, the models exhibit superior performance on datasets not used during training, indicating their potential for zero-shot applications. To validate the interpretability of the models, we performed thorough analysis on the Ind vs. Eng dataset and discovered that the SPE models accurately identify the dominant language in code-mixed text for both sentiment classification and question answering tasks. Baldwin's idea of gradual evolution through individual actions has been largely disregarded in contemporary evolutionary biology. We show that a quantitative expression of Baldwin's concept is linked to the average impact of gene replacements, as expressed through the Fisher diffusion equation. This average value represents the net change in the phenotype resulting from each new beneficial gene variant. A novel solution to the Fisher diffusion equation allows us to analytically determine the average effect of beneficial gene substitutions and their relation to the rate of phenotypic change. We also derive a formula to calculate the average effect of deleterious gene substitutions and their contribution to the reversal of phenotypic changes. We demonstrate that in situations where a population's fitness gradient exhibits smooth, continuous changes over time, the average effect of beneficial gene substitutions can be negative, indicating that large initial differences between individuals can actually hinder the evolution of complex adaptations. We also provide the condition under which the average effect of beneficial gene substitutions becomes non-negative, thereby promoting complex adaptations. Our study offers a fresh perspective on Baldwin's idea and provides a new tool for exploring its applications in modeling evolution. Moreover, the Fisher diffusion equation has various applications in biology, statistics, and physics; therefore, the solutions obtained in this study can be useful for resolving real-world problems across multiple disciplines. The approach employed in this research is versatile and can be applied to other evolutionary processes involving individual actions; therefore, its applications can extend beyond the specific example of Baldwin's idea considered here. The presented solutions are consistent with the existing results for the Fisher equation, as well as the general theory of evolution, including the effect of genetic variation and random mutations. The approach proposed in this study is innovative in its ability to analytically determine the average effect of beneficial gene substitutions and may be used as a starting point for future research on other individual-level evolutionary processes. Moreover, the probability distributions derived over time can be extremely useful in understanding how large individuals influence the evolution of complex adaptations and how they contribute to the development of high metabolic rates, innovative tools, and advanced cognitive abilities. The lessons learned from the applications of Baldwin's idea can also be applied to other individual-level evolutionary processes and may offer a new perspective on past achievements in evolutionary biology. The discovery that the average effect of beneficial gene substitutions can be negative may also challenge the traditional notion that large individuals always contribute to the development of complex adaptations. The solutions obtained in this study are consistent with the existing results for the Fisher equation, as well as the general theory of evolution, including the effect of genetic variation and random mutations.

A closed-loop feedback system, resembling human foot mechanics, has been implemented on a two-legged robot. The feedback mechanism, rooted in the stretch-shortening cycle of muscle-tendon units, is incorporated into the robot's sole and connected to a sensor that measures pressure during the stance phase. This data is used to develop an adaptive control system, which regulates the tempo and rhythm of the robot's gait. The feedback system enables the robot to adjust its gait cycle by responding to pressure data in real-time. Through this approach, the robot can achieve a synchronized stride period, regardless of the width of its feet, and maintain a steady pace in the presence of uneven terrain, all while staying upright and moving forward. The effectiveness of this control strategy is demonstrated via numerical simulations and experimental trials with the robot, wearing sole-equipped feet, navigating different gait cycles and uneven surfaces. The research presents an innovative solution for creating more natural and efficient robot gaits, offering a novel perspective on robot locomotion inspired by human biology. The presented approach successfully generates robust and adaptive gait control mechanisms for bipedal robots. The future prospects of this research involve applying this feedback mechanism to jump and exploration behaviors in robots, and eventually transferring it to wearable technology for human motion control. Previous studies have demonstrated that employing learned descriptors in camera relocalization yields exceptional results, particularly under challenging conditions. In this research, we examine whether descending descriptors to feature points can facilitate camera pose estimation. Consequently, we propose a novel framework, PDLR, which employs descending descriptors in conjunction with a global optimizer to tackle the problem of monocular SLAM. Initially, conventional image features and descriptors are generated within the framework. Subsequently, a set of selected feature points are processed using a descriptor optimizer that incorporates descending descriptors, thus creating refined descriptors for those specific features. A global optimizer then leverages the modified descriptor set, along with keyframe connections, to perform camera relocalization and generate new rotation and translation estimates. Moreover, 2D-3D feature correspondences are established to further enhance the performance of the system. Experimental findings on KITTI, Aerial, and Sensoray datasets indicate that PDLR delivers superior results, outperforming existing methods in difficult scenarios. Notably, the use of descending descriptors was found to significantly boost the performance of the system when feature points become sparse. Moreover, computational efficiency analysis suggests that the proposed framework achieves a striking balance between accuracy and speed. In this study, we explore semi-supervised learning in a decentralized setting with knowledgeable clients and a collaborative server. The server initiates a personalized semi-supervised training process by sending unlabeled data and model parameters to clients, which then refine their local models using labeled data. The improved models are exchanged with the server, enabling it to integrate the updated parameters and share them with other clients. This efficient information exchange empowers clients to benefit from each other's expertise, although only a few clients have access to labeled data. However, we discovered that the existing SSFL methods result in knowledge drifts among the shared parameters, limiting the learning potential. To address this challenge, we developed Drift-Free SSFL, a novel semi-supervised learning framework that combines personalized training with efficient inter-client knowledge sharing, and successfully applied it to vision tasks; the results demonstrate its capabilities under conditions of limited labeled data and restricted communication bandwidth. The code for Drift-Free SSFL is accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/damuii/Drift-Free-SSFL. The interior of a neutron star is undergoing a radical transformation in the moments following its merger with another neutron star. A crucial aspect of this process involves the magnetic field's behavior within the accretion disk formed by the merged star. A previously developed model, which simulated this process and the resulting disk's magnetic evolution, is the subject of a new investigation presented in the paper. This new study confirms the accuracy of the model, which indicated that the interior of the disk remains coated in magnetic field, with the majority of this field being mirrored on the surface of the disk. A novel discovery resulting from the study is the potential for a significant magnetic field to be preserved within the disk, particularly if certain conditions are met. These conditions include slower disk rotation and larger inner disk boundaries. The preservation of the magnetic field in the disk has significant implications for the production of fast radio bursts, which may be triggered by shocks within the disk. A preserved magnetic field could provide the necessary energy required for these bursts through magnetohydrodynamic waves. The study also raises the possibility that some of the magnetic field from the merged stars survives the merger process and becomes embedded in the disk, which could provide further energy for these bursts. The study paves the way for a future simulation, which will investigate the impact of this preserved magnetic field on the production of fast radio bursts. This future simulation could help answer whether the magnetic field in the disk plays a role in the creation of these bursts or whether they are instead created through a different process. Moreover, the study could also aid in identifying key indicators that could be used to distinguish between different scenarios for the origin of fast radio bursts. A future simulation could also explore whether the magnetic field in the disk could be utilized to extract energy from the star, which could result in the emission of a pulsational X-ray flux. This time, the flux could be emitted at a rate that is higher than the Eddington limit, which could lead to a variety of observable effects. A model of this process, which involves the extraction of energy from the star, is part of a future simulation that could help answer these questions, which may provide a new perspective on the observed emission from a system known as GX 3404. The future simulation could also help to shed light on whether the magnetic field in the disk could be responsible for the observed emission of a pulsational ultrafast X-ray burst, which may be triggered by the extraction of energy from the star. A newly introduced termination criterion is incorporated into interior point methods without significantly increasing computational costs, enabling decision-making about when to stop iterative calculations earlier than necessary. This termination criterion is based on an analysis of the variable metric BFGS method for unconstrained optimization and is incorporated into a range of interior point algorithms for linear programming and semidefinite programming. Experimental results for linear programming show that incorporating this termination criterion leads to minor declines in performance quality but a substantial reduction in computational time, averaging around 30-40%. Furthermore, early termination does not add complexity to the implementation of interior point methods, and its benefits can be applied to other methods for unconstrained optimization as well as to a primal-dual interior point method for semidefinite programming, yielding better efficiency with fewer iterations. However, its effects on efficiency with various interior point methods for linear programming have been found to be inconsistent, often resulting in inferior performance. The reasoning behind these outcomes involves the level of overestimation associated with the method in question; when the overestimation level is low, as with the psdSDP method, incorporating the termination criterion leads to inefficient outcomes since the method is already well-suited to detecting when inner iterations can be terminated. Conversely, when the overestimation level is high with Newton's method, incorporating the termination criterion yields better results, suggesting its potential utility with other methods that suffer from considerable overestimation levels. As a consequence, further research will be devoted to determining whether the termination criterion can be effectively utilized with a variety of interior point methods for linear programming and semidefinite programming. The study ultimately concludes that early termination of inner iterations presents a computationally efficient improvement that has been found to date. The newly introduced termination criterion has been implemented in open source and will be made publicly available. The open-source implementation has been combined with another previously introduced technique for terminating inner iterations - the 'Galuedes effect' - in order to facilitate its utilization with interior point methods for linear programming and semidefinite programming through a different approach. This notion eradicates fluctuations in gauge conditions, thereby maintaining invariance. A differential equation, referred to as the ERG, systematically fine-tunes the ERF to pinpoint the ground state of the unitary Fock space. In doing so, the ERG successfully navigates around issues of non-perturbative renormalisability but still manages to define a gauge invariant and gauge-variant correlation function relationship. Specifically, the ERG correlation function formula demonstrates an inherent connection with an integral of the associated gauge non-invariant transverse Yang-Mills theory differential equation. We resolve this challenge by establishing a gauge transformation rule for ERF components such that the ground state remains unaffected by the transformation. The Isometric Log-Ratio (ILR) transformation efficiently converts a point process's event intensities into unified dimensionless components, thereby making them easier to compare and interpret. When combined with Gaussian Theory, the ILR transformation enables a new model for predicting future event times within a pre-defined framework. In this study, we introduce a novel method for estimating the ILR scale parameter, along with the correlation structure of point processes. The performance of this scale estimator is evaluated in simulations, and compared with existing approaches. The findings indicate that the new scale estimator outperforms the competition, and like other methods, is compatible with the prediction of future event times. The methodology developed in this study is demonstrated using data from the observation of flares on the star Procyon. The results show that the new scale estimator and prediction method are versatile and can be applied to any type of data, whether or not the events are temporally ordered. The code and data necessary to reproduce the analysis are freely available online at \href{https://osoi.github.io/ILRscale/}{osoi.github.io/ILRscale}. \newline

We've developed a system that systematically categorizes text messages based on their predefined formats. The system comprises two primary components: one detects the overall message format, and the other identifies specific data points within that format. Our results show that the system's overall performance increases when we train it with data labeled according to a specific protocol, and that it outperforms a baseline model by a significant margin, even when we train it on data that's not in line with the protocol we're aiming for. To take it to the next level, we've created two biasing techniques that help the system give more weight to certain messages and make its decisions more consistent. The first technique simply weighs the importance of each data point, and the second technique actually changes the data to fit a particular protocol. We show that both techniques boost the system's performance and that the strongest results come from training the system on a large dataset of labeled data. We also show that the system's format detection isn't as good as we'd like it to be, and suggest a few ways to make it better. Finally, we make the case that the system's main strength lies in its ability to adapt to messages that don't follow a particular format, and we point out a few areas where this capability would be especially useful. The objective of form completion is to fill in a partially completed form using available information. Most existing form completion methods are designed with the assumption that the support data includes a full database, but in reality, this is not always the case. When the support data does not contain certain form items, executing the method results in inaccurate forms. To overcome this challenge, we propose a framework that incorporates two key systems: a data enrichment system and a query verification system. The data enrichment system temporyrally retrieves missing items by asking relevant questions, while the query verification system uses reasoning to verify whether the obtained items are valid. We conducted a study using two widely used datasets, which showed the proposed framework's execution accuracy improves significantly in the absence of database contents and achieves comparable accuracy to methods that assume a full database when the support data is sufficient. Additionally, the study found that the framework's execution times are short and only slightly longer than methods that assume a full database. Notably, the framework's support data can be human-readable, enabling the filling of forms using simple questions and verifications that are easy for humans to understand. Overall, the proposed framework represents a significant advancement in form completion, expanding its applicability to scenarios where the support data is limited, and achieving better results than existing methods in such scenarios. Our framework also supports the exploration of new forms, which is an essential capability. As a result, we have developed a system based on the proposed framework and successfully applied it to new forms of completion, including filling in gaps in graphical form and generating new conditional compliance forms. Our study shows that the obtained results are better than existing methods on graph-based form completion and comparable to these methods on conditional compliance forms. The support data used in our study is available at https://github.com/AI4SARL/form_completion. This study delves into the two-point angular correlation function and clustering analysis of 1.5 million galaxies from the LoTSS dataset across 4.5 square degrees at a redshift range of 0.03 to 0.9. The research utilized the LEGAS survey area, encompassing a total of 1788 wide-field plates, to calculate the angular distribution of galaxies at fixed widths and orientations. The results revealed increasing densities of galaxies by approximately 25 percent at higher redshifts, as well as a stronger correlation on larger scales at lower redshifts. The research observed excellent agreement with the Lambda Cold Dark Matter cosmology model, with the results fitting within 1 sigma of predicted models for galaxy distributions. The results further demonstrated that angular correlation statistics provide a useful, alternative method for testing cosmological theories. Based on these findings, the research placed constraints on the model's predictions, with the results indicating that the matter density parameter Omega_m is estimated as 0.27 +/- 0.04 (1-sigma error) when considering the LoTSS dataset alone. The broad application of the used analytical technique allows for its future use in testing various cosmological theories across a range of deep, wide-area radio surveys. The research also highlighted the potential for cross-validation by comparing angular and spatial galaxy distributions across multiple surveys. The rank lasso problem is a heavily resource-intensive task, especially in large dimensions, making it a difficult problem to solve. Even the most advanced methods have high computational costs, leading to inefficient processing capabilities. Due to the rapid growth in data, processing large dimensions has become even more problematic. We propose an innovative solution, an adaptive-sieving-based algorithm, to efficiently tackle the rank lasso problem in big data environments with high dimensions. This proposed method utilizes an adaptive sieving strategy, closely mimicking the solution process, to reduce dimensions and speed up computation. We thoroughly evaluated the efficiency and effectiveness of our proposed algorithm in comparison to other renowned methods. The results show that our algorithm outperforms the competitors by significantly reducing run-time; specifically, it solves smaller, dimension-reduced problems while still accurately solving the original problem. We further validate our method through theoretical proofs and place the lower bound on the error tolerance. We demonstrate its efficiency via numerical experiments, showing that the proposed algorithm rivals the performance of other methods when run-time is considered. This proposed algorithm successfully resolves the scalability issue of the rank lasso problem. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/ChunyunZhang/Adaptive-Sieving-based-algorithm.
