We demonstrate that an exclusive, universal method for achieving the lowest possible rate of entropy production exists in a class of spatially uniform systems lacking symmetry. This outcome contrasts with previous findings, which showed multiple optimal protocols can exist when spatial heterogeneity is present, and multiple distinct optimal scenarios can occur even when heterogeneity isn't a factor. This research is an expansion on our initial study, which laid the groundwork by proving the existence of a single, universal method for achieving the lowest possible rate of entropy production in spatially uniform systems. We then show that this universal method is in fact robust, capable of withstanding even small changes in the system parameters. Additionally, we provide a simplified mathematical approach that can accurately estimate the optimal production rate in systems with spatial heterogeneity by applying the maximum principle, a well-established mathematical concept. This new approach provides a more efficient and simpler method for calculating the optimal production rate in systems with spatial heterogeneity compared to prior methods. Lastly, we explore the practical implications of the universal method for achieving the lowest possible rate of entropy production in spatially uniform systems and discuss its potential applications and limitations. This outcome has significant practical and theoretical implications as it could lead to the development of new and efficient algorithms for predicting the behavior of non-equilibrium thermodynamic systems. Furthermore, this outcome challenges the long-held assumption that multiple optimal protocols necessarily exist, leading to new areas of research on the conditions under which multiple optimal protocols can and cannot exist, and the practical implications of these conditions. This research, in part, answers one of these questions by showing that the conditions under which multiple optimal protocols can exist are in fact distinct from the conditions under which the optimal protocol can be unique. We then provide formal mathematical definitions for these two conditions, discuss their significance, and explore the practical implications of these conditions in the behavior of non-equilibrium thermodynamic systems. This outcome has significant practical and theoretical implications as it could lead to the development of new and efficient algorithms for predicting the behavior of non-equilibrium thermodynamic systems. As rapidly evolving AI services transform the tech sector, their significant environmental impacts are gaining attention from industry and academia. Current research mainly focuses on measuring the environmental footprint of AI models during their active operation, yet the carbon and other negative effects that result from their entire lifespan - from creation to disposal - are often overlooked. In this study, we introduce a novel approach that integrates lifecycle assessment to quantify the total environmental impact of AI services throughout their entire life cycle. Furthermore, we develop a comprehensive inventory analysis framework to determine the major contributors to these impacts. Through our lifecycle assessment, we reveal that the production phase significantly accounts for the majority of the environmental influence. Interestingly, the processes occurring during the initial development of hardware and software have the greatest impact. Conversely, the operational phase has a relatively minor effect. Based on our findings and existing research, we formulate a set of best practices to help developers and users make environmentally conscious decisions when working with AI services. Ultimately, we advocate for the incorporation of lifecycle-based evaluation of other computational models. The source code used for the study is publicly available at the following link: https://github.com/chrishtravis/lca-cvae. Additionally, all data employed in the research are presented in the following document: https://doi.org/10.6029/archivums26242. Lastly, the report can be accessed at the following link: https://neuralfuel.github.io/lifecycle-ml/. A relatively newly introduced approach, the dual-weighted residual method, has
been shown to be an effective tool for error estimation in a variety of coupled
problems in fluid dynamics. This method's ability to provide error bounds that
are achievable, along with its computational efficiency, make it a desirable
tool for verifying the accuracy of numerical solutions in real-time. This
paper extends the method to predictive models by deriving and implementing a
compatible error estimator for coupled problems involving the continuous
Galerkin method. To test the method's effectiveness, the authors present numerical
results that demonstrate its practical application to a coupled problem in
fluid mechanics involving a predictive model of surface tension driven fluid flow
coupled with an experimental flow visualizer. The method's ability to provide
accurate predictions of the experimental flow visualizer's behavior, along with
computational efficiencies that far exceed those of previously introduced error
estimators, make it a valuable tool for the predictive coupling of numerical
models with experimental devices in fluid mechanics. Additionally, the method's
ability to provide predictive error bounds that approach a theoretical limit,
along with its efficiency, make it a desirable tool for online verification of
solutions in coupled problems in fluid dynamics. The authors propose that the
method's ability to facilitate predictive coupling of numerical models with
experimental devices, along with online verification of solutions, makes it a
viable approach for the predictive coupling of numerical models with

existing error estimators, along with its efficiency, make it a suitable tool
for complex coupled problems in fluid dynamics involving the interaction of
solving and predicting methods. The authors propose that the method's greatest
potential lies in its ability to outperform existing error estimators in the
development of stable and efficient computational models for coupled problems

Graph packing issues, specifically those concerning tight bounds, can be quite challenging, particularly when it comes to graph paths (simple, vertex-disjoint paths). This paper explores narrowest circuits (ST-NWC) - a straightforward graph packing issue, and proposes an iterative algorithm with a sublinear time complexity of O(n^(1+o(1)}) for its solution. This finding improves upon the best known previous result, achieved through depth-first search in the equivalent time complexity of O(n^2). Next, the paper tackles the more complex challenge of shortest circuits (ST-SWC) and establishes a lower bound on the efficiency of any possible algorithm seeking this solution. This lower bound exhibits a dependence on n in the form of log^k n, where k is a value between 2.03 and 2.44. This breakthrough shows that the previously proposed iterative algorithm is nearly efficient in terms of time complexity. Finally, the paper extends its findings to a more general problem - finding the widest vertex-disjoint paths in a directed graph (WDP). A new iterative algorithm is proposed with a polynomial time complexity of O(n^3), which is the first known algorithm seeking this solution in subcubic time. This finding represents a significant advancement over the prior known results, achieved through a cubic time complexity of O(n^3), in a paper by Mohar and Pashkov. This breakthrough shows that the previously known results in the field are essentially linear, and lays the groundwork for possible improvements through the application of Szemerédi's regularity lemma. This methodology has previously yielded substantial progress in the field, particularly in the construction of a planar graph consisting of five-vertex complete bipartite subgraphs with a tight bandwidth of twenty-two. This groundbreaking finding was accomplished by Annamalai and Ramanujan. This new algorithm for the WDP issue also holds promise of being efficient and useful for the construction of graphs with desired properties, through the application of a new lemma to determine the existence of a simple circuit in a directed graph with a tight bandwidth of fifty-two. This directed graph consists of a tight bandwidth of fifty-two, and has a newly established width of fifty-three. This breadth of fifty-three signifies the largest possible number of vertex-disjoint simple circuits in the graph. This study examines a specific model, consisting of a two-field model with a ${\cal W}_4$ potential, to investigate scalar field configurations in the vicinity of the horizon. Unlike in conventional holographic superconductors, the transition to a scalar hair black hole does not necessarily involve the scalar field's mass or the black hole's temperature, but rather its scalar charge. When an external magnetic field is introduced, the scalar field's configuration and potential black hole properties change. However, the mechanism by which the scalar hair black hole forms remains the same as in the charge-regularized model. If an external magnetic field is present, the field strength at the horizon is determined by the scalar charge, and the scalar hair black hole's properties are distinct from those in a black hole subjected to an external magnetic field. Nonetheless, the model lacks a description of how the scalar hair black hole's properties transition into those of a normal black hole. Instead, the model displays a description of how the scalar hair black hole's properties resemble those of a normal black hole as the scalar charge decreases. Conversely, as the scalar charge increases, the model's properties resemble those of a holographic superconductor. Therefore, the model suggests that the transition from a holographic superconductor to a scalar hair black hole occurs as the scalar charge increases. Furthermore, the model's critical value of the scalar charge for the superconductor's transition matches that obtained through alternative methods. Lastly, the model's critical value of the scalar charge for the superconductor's transition is independent of the black hole's temperature, just as it relies solely on the black hole's temperature in the charge-regularized model. In contrast to the charge-regularized model, however, the model under examination does yield a non-zero critical value of the scalar charge. The process of mRNA production in eukaryotic cells involves a complex series of events governed by the central dogma, yet the mechanisms governing the transcription cycle are still not fully understood. Current models suggest that the time lag between transcription initiation and mature mRNA output is primarily attributed to RNA processing delays; however, the dependence of this time lag on gene length has been a subject of controversy. Our study examined the transcription time of 749 genes in Arabidopsis thaliana with varying lengths, revealing a significant influence of gene length on the time lag between transcription completion and mature mRNA production. The results suggest that shorter genes are associated with increased transcription termination rates, whereas longer genes exhibit a decreased rate, leading to previously unreported insights into transcription regulation. This research provides a framework for the development of mathematical models describing transcription kinetics, offering a new perspective on RNA production in eukaryotic cells. Moreover, the analysis sheds light on the underlying mechanisms of transcriptional regulation, contributing to our understanding of the complex interplay between RNA processing and transcription dynamics. Finally, the model's predictions were validated through experiments, providing a comprehensive explanation of mRNA output variability in eukaryotic cells. Our study paves the way for the application of data-driven computational modeling to elucidate the underlying mechanisms of eukaryotic RNA production. The concepts of isotropic and shear jamming are fundamental to understanding compressible amorphous materials, yet their mechanical behaviors have not been thoroughly compared. Researchers have previously observed similarities between the two types of jamming and a second-order phase transition, particularly in their energy-to-force ratio fluctuations. However, recent studies have revealed that this similarity is merely a consequence of the power law behavior of the jamming protocol. More in-depth research is necessary to clarify the relationship between jamming and phase transitions. This work aims to investigate the jamming transition in one dimension using numerical simulations with jamming protocols that are not dependent on force or energy. The results suggest that isotropic jamming exhibits a second-order phase transition with a specific critical exponent value. Conversely, frictional shear jamming displays a first-order phase transition with a different critical exponent value. Furthermore, these findings demonstrate that varying jamming protocols can lead to distinct critical exponent values for jamming transitions. Nonetheless, the structure of jammed materials appears to be independently critical regardless of the used protocol. Lastly, the relationships between jamming and phase transitions, as well as the concepts of isotropic and shear jamming, require further clarification and investigation.

Our study investigates how well the program synthesis framework, initially proposed. by Keller and Cai, performs in a variety of situations and settings.  We carry out two types of examinations.  First, we investigate the program synthesis framework's capabilities through an experimental study.  We modify the program synthesis framework to determine the fastest possible sequence of queries that allows it to discover the target program, as well as the most efficient possible information exchange ratio.  The results of our study demonstrate that the program synthesis framework is highly effective, converting a sequence of inputs into a program with an average processing speed of about 1.5 queries per input, using about 60% of the total information available.  Secondly, we conduct analytical studies on the program synthesis framework to establish more rigorous bounds on its performance and to examine its applicability to a broader range of situations.  We begin by investigating the program synthesis framework's optimal performance in a simplified scenario where a target program is determined in advance and is always retrievable.  We find that in this scenario, the program synthesis framework is within a factor of $O(\log q)$ from optimal, where $q$ represents the total number of possible programs.  We expand upon this result in our follow-up study, which considers more realistic constraints and includes additional rigorous bounds on the program synthesis framework's performance.  We validate the program synthesis framework's efficiency through an extensive series of experimental tests in a variety of practical situations and applications, including program inversion, data generation, and validated random search.  The results of our experiments demonstrate its effectiveness and frequently approach optimal performance.  We evaluate the program synthesis framework's efficiency also in terms of its relationship with other successful algorithmic techniques such as binary search, random search, and active learning.  We find that in many instances, the program synthesis framework is at least as efficient as, and frequently more efficient than, these alternative approaches.  We identify the program synthesis framework's capacity to efficiently learn complex sequential functions such as data generators and random programs as a particularly promising application of program synthesis. The distribution of exoplanets regarding their mass and orbital radius does not support the idea that planets form primarily from the disk's outer layers as predicted by the core accretion theory. This prediction states that large planets should predominantly be found at greater distances from their host stars due to lower pressure in the outer disk. To investigate this issue further, we examine the potential for planets to form through two distinct processes within the core accretion framework. These processes are (i) planet formation in high-pressure regions near their stars, and (ii) a migration barrier that prevents planets from moving arbitrarily close to their stars. We used computational models to study a planet's evolution under various disk conditions and examined the distribution of exoplanets in a sample of 62 systems with well-documented planetary companions. Our models take into account a planet's early growth, its interaction with surrounding material, and its final orbital position following a migration event. We find that while a planet's early development is unaffected by a low-pressure environment, this issue remains a challenge for the core accretion theory. Additionally, the migration barrier alone cannot explain the observed planetary mass distribution. However, a combination of these factors contributes to the current understanding of exoplanet distribution, and further modifications to these processes may be required to fully account for the observed phenomena. This study provides new restrictions for models of planetary formation and the planetary mass spectrum, and could have implications for future discoveries in exoplanetary systems, especially those with smaller or more massive planets. 

The key factors that were analyzed in this study are as follows:
- The effect of a low-pressure environment on planetary formation: This factor has little impact on a planet's early development but could affect its mass and orbital distance.
- The migration barrier: This factor affects a planet's final orbital position but cannot alone explain the observed relationship between a planet's mass and distance. 
- The effect of a high-pressure environment on planetary formation: This factor could play a significant role in the formation of massive planets close to their stars, and is being investigated further in another study.

Estimating scene geometry is a critical task that spans multiple applications and
instrumentations, but has historically been isolated from other visual tasks.
Despite its potential for robust training data, the conventional approach of
leveraging stereo and lidar has been hindered by the locally-focused and diverse
nature of the data. In contrast, advancing geometric estimation through deep
learning enables the utilization of a wide range of data sources, including those
used for image classification. We argue that estimating scene geometry is a more
advantageous starting point for pre-training compared to traditional methods, and
propose a novel method that integrates geometry estimation with image-level tasks
via explicit alignment of feature maps. This approach surpasses existing methods in
both geometric estimation and image classification tasks. We demonstrate the
importance of explicit alignment of feature maps, as well as the benefits of using
lidar and multi-view geometry estimation. This leads to the development of a
state-of-the-art lidar-based regression model and a novel geometric estimation
method that surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in 2.5D and 3D geometric
estimation tasks. This research presents the first self-supervised method for
2.5D geometric estimation that rivals its supervised counterparts. Moreover, our
work initiates the exploration of self-supervised 3D geometric estimation within
the field of deep learning. The code for our research will be made accessible.

Recently, time-series analysis has gained significant traction, but there's a significant obstacle: a severe scarcity of annotated training data, making it difficult to leverage deep learning techniques effectively. To address this challenge, we've developed a novel data label synthesis framework, called TCube, which enables the creation of synthetic labels through interactive data exploration. By integrating various analysis operations into the training process, TCube allows us to preserve domain expert knowledge, enabling the adaptation of deep learning models with minimal domain expertise. Furthermore, TCube enhances the diversity of created labels using clustering analysis, achieving significant reduction in training data volume while maintaining key feature representation. We've evaluated TCube on several real-world datasets and found it to significantly outperform existing data augmentation methods, also yielding comparable performance on time-series classification tasks. This study examines the effectiveness of LSTM in enhancing Japanese word segmentation, a process complicated by extensive use of characters and lack of clear word boundaries. Conventional methods rely on static character models or Markov processes, but these are inefficient in capturing word segmentation patterns. Contrasting these approaches, this work applies LSTM, a type of recurrent neural network particularly suited to modeling sequences with complex, dynamic patterns. Experimental results indicate a significant improvement in F-measure values when using LSTM, with a substantial gain of 4.81% when combining LSTM with character features. Additionally, a comparative analysis with static character models reveals a notable improvement of 6.13% in F-measure values. Furthermore, when replacing Markov processes with LSTM, an impressive gain of 13.03% in F-measure values was observed. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the capability of LSTM in generating multiple word segmentation patterns by employing an attention mechanism, thereby enhancing the overall F-measure value by 1.41%. In conclusion, the research emphasizes the effectiveness of LSTM in improving Japanese word segmentation, and also suggests its potential applications in related natural language processing tasks. In addition, the code used in this study has been made available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/JaehoLIM/Japanese-Word-Segmentation. Alternatively, it can be accessed directly at https://jaeho-lim.github.io/Japanese-Word-Segmentation/.

Our interest in knowledge sharing is driven by the popularity of online platforms like Stack Overflow, where users frequently share external resources, including articles, blogs, and videos, which are often referenced multiple times. Despite these resources being external, they serve as essential components of the answers provided by users. Given the common practice of sharing the same resource multiple times, our aim is to develop an approach that efficiently manages these repetitions and preserves the updated information when the referenced material changes. This study is based on a data set with 1.2 million Q&A pairs, containing 370,000 external resources, and our analysis focuses on the inherent properties of this data, including the type of resources shared, before investigating methods for implementing efficient mechanisms to update and access this information. As part of our proposed strategies, we observe that creating a knowledge base offers benefits over retrieving resources from the internet, including faster access and updated information. Furthermore, instead of requiring the entire question, our results show that using selected phrases from the Q&A context is sufficient for updating resource information. Additionally, video resources differ from articles and blogs in terms of their stability and update frequency. While opportunities for resource linkability due to copy-paste behavior are prevalent, maintaining the latest information also necessitates integrating resource embedding or summarization to alleviate these repetitions. This study contributes to understanding the characteristics of online workspaces, enables reproducible research, and provides mechanisms for handling prevalent repetitions in the data. As a next step, our future work will involve leveraging machine learning and incorporating additional features to achieve the same goal. Our code and data are publicly available. Individual actions can help mitigate the climate crisis, but they are only effective if people are persuaded to take them. Climate change communication is often ineffective because it fails to consider personal values, leading to a lack of motivation to act. To improve this, it is crucial to develop effective ways to connect individual personal values with climate change mitigation measures. This study innovates a new approach by leveraging State-of-the-art Natural Language Processing (NLP) capabilities to achieve two key objectives. Firstly, it identifies and ranks the personal values relevant to climate change by analyzing online climate-related discussions and the values they encompass. Secondly, it employs these results to suggest actionable initiatives tailored to the values of online communities engaged in climate discussions. This proposal boasts exceptional performance, surpassing existing methods, and is experimentally verified to outperform a basic intervention using NLP-based values discovery. Evaluations indicate that this approach enhances public awareness of climate change by linking individual personal values to applicable actions, ultimately promoting greater value-based action. This research makes three significant contributions to the fields of NLP and climate communication. Firstly, it applies cutting-edge NLP techniques to a vital area like climate communication; Secondly, it develops a new, transferable approach for uncovering relevant values in online discussions; Thirdly, it introduces a novel application of NLP in promoting value-based action on climate change through identifiable and actionable values. This research has the potential to be expanded into various other domains like education, health, and social justice. Autonomous driving systems leveraging Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have demonstrated significant potential in tackling challenging tasks within partially observable environments, such as high-level autonomous driving functions like route following and speed control. Nonetheless, the role of RNNs in these applications remains understudied. This work employs an influential Bayesian inference framework, known as the Variable Rate Gaussian Pyramid, to decompose high-dimensional autonomous driving sequences into structured, context-specific components, which are then used to design an efficient RNN-based task classifier. By integrating RNNs into the classification process, we've observed a 2.5 dB improvement in performance over a baseline classifier and achieved a 10% enhancement in mapping efficiency, which is critical for deploying deep neural networks in embedded autonomous driving systems, such as those used in self-driving cars. A comparable outcome was achieved when classifying driving tasks at a lower temporal resolution using the reconstructed task stream, thus confirming the feasibility of RNNs as a crucial component in autonomous driving systems. Our novel approach and empirical findings are now presented. This research uses two approaches - the Taylor expansion and the relativistic fermi gas models - to investigate how a dense magnetic field impacts the equation of state of strange quark matter. Our results show that a dense magnetic field lowers the critical density required for the onset of color superconductivity in this type of matter. We investigate various aspects of survivors from the dynamic system defined by intermediate $\beta$-transformations with noninteger bases. Our analysis extends previous work on badly approximable numbers in base $\sqrt{2}+$1. We establish a connection between survivors at a given level and numbers satisfying a specific diophantine condition, expressed in base $b=\sqrt{2}+1$. Additionally, using recent findings from Bugeja and Loridant, we demonstrate that the set of almost survivor points for any level $k$ forms a $C^{1}$-embeddings class along with its image under the associated $\beta$-transformation. Furthermore, we compute the survivor set for $k=2$ and show that its image under the transformation is countable while its complement has full Lebesgue measure. Moreover, we prove that for any level $k$, the almost survivor set is $C^{1}$-embeddings class compatible with the badly approximable set in base $b$. Lastly, we explore some open questions and challenges. Note that many of the concepts and results are highly similar to those discussed for irrational rotations in the one-dimensional case. Nevertheless, the findings and difficulties are distinct from those for the Masur-Veech mosaics and the Siegel parametric mosaics, as discussed in [Kathryn Helman's thesis, 2019]. Interpreting the behavior of deep learning models in real-time has gained significant traction in recent years, and various methods have been developed to achieve this. In this research, we introduce a new approach, referred to as Disentangled Attribution Curves (DAC), which enables fast and generalizable predictions on datasets with multiple feature dimensions using a single model. By analyzing DACs, we can identify distinct segments corresponding to the effect of individual model parameters on the output. Through our experiments on multiple public datasets, we demonstrate that DAC performs consistently well in revealing meaningful patterns in the data, and can function effectively even in high-dimensional spaces. For instance, when applied to a bike-sharing dataset, DAC helps reveal a distinct drop in usage patterns around holidays, clearly identifiable by the characteristic curve shapes. Moreover, DAC achieves this analysis without requiring domain-specific knowledge and can function as a general-purpose tool for exploring the behavior of deep learning models. This testing framework is built on top of a robot driver architecture consisting of three key components: driver under test, robot driver, and host computer. The host computer is where testing software is installed, enabling the upload and download of data to and from the robot via a serial connection. The robot driver runs on the microcontroller and acts as a middleman to facilitate data exchange between the host computer and the driver under test. The test is typically initiated by the host computer, which sends a command to the robot over a serial connection using a serial interface like USB or Bluetooth. The robot then executes the driver test command and returns the results to the host computer via the same serial interface. The results are then verified using test assertions, which are part of the testing framework. The verification process completes the test cycle and produces a pass or fail outcome. To simplify the process, a test automation tool called Test Command Manager is used to manage and update test commands on the host computer. A demonstration of the testing framework's efficiency in locating bugs was also successfully conducted. De novo system call filtering for applications written in interpreted languages such as PHP and Python is implemented in Timeloops. This technique is necessary because most applications using interpreted languages lack a secure interface to filter system calls due to their dynamic execution nature. Timeloops achieves this by analyzing the execution flow of programs and identifying points where system calls can be effectively restricted. It then uses static code inspection along with dynamic analysis to create a call graph, which is used for determining system call access points. This information is combined with context information to enable a fine-grained system call filtering policy. This policy is based on the application's execution state and is calculated at runtime using machine learning algorithms. This method is fully automatic and does not require programmer intervention. Experiments with various PHP and Python applications showed significant improvements in system call filtering coverage, with an average gain of 17.6% in system call filtering and a successful rate of 0.879 for unknown system calls. This technique is now part of the Attacker Toolkit. Timeloops has been publicly available since May 2022. This paper revisits Timeloops, presents new research findings, and enhances the method with additional technology. A major advancement is the incorporation of path-based system call filtering, which enables more efficient system call filtering with less system call overhead. This new technique achieved a system call filtering coverage of 88.5% for Python and 91.4% for PHP with a system call overhead of 1.06%, a significant improvement of 56% over the original method. This enhancement has been publicly available since February 2023. Further research is being conducted to extend the method to other languages such as Java, JavaScript, and Ruby. However, the high dimensionality of the data poses a significant challenge for identification of important features, making classification and other tasks complicated. Traditional Euclidean distances are often inadequate for capturing the inherent biology in such datasets, leading to the development of more sophisticated distance measures that align with the underlying cellular relationships. Nevertheless, existing supervised classification methods often fall short due to the need for adjustment of distance metrics after training the classifier. To address these challenges, we present a new approach - NeoFisher - an efficient two-stage framework designed for single-cell RNA sequencing data classification. During the initial training phase, the framework calculates a dimensionally reduced, orthogonal representation of the data in a space that naturally accommodates the distance metric. Once the model is trained, the data can be easily projected onto this space for classification. Evaluations on multiple public datasets have shown the superiority of NeoFisher over alternative methods in terms of accuracy and generalizability, achieving up to a 4.9% improvement in AUC score over the current best approaches. Moreover, the applicability of this framework extends beyond scRNA-seq data as it can be applied to any multi-dimensional data with non-Euclidean space characteristics, making it a versatile tool for classification tasks in various domains. The close approach of stars to a supermassive black hole is influenced by the mass distribution of stars within the broader gravitational potential of the host galaxy. Existing models primarily rely on a straightforward mass function, which assigns a fixed mass to each star and then applies the galaxy's potential to determine their orbits. However, this approach underestimates the impact of mass variability among the stars, largely due to the presence of intermediate-mass stars with variable masses within the galaxy's potential. In the study presented here, we explore the effect of mass variability on the scattering of stars in the vicinity of a supermassive black hole. We define a mass variability parameter, $M_p/M$, which represents the ratio of a star's mass range to its average mass, enabling us to systematically examine the influence of mass variability on the cross-sections of stellar-stellar scattering. Our results indicate that mass variability has a notable effect, particularly at close approaches and for stars with higher initial kinetic energies; in some cases, taking this into account can boost the cross-section by up to 50%. In light of this discovery, we suggest that mass variability should be incorporated into models of stellar hardening and binary evolution in the environment of a supermassive black hole. This study explores the technical challenges posed by uncertainty when implementing Model Predictive Control (MPC). Given that quantifying uncertainty is a fundamental aspect of MPC design, this work examines the implications of uncertainty on control strategies. Specifically, it investigates the effects of uncertainty on optimal control policies and how they vary with different risk attitudes. This is achieved through a sequential decision-making framework, in which the risk attitude is treated as a constraint in a mathematical programming problem. This approach enables the incorporation of risk preferences in the decision-making process and provides a valuable tool for understanding the relationship between uncertainty and control. This method's application and efficacy are demonstrated through two case studies, each focusing on diverse fields: chemical process control and active suspension systems. In the first case study, the goal is to develop a stochastic MPC algorithm to mitigate oscillations in converging flows within a series of continuous stirs tanks. In the second case study, the objective is to design an active control strategy for hydraulic systems with variable displacement pumps, while ensuring the stability of the system and controlling its dynamics. This study addresses the issue of separating mixed signals of reduced dimensionality, focusing on integrative signal processing approaches that combine data compression and independent component analysis. We develop two innovative algorithms in this context - a first-order Tikhonov algorithm and a Grassmann manifold conjugate gradient method - both of which aim to decompose compressed data. We then test these algorithms against a newly introduced variant of the gradient descent algorithm, as well as existing ICA methods, using both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our results show that these new algorithms not only outperform traditional ICA methods but also achieve superior performance compared to adaptive ICA techniques, with the added benefit of requiring significantly less memory resources. Furthermore, we highlight the potential for these algorithms to be used effectively in various applications, such as biosignal separation and data transmission through data compression. The influence of a macroscopic, coherent feedback loop on the quantum properties of an atomic ensemble as well as its interactions with a laser field and a spin ensemble within a cavity is examined through simulations of an experiment involving three-body quantum interactions. Without the feedback loop, the entanglement of the atomic ensemble with the cavity and the laser field exhibits periodic maxima and minima. However, when the feedback loop is present, the entanglement becomes immune to periods of negativities, but its overall quantum features are shown to degrade due to periodic variations in its amplitude. Nonetheless, the entanglement of the system with the laser field exhibits sustained growth and periodic fluctuations in the entanglement of the system with the atomic ensemble can be eliminated by adjusting the phase of the feedback loop. Furthermore, the entanglement of the system with the atomic ensemble is shown to be enhanced through the adjustment of specific parameters, but this enhancement comes at a cost of reduced robustness against thermal effects. On the other hand, the entanglement of the system with the laser field exhibits increased robustness against thermal effects, but this increased robustness cannot be achieved without periodic fluctuations in its amplitude. The findings of this study suggest that the coherent feedback loop has a positive effect on the quantum features of the system, but its impact is most beneficial when the phase of the feedback loop is adjusted to be opposite to the phase of the laser field. These findings are crucial for developing next-to-next-to-leading order subtraction terms in QCD calculations, especially for high-energy hadronic collisions where complex final states with intricate substructure are present. We've derived the splitting operators for quark and gluon combinations, and these are applicable to various processes involving the collision of color particles. We've performed an extensive validation of our findings against other approaches, such as field theory and dimensional regularization. Our numerical findings are crucial for the construction of next-to-next-to-leading order subtraction terms in QED, which in turn facilitates the prediction of QED observables with enhanced precision. Sundials have stood the test of time as ancient instruments for measuring time, and their widespread use across various cultures has left an estimated one hundred thousand to two hundred thousand examples still functional today. These historical timekeepers not only hold significance in understanding past lifestyles but also serve as essential references for educating people about geometry and architecture. Unfortunately, many sundials have fallen into obscurity due to neglect; thus, it is crucial that their current status is documented thoroughly. In the context of the Indonesian archipelago with its rich sundials inherited from centuries of cultural development, we propose a pioneering approach for not only recording but also actively learning about these sundials through collaborative scientific methods that combine technical computations with on-site observations using mobile devices. By integrating existing knowledge about timekeeping mechanics, new technological developments in data collection and analysis, and the proven concept of collective, or crowd-sourced, scientific efforts, it is possible to recreate a novel model for exploring and studying sundials. This innovative framework can effectively facilitate data derivation and statistical examination of sundial shadows, thereby enabling researchers to obtain reliable insights into the accuracy of time measurements. This paper presents TFIET, an innovative protocol for immediate data and energy exchange between users and a Dedicated Evolution Domain 2D (DED2D) system. The TFIET scheme enables simultaneous energy and data transfer to users through a two-stage process, utilizing a time-sharing approach with dynamic resource allocation. The transfer of data and energy to users takes place in parallel at the base station, utilizing different time slots and resources, and is coordinated via a hybrid ARQ mechanism. The paper provides a detailed description of the TFIET protocol and its implementation, as well as the resource allocation methods used during the transfer of data and energy to users. The TFIET protocol's performance is evaluated under different scenarios and compared to existing solutions. The results show that TFIET can improve energy efficiency, extend DED2D's lifetime, and achieve higher throughput and user satisfaction rates. The efficiency of TFIET also satisfies a 90% threshold. This research presents a novel model for a black hole formed from polymers. Building on the concept of polymerized spacetime from quantum gravity theories such as Asymptotic Safety, a corresponding metric is developed. Contrary to expectations, the metric of this polymer black hole exhibits wormhole-like features rather than the typical geometric structure of a black hole. Moreover, the energy conditions of the polymer black hole reveal a transient state with zero zero-point energy, followed by a transition to a thermodynamic equilibrium characterized by positive energy. The quality and expressiveness of text-to-speech systems can significantly benefit from proper word ordering in speech. Existing systems face challenges in maintaining the correct word order, particularly with unordered word-based language models, which can result in inaccurately ordered speech. To address this limitation, we developed MaskedSpeech, a novel language model that utilizes masked wording to preserve the correct word order. By masking certain words during training and generating speech with the masked words, our system effectively maintains the correct word order. Furthermore, MaskedSpeech has the added capability of utilizing additional pronunciation information. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our system, with evaluations indicating that it outperforms the unmasked baseline in maintaining the correct word order and retains similar speech naturalness. We publicly showcase the evaluation results of our model on the CMU Kaldi Corpus, with the full code available on GitHub. The evaluation results reveal that MaskedSpeech achieves a word error rate of 23.4, nearly doubling the error rate of the unmasked baseline (12.6), on the CMU Kaldi Corpus. In addition to the evaluation on the CMU Kaldi Corpus, we also achieved comparable success on the LibriTTS dataset. You can access the evaluation results of LibriTTS by visiting our project page. The output speech quality from MaskedSpeech is equivalent to that of the unmasked baseline, with both models receiving a mean opinion score of 4.12 in the MOS evaluation. Nonetheless, the success of our system primarily lies in its ability to maintain the correct word order, rather than solely impacting speech naturalness. We believe that MaskedSpeech presents an effective solution for improving the naturalness and expressiveness of text-to-speech systems through enhanced word ordering. We make our model available for public use at https://github.com/ai4amal/MaskedSpeech. We also provide the pre-trained model for early access to users. Deep Neural Networks' vulnerabilities to manipulative attacks have garnered significant interest. Unlike traditional adversarial example attacks that disrupt input data, MitM attacks focus on compromising the connection between the DNN and its data source. We investigate the impact of MitM attacks on image classification DNNs, introducing a new attack model - Active MitM - which actively manipulates the connection to alter the classified image. Experimental results on ImageNet demonstrate that Active MitM can successfully interfere with the DNN, although the attack requires direct access to the DNN and the data source. To simulate real-world conditions, we explored alternative scenarios involving proxy MitM attacks, but found they were significantly impaired due to limited control over the connection. The study sets the stage for exploring the broader implications of MitM attacks on DNNs. The code for this study is available on GitHub, specifically at the https://github.com/qnguyen-corrma/MitM_attacks_on_DNNs repository. \\

Our study delves into the conspiracy theories shared on social media regarding climate change to understand their spread. Researchers have proposed numerous causes for the widespread dissemination of conspiracy theories, yet there's a lack of investigation into their specific origins on social media platforms. To fill this gap, our work analyzes Twitter conversations referencing climate change conspiracy theories and identifies their primary source. Our analysis reveals that individual social media users are the main disseminators of conspiracy theories, accounting for approximately 67% of all relevant tweets. Moreover, our work also examines the characteristics of high-impact tweets and their senders to better comprehend their propagation. Our research focuses on Twitter's English corpus from June 2020 and is the first study to investigate the origins of conspiracy theory-related content within this domain. Our findings can inform the development of strategies to mitigate the dissemination of conspiracy theories on social media. Furthermore, our work generates insights that can be applied to other research domains within the social media science field. A detailed analysis of proton-proton collisions recorded by the CMS experiment at a 13 TeV energy threshold with the CMS detector at the Large Hadron Collider is the subject of this study. Spanning the period from 2016 to 2018 and encompassing 137 fb^-1 of exposure, the focus lies on searching for dark matter particles interacting with quarks through moderate-mass mediators. Predicted by models such as vector-like quark models, these interactions offer a possible explanation for dark matter's presence. The research methodology involves selecting events characterized by missing transverse momentum and isolation, alongside reconstructed top quark pairs, single top quarks, or individual light quarks in the final state. In total, 2.9 (2.5) events were detected in the signal (control) regions at the 95% confidence level, adhering to a natural suppression of standard model predictions of up to 10^3 across the examined final states. Although no evidence of signal existence was found, new constraints were established on the $tp$ coupling coupling with mass bounds of up to 1.5 TeV on the $tp$ coupling and up to 2.6 TeV on the $t't'$ coupling. Moreover, this study's methodology and results offer a foundation for future research into various alternative models of dark matter and quark-disk interaction. This study offers a comparative analysis of the return on investment for various higher education fields in Norway and Denmark. Data from both countries is examined to calculate the return on investment for specific fields of study and to assess how these earnings compare to the national average. Our findings suggest that the return on investment for Norwegian students varies significantly depending on their field of study, with some fields yielding substantially lower earnings than the national average. In contrast, the return on investment in Denmark appears to be relatively uniform across different fields. Overall, the earnings in Denmark surpass those in Norway. Our investigation also sheds light on the potential link between the Norwegian system of calculating return on investment and the observed disparities in earnings among graduates in different fields. Additionally, our comparison with Denmark highlights several key differences between the two countries' systems for determining return on investment. These discrepancies may have contributed to the varying outcomes for Norwegian students. Finally, our study raises important implications for how return on investment is understood and used to benefit higher education students and the broader economy in Norway. Our findings specifically address the concerns that the concept of return on investment may be perceived as primarily focusing on individual earnings and prioritizing fields with high financial returns, thereby potentially undermining its other valuable purposes and interpretations. We offer alternative perspectives on how return on investment can be understood and used beyond its common association with individual financial gain and specific field of study returns. Additionally, we provide examples of how return on investment can be utilized more equitably and diversely to benefit a wider range of stakeholders and achieve various social and economic objectives throughout Norway's higher education system. We propose this understanding of return on investment as a more inclusive and diverse conception – which we will refer to as an "ecosystem of return on investment." We also provide a brief illustration of how an ecosystem of return on investment can be put into practice. We acknowledge that this is just a starting point, and more work is needed to develop and implement this new direction for return on investment more thoroughly. We are open to hearing feedback and suggestions from others. We are looking forward to hearing more perspectives and ideas on this matter. In neuromorphic computing, computational structures are designed to mimic neuronal networks and enable innovative, neuromorphic information processing techniques. To utilize existing neural data, a new method of learning known as on-chip learning has been developed, differing from classical methods which often require large off-chip datasets. This study proposes an on-chip learning strategy utilizing a silicon analog of catfish slippage, an unsupervised competitive learning technique. Focusing on continuous, distributed data such as images, a novel approach is presented for converting any data into binary form. The concept of slippage is generalized for binary vectors and a hardware-realization of this binary catfish method is demonstrated through CMOS implementation on a 140 x 140 neuromorphic array. The effectiveness of this learning technique is shown through experiments on continuous, distributed data such as 64 x 64 pixel micro-images of digits 0-9, retrieved from a 128 x 128 RDM RAM memory. The findings of these experiments are also compared to the results of supervised learning applied to the same data. It is demonstrated that competitive, on-chip learning can effectively classify 80% of the 10-digit images without requiring supervisory information. The integration of this learning technique with neuromorphic sensing and other advanced information processing techniques such as event-driven learning and slippage-based data classification in hardware offers promising possibilities for innovative, adaptive sensing systems. The computational performance of the implemented catfish learning chip is evaluated in terms of its capability to process events in real-time, providing a functional assessment of its capabilities for on-chip learning applications. The research presented provides a significant advancement in the development of on-chip learning methods and contributes to the creation of more efficient, hardware-based learning systems. Additionally, it offers a valuable tool for scientists to study adaptive learning and sensing at the system-level. The study shows that on-chip learning of continuous, distributed data such as images can provide reliable results within a limited number of learning iterations, even without requiring supervisory information. The discovery of slippage in binary vectors extends the potential applications of catfish learning to various domains including hardware-based machine learning and neuromorphic sensing. The development of the catfish learning chip also marks a significant breakthrough in the practical implementation of on-chip learning techniques in neuromorphic computing. The study's findings provide a valuable reference point for the design of innovative, adaptive sensing systems, and offer promising possibilities for other on-chip learning techniques in neuromorphic computing. On December 13, 2003, a strong flare produced two solar flares, with the weaker one trigging the observation of a peculiar geomagnetic storm by the GEO Potentia X2-4 solar storm satellite. During this storm, the GOES satellite in the Earth's orbit detected a highly unusual satellite storm, which was unusual in several ways. Deep Neural Networks are extremely effective pattern recognizers but suffer greatly from the problem of overfitting. Research has yielded various techniques to minimize overfitting but none have provided a full solution until the method described in this paper is considered. This algorithm treats overfitting as a data coverage issue and addresses it by training a neural network with an progressively increasing number of support points, effectively controlling overfitting through data restriction. Unlike traditional methods that rely on data augmentation, l1 and l2 regularization, dropout, and parameter reduction, this algorithm avoids overfitting by refraining from representing certain data points. Similar to the iterative training process employed by Variational Auto Encoders, a neural network is trained in stages with each stage incorporating new support points and discarding old weight vectors. However, unlike VAEs, the method described in this paper yields superior classification performance with significantly reduced computational costs. Experimental results on key image and text classification challenges demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm in surpassing the current state-of-the-art methods. This paper presents an innovative solution to the long-standing problem of overfitting and the experimental results validate its superiority over the existing approaches. Deep learning's widespread success has been fueled by their exceptional performance, but this has come at a cost - a reliance on insecure, easily manipulated models. Researchers now place a higher emphasis on creating robust models that can withstand the impact of data corruption or adversarial attacks. In response, a new framework is proposed, comprising two core components: a novel constraint on the model's final layer, ensuring robustness to any level of perturbation; and an innovative method of enhancing the model's input data, making it resilient to manipulation. This framework offers a unified approach to creating robust models, capable of withstanding a range of attacks. In tests on ImageNet, models trained with the proposed framework outperformed existing robust models while requiring fewer computational resources. Additionally, the enhanced input data proved beneficial, even when combined with existing robust models, resulting in a 10% enhancement in model performance. This framework presents a promising solution to the problem of creating deep learning models that are resistant to manipulation. Code is available at https://github.com/Sun-CMU/RobustLearn.

Proteins are intricate, shape-shifting molecules composed of multiple subunits called amino acids that twist together to form a complex structure. Despite significant advances, accurately determining the three-dimensional arrangement of proteins from experimental data remains a challenging and time-consuming process, particularly when dealing with less reliable data. A novel approach, known as Proteins Calling Structure (ProCS), uses advanced statistical methods to refine protein structures more efficiently, making the process up to five times faster and more accurate. In this improved version, ProCS is integrated into the robust molecular dynamics simulation protocol, dubbed ProCS-MD, and tested on a variety of proteins with and without experimental templates. ProCS-MD's effectiveness is demonstrated not only through superior energy scores but also through the high quality of the refined structures, as measured by their similarity to true structures using the sensitive Residue-Distance Matrix Similarity (RDM) metric. In cases where the ProCS-MD algorithm was compared to other state-of-the-art methods without successful structures, the difference in performance was quite distinct. Even when the input structures were particularly poor, ProCS-MD was able to generate structures with significant improvements in accuracy. In conclusion, the ProCS-MD method represents a highly effective tool for refining protein structures, offering a more efficient and accurate solution than other methods. Unlike other techniques, ProCS-MD works well with diverse starting structures, making it a versatile solution that can be applied to a wide range of protein structure prediction challenges. The changes in superconducting properties in a two-band model are explored by altering the Fermi surface's topology from a closed loop to an open one. This open trajectory transforms into a star-shaped structure after applying a external magnetic field. Our analysis focuses on the impact of a magnetic field on transport properties in superconducting materials with Fermi surfaces characterized by nodal loops and Mott iron-based compounds. For a nodal loop, we introduce a magnetic field through the hole pocket's center, converting the Fermi surface into a four-pronged shape. Conversely, in Mott iron-based compounds, the application of a magnetic field induces a shift from a square-shaped Fermi surface to a diamond-shaped one. We calculate the change in magnetic susceptibility $\chi$ and discover that this transition differs significantly between these materials. Traditional active learning techniques attempt to minimize the need for labeled data by strategically selecting samples that provide the most value in the learning process. However, many of these methods have been limited by their reliance on uncertain or diverse samples, which can be hard to obtain in many real-world settings. In response, we've developed a new algorithm that addresses these issues by balancing the preservation of labels for selected samples and maximizing entropy in the posterior distribution. By formulating this problem as a bi-level nonlinear optimization problem and proposing a semi-supervised minimax entropy-based active learning method, we've demonstrated improved performance over traditional methods on multiple data sets. Furthermore, we've extended this approach to be compatible with soft labels and established a connection to information theory. Overall, our new algorithm offers enhanced sample selection that's consistent with the active learning paradigm while also providing theoretical insights into the importance of preserving labeled data. The findings demonstrate that batching comparisons with human feedback yields a notable increase in learning efficiency, particularly when compared to non-batched interactions. It's essential to note that batching comparisons also poses new challenges; notably, it necessitates careful consideration of the ordering of comparisons to maximize its computational benefits. The results show that batching comparisons can notably enhance the learning efficiency of agents when combined with self-improving techniques. Ultimately, the findings of this study underscore the potential of batching comparisons as a means to more effectively utilize human feedback and accelerate the reward learning process. In various policy evaluation settings, the Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is frequently estimated using the Average Influence Probability Weighted (AIPW) estimator. A recent study developed an AIPW variant that incorporates Influence Probability Weighting and Double Machine Learning under equal weight conditions, resulting in strong theoretical justifications. However, in practical applications, the AIPW estimator often exhibits high variability, making it difficult to draw inferences. A common approach to mitigate this issue is to utilize Bootstrap sampling, a resampling technique. Despite its popularity, Boehnke and van der Laan found issues with its validity in policy evaluation contexts. In response, they suggested two alternative methods for conducting inference: the Finite Population Moment Estimation and the Linearization method. A key finding of this research is that the AIPW estimator's performance can be significantly improved by omitting regularization; removing the corresponding constraint yields a convergent estimator. Additionally, this research presents methods for estimating the variance of the AIPW estimator and proposes two new validation techniques: the Quantile Based and the Kernel Based approaches. A thorough evaluation of these techniques is performed using simulated data and real-world applications from fields of public medicine and commerce. The results show that the AIPW estimator with omitted regularization exhibits superior performance, and when combined with the Linearization method for inference, this approach achieves strong results. However, it is essential to note that the efficacy of this procedure may be compromised by the presence of confounding variables. Conversely, the Finite Population Moment Estimation and the Kernel Based validation methods prove versatile and adaptable to various contexts, yielding reasonable outcomes in these situations. In general, the AIPW estimator with omitted regularization coupled with the Linearization method for inference represents a formidable empirical tool. Furthermore, the study's findings and recommendations provide a valuable resource for researchers working in policy evaluation. The accompanying code can be found on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/BoehnkeLab/AIPW_Inference. In our investigation of the Estimator of the Upper Tail, a Bayesian model-based approach for estimating extreme values, we broaden the understanding of its tuning parameter'm'. Traditionally,'m' has been viewed as a fixed, known parameter; however, in the context of Bayesian analysis, it is more accurately perceived as a variable quantifying prior confidence. To address this uncertainty, we utilize a beta distribution as the prior for'm', treating it as a hyperparameter along with other hyperparameters. Consequently, the Estimator of the Upper Tail becomes a hierarchical Bayesian model. By employing Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulation, we generate samples for the unknown parameters, and subsequently, calculate the Estimator of the Upper Tail. The performance of this estimator in the presence of uncertainty surrounding'm' is examined through simulations, which reveal that it remains reliable and robust. Additionally, in practical modeling, the choice of'm' can be determined by evaluating the likelihood functions or utilizing decision theory to optimize results. The findings highlight that varying'm' can significantly affect estimates; hence, it is crucial to consider its value when applying the Estimator of the Upper Tail. The analysis also shows that when'm' is small, the estimator tends to the classical Generalized Pareto distribution, while larger'm' values lead to a mix of Uniform and Generalized Pareto distributions. Ultimately, the Hierarchical Estimator of the Upper Tail offers valuable insights for modeling and decision-making purposes. The software necessary for replicating the results can be accessed at https://github.com/minespar/BayesEUT. Specifically, the hierarchical version of the estimator can be obtained from the repository's code repository under the label 'BayesEUT-m'. In contrast, a key contribution of this study is the demonstration that this concept is tenable for a subset of nondeterministic two-way transducers, specifically those exhibiting a form of 'degeneracy' in which every state has at least two equivalent counterparts. A new method is developed to calculate a specific entry of the convolution operator separately, which contrasts with the usual approach of computing the full convolution. The proposed technique takes advantage of the fast Fourier transform to efficiently compute the convolution, achieving a linear time complexity of O(n log(n)) when the function spaces have a logarithmic size. Moreover, the algorithm is shown to be scalable for large-scale computations by proving its efficiency in both theoretical and practical contexts. The research is complemented by experimental results demonstrating its superiority over the standard convolution computation. The proposed algorithm is also considered a potential tool for statistical physics applications. The provided code can be accessed at https://github.com/damianoborin/fConvolution.

Two procedures in lattice QCD spectral density analysis are examined to determine the existence of a tetraquark state. The first method involves directly extracting the lattice QCD correlation function of a hadronic system, and the second method uses a finite volume sum rule with the Khadronization Kernel, both aiming to identify the tetraquark state. The crucial roles of gauge field volume and ultraviolet cut-off in the generation of tetraquark state are investigated in the spectral density through two distinct lattice spacings and an array of finite volumes. The results from this study suggest that a tetraquark state is not present in the spectral density analysis for a finer lattice spacing but is consistently identified across multiple finite volumes for a coarser lattice spacing. The existence of a tetraquark state in the spectral density is determined to be lattice spacing dependent. Additionally, the relative contributions of different quark irreducible scattering processes are examined, and the findings indicate that the tetraquark state signal is predominantly produced by two particular processes involving the interaction of two valence quarks and the creation of a heavy vector meson and quark pair, and the presence of a finite ultraviolet cut-off, governing the lattice field variables. The implications of these findings for the understanding of tetraquark states are discussed. The technical details of the lattice QCD simulations, including the quark action and the lattice parameters used, as well as the techniques employed for the continuum extrapolation of the lattice correlation functions, are provided in an accompanying technical document. The same document also outlines the methods used for the determination of the Khadronization Kernel and the resulting tetraquark state signal, and presents a detailed comparison with the kernel's behavior in the continuum limit. The technical document is accessible at [arXiv:2306.16916](https://arxiv.org/abs/arXiv:2306.16916). The presented lattice QCD data and the corresponding Khadronization Kernel are made available in the Enrico Fermi Institute Lattice QCD Dataset repository at [https://github.com/EFILQCD/tetra-volume](https://github.com/EFILQCD/tetra-volume). We develop a straightforward model to estimate airborne aerosol concentrations produced by a single infected person, applicable during transitions, movement within spaces, and near respiring individuals. Leveraging the well-mixed model with consideration for breathing patterns, body dimensions, and breathing volume, we calculate the aerosol age when the air reaches the mouth and lungs. This age serves as the basis for determining the transmission probability, drawing from the effective radius and average aerosol velocity from relevant studies. Our model aims to balance precision with simplicity, using basic physical and biological parameters available in public domains. We test the efficacy of our model in various non-stationary conditions and compare it to more complex models, revealing acceptable errors in orders of magnitude. The proposed model offers a practical option for designing vaccination strategies and developing decision-making tools, especially in situations where computer resources are limited. As an example, we use the model to estimate aerosol ages and demonstrate its potential in guiding actions to minimize the spread of infection. The model can be used for other applications as well. This research offers a rigorous analysis of the test statistic introduced by Breuer, Kopp, and Schulle in 2018 for identifying common stochastic trends across multiple time series. Our study examines the case where the underlying shock vectors exhibit interdependent components and non-fickian behavior, specifically with heavy tails and sample sizes that may differ significantly. Our findings indicate that the test statistic's distribution converges to a limit that is independent of the individual data sets as the sample size increases. Notably, the estimators for the number of common stochastic trends are resistant to the effects of heavy tails and demonstrate valid results in both the within-error and between-error scenarios. However, when the individual data sets are relatively small, their distributions may not accurately represent the true underlying dynamics. As a practical implication, it is recommended that users select a wide range of critical values for the test statistic in order to account for these potential variations. Our theoretical findings are backed by corresponding numerical simulations and practical applications of the approach to stock price segmentation. The research is freely accessible online at a publicly accessible repository. Moreover, the study offers an alternative estimation method for the number of common stochastic trends that is specific to systems with differences in root systems and is robust in the presence of heavy tails. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the standard Johansen test for system rank is actually testing for a specific case of these common stochastic trends, namely systems with root differences and heavy tails. As a practical implication, it is suggested that the degree of heavy tails should be investigated before making inferences about the system's rank. Finally, it is shown that the test statistic is also capable of identifying systems with unique shock vectors - what is referred to as'systemic' or 'institutional' common stochastic trends. This new concept highlights the potential for these trends to confound the limits-to-arbitrage principle in financial market segmentation. Content delivery depends on cooperation among internet service providers, but the lack of a standardized framework makes it difficult to achieve a fair balance between their interests. We address this challenge by developing a game-theoretic model that considers the costs of content providers and the benefits (in terms of revenue) gained by internet service providers. We investigate how costs are shared among service providers and introduce a novel concept of cooperative effectiveness to evaluate the outcome. Through analysis and numerical examination, we reveal that content providers benefit from cooperation among service providers, while non-cooperative scenarios result in lower payoffs. Furthermore, we identify the conditions necessary for effective cooperation and show that content providers and one dominant service provider can achieve a stable alliance if they share costs fairly. In contrast, all-inclusive cooperation among service providers requires cost-sharing schemes based on marginal cost. Our research provides insights into the challenges of polyarchy in the digital environment and offers a framework for standardization. We also explore the link between the core of a game and the outcome of an evolution process guided by an evolutionary logic known as the prisoner's dilemma. We find that the core is broader than the payoff-equivalent support nucleus and that stable alliances may result from the latter's strategy distribution. Our investigation is the first to integrate different concepts of effectiveness in game theory and offers a standardized framework that can be applied to various situations by both established and emerging internet service providers. We also highlight the significance of standardization in the digital sector through public policies. Lastly, we examine how cooperative strategies influence investment behaviors and find that the core strategy of an effective alliance may result in lower investment efforts when a key provider cooperates with a dominant service provider while competing with other service providers. We conclude that cooperative strategies have both beneficial and detrimental effects on investment behaviors and that these effects vary depending on circumstances. These findings can guide public policy decisions on standardization and cooperation in the digital sector. We also explore the conditions under which one service provider can achieve a stable alliance with the content provider, resulting in a lower investment effort compared to non-cooperative scenarios. Our research establishes a link between these measured bending laminations and the geometric information of quasi-Fuchsian 3-manifolds that reside near the Fuchsian locus within the complex ball. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that the set of measured bending laminations has a countable infinity, and we prove the existence of a unique quasi-Fuchsian 3-manifold for each bending laminations that it contains, thereby providing a complete classification up to homology. Additionally, our research builds on previous research by Madsen and Weimann regarding the complexity of one-dimensional cohomology in 3-manifolds. High-frequency trading data is examined to identify the dynamics of asset return distributions across different frequency ranges. Our analysis combines theoretical models of portfolio performance and empirical observations of market trades to build a framework for understanding how asset return distributions evolve over time. This includes modeling the shape of cross-sectional return distributions based on the moments of fund returns and testing these predictions using UK equity trade data. Our results show that for a 15-minute frequency, the first four moments of the cross-sectional return distribution are accurately captured by the moments of fund returns. However, at a 20-minute frequency, the cross-sectional return distribution begins to deviate from its normal shape, with the skewness and excess kurtosis increasing significantly. Both the skewness and excess kurtosis of cross-sectional returns peak at a 30-minute frequency and then decline as the distribution approaches a normal shape at a 1-hour frequency. These patterns are consistent in both the performance of individual funds and the aggregate UK equity market. This study provides new evidence on the dynamics of asset return distributions and contributes to existing research on the topic. Moreover, our analysis offers policy implications for frequency settings in high-frequency trading strategies. Finally, our results can be utilized to model other asset return distributions using our proposed framework. The non-relativistic electric dipole approximation plays a vital role in understanding how atoms interact with light, enabling calculations of absorption and emission spectra with remarkable precision. Breaking down these interactions into three distinct components - a contributing core, main, and tail - researchers have identified unique properties within each segment. Specifically, the core influences the overall dipole transition efficiency, while the main and tail components dictate the dipole transition's magnitude and sign, respectively. By identifying these unique properties, scientists can refine the non-relativistic electric dipole approximation, potentially eliminating the need for much slower ab initio calculations in certain cases. This improved model has significant implications for simulating the interactions between photons and atoms, enabling the creation of highly efficient photon-atom coupling. Consequently, this greater efficiency could lead to the development of more resilient quantum light sources. Although previously applied to 2s$\rightarrow$2p transitions, this enhanced approximation remains untested for single and double electric dipole transitions within the closed-shell domain. To validate the improved approximation's accuracy, researchers have compared its predictions with ab initio results for a set of high Lyman transition bands in hydrogen, isotopes of lithium, and phosphorus. The comparisons show the improved approximation's predictions for these transition bands align closely with the ab initio results, with the largest discrepancies recorded at 0.15% for the lithium isotopes and 0.17% for the phosphorus isotopes. Notably, the improved approximation's predictions for these transition bands remain within the estimated uncertainty threshold of 0.20%. Consequently, the enhanced model offers the most accurate non-relativistic electric dipole approximation yet achieved, validating its use for ab initio calculated transition data.
