To investigate the origin of galaxy warps, we conducted a study on 13 late-type spiral galaxies with warped outer rings. The majority of these galaxies were found to have an outer ring in the same plane as their core. However, the extent and inclination of this outer ring relative to the core varied significantly. Through a seriesassistant analysis, we considered a hypothetical lognormal distribution for the tidal influence that contributes to galaxy warps. We observed that the probability of finding galaxies with warped outer rings was around 30-40%, with this statistic increasing to 60-80% for galaxies with U-shaped warps. These probabilities were based on a comparison with a control sample of 15 galaxies. We noted that the probability of finding galaxies with warped outer rings was higher in interactions involving a ratio of mass to the perturber of $M_{\rm pert}$ to $M_{\rm gal}$ equal to or greater than 0.1, with this statistic peaking at 0.4 for such interactions. These findings provide support for a interaction-based explanation for galaxy warps, with the occurrence of warped galaxy rings in disk systems potentially attributed to the influence of galactic tides and interactions. Additionally, we noted that the probability of finding galaxies with warped outer rings in group or cluster environments was around twice as high as in interactions involving a single perturber. These, however, may be partially masked by the impact of feedback from active galactic nuclei. Furthermore, we noted that the occurrence of galaxy warps in groups or clusters was more prevalent in galaxies with U-shaped warps, with this statistic peaking at 60% for such warps, as opposed to just 20% in galaxies with S-shaped warps. These findings suggest that the influence of galactic environment on warped galaxy formation could be the result of either strong or weak tidal forces, with the former contributing to U-shaped warps and the latter to S-shaped warps. These findings, however, need to be verified through further analysis of high-resolution simulations of galaxy interactions and formation. In addition, we also conducted further analysis on the time it would take for galaxy wars to form after a galactic interaction. Our results suggest that this time frame could be as low as 1 billion years in cases where the mass of the perturber is 10% of the mass of the galaxy, with this time frame increasing to 3-4 billion years in cases where the mass of the perturber is 1% of the mass of the galaxy.

Imitation learning seeks to align an agent's behavior with that of an expert by generating expert-like data, but does so without necessarily closing the gap between their environments. As a result, discrepancies between the two spaces can hinder imitation. To overcome this limitation, we develop a framework for comparing distribution differences and predicting expert behavior within a shared latent space. This approach employs a common encoder to translate both expert and agent interactions into a unified latent environment, thereby eliminating discrepancies in the process. We support our method with a demonstration of its superior performance on a challenging simulation of marine rescue operations. Additionally, we illustrate the benefits of extracting latent environments through an analysis of the extracted variables in the same marine rescue domain. Finally, high-level environment features are used to guide an agent's decision-making in a real-world industrial setting. This research highlights the significance of environment structure in supporting an effective imitation learning strategy. Conversely, a mismatch between environments and the resulting loss of key features hinders an agent's ability to acquire essential knowledge. In response, we suggest a practical solution to address this issue in a practical setting. The proposed method offers an viable alternative to existing imitation learning techniques. It provides an accurate representation of the target domain, corrects environmental mismatches, and facilitates knowledge acquisition by the agent. Furthermore, the latent environment can be utilized as a starting point for designing more effective transfer learning methods, as evidenced by the performance of an evolution strategy in the marine rescue domain. We show that utilizing the latent environment rather than the observed domain results in an improvement of the transfer learning method. The proposed method also has an efficient computational complexity. A thorough comparison with existing approaches is presented in the supplement. The code to reproduce the results is available on our website. Research suggests that angular momentum in clouds of gas plays a critical role in the process of protostar formation, and thus studying this aspect is of great importance. We conducted a computational investigation into the influence of angular momentum on the development of disks surrounding protostars, and found that higher angular momentum levels in gas clouds are more likely to lead to disk fragmentation. Additionally, we discovered that the direction of angular momentum in the cloud has a significant impact on the potential fragmentation, and that other factors, such as magnetic fields and radiative transfer, can also affect the process of protostar formation and disk development in this context. Our findings ultimately highlight the need for further observations and studies into the properties of the environment in the formation of stars. This research offers a fresh perspective on understanding coverage of association rules and redundancy within a knowledge base, drawing on the foundations of modal logic. By translating association rules into a specific modal logic, we gain essential insights into the nuances of entailment among these rules, enabling us to quantify the redundancy among them. In particular, we observe that an association rule is logically implied by another rule if and only if the first rule is derivable from the second within a specific logical framework, characterized by the addition of novelties through a series of successive updates. This relationship allows us to investigate the computational complexities of decision problems arising from the application of this new logical framework. Specifically, we find that deriving an association rule from another instance, subject to a knowledge base constraint, constitutes a computationally intractable problem, albeit with a related solvable variant when the target rule is explicitly present within the knowledge base. To address these complexities, we introduce a heuristic approach grounded in a new type of logic, which we term associative, and establish the basic properties of this new logical system. This associative logic emerges as a convenient means to approximate the more intricate modal logic underlying association rules, yielding significant computational benefits. In particular, we find that deriving an association rule from another, subject to a knowledge base constraint, becomes a solvable problem within a linear time scale when the target rule is explicitly present within the knowledge base. To showcase the applicability of these results, we report on the implementation of an enhanced version of CBA, the classical data mining algorithm for association rule mining, incorporating our new type of logic to efficiently eliminate redundant rules. Experimental outcomes indicate a pronounced time efficiency gain of up to 80% when the proposed approach is compared to a straight application of CBA. In particular, we observe a noticeable performance boost on two diverse datasets, achieving superior results when the number of generated rules is relatively small, and sometimes comparable outcomes when the volume of rules increases substantially. In general, we suspect that the degree of rule generality could serve as a decisive factor in determining the applicability of our new approach. In light of these experimental findings, we propose the following potential research direction: an in-depth statistical investigation of the characteristics of the generated rules could yield valuable insights for data mining purposes. In fact, we suspect that the number of general rules might possess an exponential growth tendency with respect to the number of specific rules, presenting an intriguing hypothesis for future research to assess. Individuals struggling with mental health issues have a higher likelihood of engaging in certain undesirable behaviors. Research has demonstrated that mental health treatment can significantly reduce the rate of repeat offenses, with crimes involving violence and property crimes being the most responsive to treatment. Nevertheless, identifying the specific disorders linked to specific crimes is a complex task due to the diverse interactions between mental health conditions and criminal activities. We have developed an innovative system that utilizes deep learning to create individualized connections between specific disorders and crimes, taking into account the varying levels of impact associated with each disorder. The core of this innovative approach lies in a Dual-Stage Transformer model that first establishes broad links between disorders and crimes, before refining these connections with a transformer-based network that draws from rich, accurate data sets. Comprehensive experiments have yielded promising results, with our model outperforming other methods in predicting specific disorders linked to particular crimes, with our model achieving a remarkable 0.242 Higher AUROC compared to the existing approaches. What's more, our approach provides intuitive insights into the connections between specific disorders and crimes, making it easier to draw conclusions from the data. Our analysis shows that the model's success can be attributed to its unique ability to draw from rich, accurate data sets, as well as its use of a transformer-based network that allows for the extraction of complex patterns from the data. This new approach has the potential to revolutionize the use of deep learning in legal proceedings by providing valuable insights into the links between specific disorders and crimes. Detecting anomalies in time series data is critical in identifying irregular patterns or behaviors deviating from the norm. When utilizing deep learning models, a significant limitation arises from the requirement for extensively labeled data, making the process expensive and impractical. This paper delves into a cutting-edge method using an unsupervised pre-training technique based on a language model, thereby enabling fast and efficient discovery of anomalous patterns without relying on labeled data. Notably, this method leverages its ability to model long-term context similar to how BERT processes language, thus making it suitable for identifying anomalies in time series data. The results highlight the effectiveness of this method in extracting relevant features and identifying anomalies with comparable or better performance to state-of-the-art anomaly detection models that rely on labeled data. Furthermore, this method also demonstrates robustness in withstanding small modifications to the input data. Therefore, this research suggests that pre-training unsupervised on generic tasks can lead to surprising capabilities in other domains. The current state of deep learning-based verification systems, along with their advantages and shortcomings, has been reviewed. Open-source re-creation instructions for existing verification tools are provided, enabling users to compare these systems under identical conditions. Empirical studies were conducted to examine the performance of different verification systems in both clean and artificially introduced noisy environments. The analysis revealed that the performance rankings of these systems were particularly susceptible to changes in the data noise levels. Consequently, the reliability of a verification system is tightly coupled with the level of data purity, and therefore, cannot be adequately assessed through clean datasets alone. The findings highlight the necessity for testing and evaluation procedures that take into consideration a range of data purity levels. The effectiveness of data augmentation techniques is widely recognized, but how they're influenced by the amount of data available is still an area of investigation. This study examines how various data augmentation techniques enhance the accuracy of models trained on small, normal, and large datasets of sizes 4, 50, and 5000 on a specific image classification task using the CIFAR-10 dataset after being normalized to have the same diversity of classes. The results show that while augmentation techniques generally improve accuracy, their benefits greatly depend on the available data size; in small datasets, improvements can be substantial but may not exceed the gains achieved through changes in hyperparameters alone, whereas they offer consistent gains in larger datasets. This study also provides insights into the performance of different models under test-time data augmentation and how it interacts with different optimizers and loss functions. Furthermore, the research highlights the potential of discarding augmented data with low prediction confidence as an effective approach to strike a balance between model performance and complexity. Ultimately, the findings suggest that the value of data augmentation lies primarily in larger datasets and that the benefits diminish in smaller datasets. Given a statistical model, the task is to estimate a function of parameters, g(p), using observed data, which may be subject to restrictions. When we have a likelihood function based on observed data, we can use weak convergence to infer the properties of its functional average, ultimately estimating g(p) in a consistent manner. However, when the data are merely assumed to satisfy certain conditions, such as independence and identically distributed, we may use weak convergence to bound the estimation error but cannot guarantee consistency in a linear interpolation manner. In case the function g(p) is part of an optimization problem, such as in empirical risk minimization, we may use weak convergence under mild conditions to estimate g(p) through an alternative route. To evaluate the efficiency of these estimation methods, we also analyze the asymptotic variance and provide non-asymptotic upper bounds for the estimation error. Numerous numerical studies back up the theoretical findings. Interestingly, in some scenarios, we discover that the simple linear interpolation method, which lacks consistency, actually yields the same order of convergence as the consistent linear error-correction method. Additionally, we extend and apply the results to various well-known estimation challenges, including constrained optimization, capacity prediction in information theory, and the behavior of empirical Bayes and Bayes methods. Lastly, we establish a new connection between empirical and frequentist perspectives by showing, under specific conditions, that the empirical Bayes method is the frequentist method of minimizing loss. This relationship enables us to derive non-asymptotic upper bounds for the estimation error in empirical Bayes methods. In contrast to previous findings, we may use weak convergence to bound the estimation error in frequentist methods without requiring specific conditions on the data distribution. This result is particularly notable as it is the first proof of its kind to our knowledge. Furthermore, we may use weak convergence to derive non-asymptotic upper bounds for the estimation error in constrained optimization problems, a task not explored in previous research. In the absence of data, we also use weak convergence to estimate the bias of estimation methods. Additionally, we extend the findings to multi-dimensional estimation tasks by analyzing the behavior of these estimation methods in high-dimensional scenarios. In the process, we derive new upper bounds for the estimation error in high-dimensional scenarios, a result valuable in its own right. In conclusion, this study showcases the utility of using weak convergence as a powerful analytical tool in solving a diverse range of estimation challenges in statistics and data science. The rise of big data and big data management systems has led to a significant shift in how to address privacy issues, moving beyond individual records to a collective consideration of groups of records. Current approaches, however, fall short in addressing a key aspect: dependency relationships between individual records. In reality, data from sensors, online transactions, medical records, etc. often exhibit high dependency within large datasets, making the assumed independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) assumption invalid. Ignoring these dependencies results in underestimating the potential data breaches and misleading evaluations of data management systems. In this study, we introduce a new model that takes these dependencies into account to assess a data release's privacy impact and compare the privacy-privacy tradeoff with existing methods. Our experiments demonstrate that failing to account for record-to-record relationships in data release valuations leads to an inadequate and overly optimistic appraisal of privacy risks. In contrast, our proposed approach yields a more realistic and higher valuation of privacy risks that aligns with the existing literature in economics. This valuation can inform data management system decisions regarding the release of data on a per-group basis. In particular, we show that releasing data in groups results in a valuation that is at least as high as the valuation obtained through the current state-of-the-art methods that assume i.i.d. records. In some cases, our findings even suggest that the value of privacy-privacy tradeoff when considering dependent records is significantly higher than the value obtained with the existing methods that assume independent records. In particular, our experiments show that the value of privacy-privacy tradeoff when considering dependent records in a dataset of online transactions can be two orders of magnitude higher than the value obtained with the existing methods that assume independent records in a dataset of medical records. This paper focuses on developing consumer-centric outcomes by leveraging the creative process of those who create their own fashion outfits. To achieve this, our research introduces an innovative approach that uses StyleTransferNet, a pre-trained image classifier, to detect outfit pieces that don't match. Utilizing user-generated content from social media platforms, we train and evaluate our model to demonstrate its superiority over traditional methods. Moreover, our analysis delves into the advantages and limitations of machine learning in assisting human creators. Ultimately, our work showcases the potential of machine learning in enabling humans to produce high-quality, unique fashion outfits efficiently. Non-classical resource theories have become a premier area of study in quantum information theory for multiple reasons. Firstly, they offer an simplified framework to examine and understand diverse physical systems; secondly, they provide a method to identify and exploit unique properties of quantum states and operations that are missing in classical systems; and lastly, they facilitate the identification of essential physical properties necessary for achieving specific tasks. The advancement in NCRTs has significantly improved our comprehension of quantum systems, enabling the development of efficient protocols for tasks like compression, decoding, randomness extraction, and randomness splitting, as well as the demonstration of quantum advantages in non-thermality, correlation generation, randomness extraction, and covert communication. Furthermore, NCRTs have enabled the identification of resource inequalities that can serve as checklists for identifying quantum advantages. Nevertheless, there is still a need for a systematic approach that can determine the useful utility of a resource in a practical protocol before designing a quantum information processing task that leverages it. We intend to tackle this problem by proposing a method to evaluate the utility of a resource in a practical protocol, as well as designing a task that utilizes the non-classical features of entanglement in quantum systems. Entanglement is a non-classical resource that has the potential to provide significant advantages in the execution of various quantum information processing tasks. The rapid growth of the internet of things (IoT) has led to a significant increase in data, which has prompted the adoption of federated learning due to scalability and privacy concerns. Nonetheless, the federated learning approach faces limitations in efficiently managing the vast amount of IoT data while preserving data privacy. In this study, we introduce FedBuff, a novel incremental federated learning algorithm that counteracts the pitfalls of traditional federated learning methods. FedBuff operates by partitioning the federated learning process into distinct layers, each utilizing buffered data to train a neural network layer from incremental batches. This innovative approach enables FedBuff to scale efficiently, maintain privacy, and achieve a moderate performance comparable to state-of-the-art models. Notably, the FedBuff repository is accessible at https://github.com/joethefish/FedBuff. Experimental findings demonstrate that FedBuff scales better than MOON and is more efficient than M-Local-SCFG and FedPerf, all of which are advanced federated learning methods. Furthermore, FedBuff achieves a comparable performance to state-of-the-art models across diverse datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Fashion MNIST, and knn-MNIST. Specifically, FedBuff demonstrates a 1.5 times improvement in efficiency and 2 times improvement in scalability over the next best approach, M-Local-SCFG. This remarkable performance showcases the FedBuff algorithm's superiority and serves as a promising solution for federated learning applications requiring efficient, private, and scalable training of neural networks. As a future direction, the integration of FedBuff with additional optimization techniques, such as distributed learning and graph neural networks, may further enhance its performance and achieve new breakthroughs in federated learning. In conclusion, the FedBuff algorithm offers a novel and effective approach to federated learning that balances efficiency, privacy, and performance. Although the algorithm still requires several modifications to match the performance of local training, the promising results indicate a bright future for FedBuff and its potential to revolutionize the field of federated learning. This study delves into the integration of kernel-based techniques with traditional projection methods rooted in partial differential equations (PDEs) and functional integrals. It explores the extension of kernel-based Newton methods to approximate fixed-points and equilibrium solutions, ultimately examining their links to classical projection methods such as the Galerkin approach. Convergence, accuracy, and computational efficiency of these kernel-based techniques are then evaluated against established methods, including the non-local Galerkin approach and the conjugate kernel method. Numerical experiments are conducted to demonstrate the performance of these techniques in solving non-local PDEs, work done in collaboration with J. P. A. Sampaio. 

In this work, we developed a new approach for finding the closest solution to a given problem with a non-local constraint, formulated as a non-convex optimization task. This method can be applied to various equilibrium problems, including those with and without equilibrium, and is complemented by an iterative scheme that produces a sequence of sub-optimal solutions. Both methods were successfully tested on non-local PDEs, showing comparable results to existing solution methods. Notably, the integrated kernel-based technique outperformed the other methods in several numerical evaluations. Furthermore, the study identified interesting connections between the kernel-based Newton method and the conjugate kernel method, suggesting a shared root in certain circumstances. Lastly, the comparison of kernel-based techniques against classical projection methods revealed superior performance of these techniques, including the non-local Galerkin approach. All numerical experiments were conducted on an Intel Core i5-2400 processor with 8 GB of RAM, running a Linux operating system. This work has potential applications in solving partial differential equations, particularly those with non-local interactions, and may also be utilized to model dynamic systems subject to fractional delays. 

Key findings of this research include: 

* The kernel-based techniques developed can efficiently approximate fixed-points and equilibrium solutions of partial differential equations to a high degree of accuracy.
* These techniques compare favorably to established methods, including the non-local Galerkin approach and conjugate kernel method.

The construction of high dimensional expanders (HDEs) through lifting of expander graphs and manifolds has significant theoretical and practical implications for computer science. This article contributes novel constructions of HDEs by employing lifting on a series of geometric expanders in low-dimensional spaces and utilizing a recent high-dimensional expansion result for simplicial complexes due to Lela Studenmund, Luca Trevisan, and Tias Foster. Additionally, we present a series of constructions, beginning with a straightforward method using 2-dimensional geometric expanders and continuing with more complex constructions involving 4-dimensional hypergraphs, by employing the properties of stable matchings in specific structures and the proof from Trevisan and Samorodnitsky on the expansion of certain complexes. These innovative methods yield evidence that four-dimensional geometric expanders can be considered as more fundamental objects of study in the field of high dimensional expanding of simplicial complexes. This research was inspired by questions from James R. Lee and partially takes from an earlier thesis by Studenmund. Our work is codesigned with a blog series by Laura Tzook and can be found at https://high-dimensional-geometries.blog. Additionally, we propose an independent line of research in the construction of HDEs based on minimizing local constraints in the distance of geometric expanders and applying this concept to the study of distance regular graphs. This new approach results in the construction of the first known graph with a geometric expansion of 1.99999999999997 in the Euclidean space of dimension five, achieving a higher expansion rate than previously recorded in the Euclidean space of the same dimension by Li and Tretkovic. The explosion in parameters that occurs when combining long-range recurrent connections with dense connections in hidden layers contributes significantly to these problems. In an effort to overcome these limitations, a new architecture called the Steered Convolutional Neural Network (SCN) is studied. The rapid spread of COVID-19 across the globe has led to a devastating public health crisis, prompting governments to seek effective policies to balance economic costs and medical outcomes. Given the constant evolution of the virus, policy decisions made earlier in the pandemic may no longer be suitable, necessitating regular reassessment. In response, we develop a new approach that combines economic and public health analysis to provide decision-makers with up-to-date policy recommendations. Our method explicitly models the interconnectedness of pandemic dynamics, commodity interactions, financial influences, and the sequential nature of temporal events. By optimizing a comprehensive objective function that weighs medical and economic consequences, we obtain the optimal policy rule at any given time. The effectiveness of our approach is validated through numerical simulations, which demonstrate the superiority of our delayed mitigation strategy over both early and unregulated scenarios. Furthermore, our results show that timely moderate measures are essential to achieving a balanced outcome. The proposed framework serves as a versatile tool capable of handling evolving pandemics, facilitating the derivation of general policy principles and scenario-specific policy recommendations. Debugging data-intensive machine learning (MLE) pipelines has become a major challenge due to their growing complexity. Current data debugging techniques are often inefficient because they require the entire pipeline to be executed from start to finish multiple times. Our new method, DataScope, locates issues within MLE pipelines directly in the pipeline's symbolic form, dramatically reducing the number of times the code needs to be run. DataScope achieves this improvement by breaking down data debugging into a series of independent tasks and optimizing each one individually. This optimization, along with a novel data flow analysis, allows DataScope to execute each task as quickly as possible. Our testing on actual MLE pipelines confirms that DataScope significantly outperforms other methods, taking less than a tenth the time to detect issues for large datasets. In free-electron lasers (FELs), particularly those that produce XUV and soft X-ray wavelengths, a typical setup begins with a chaotic, shot-to-shot electron beam phase and then attempts to establish a synchronized radiation-field-electron interaction. This is achieved through a combination of undulator chirp and taper settings on the electron beam, resulting in output that is maximized but highly dependent on the initial electron phase. To overcome this challenge, an alternative approach called chirp-taper optimization (CTO) has been developed. For the first time, this work presents a detailed analysis of CTO's impact on ultrashort pulse generation in FELs. Within a dynamic FEL simulation framework, the results show that CTO not only limits the output's overall stability but also hinders the generation of the desired ultrashort pulses. This occurrence is primarily attributed to an initial electron phase landau spike that forms during the chirp-taper drive. Consequently, all produced radiation remains dominated by a single phase, resulting in poor output efficiency. However, there are alternative strategies, such as phase Landau damping by beam transfer, that can help mitigate this issue and enable the optimal operation of CTO in FELs. By assuming small vertical velocity fluctuations in comparison to horizontal fluctuations, the authors derive a simplified model to represent atmospheric perturbations. This modified model preserves the conservation laws of the original equations and includes an anomalous dissipation term resulting from the discretization of the simplified equations. Unlike the original equations, which predict instability in the form of gravity waves, this modified model predicts only damped waves. Consequently, a numerical solution to the modified model is presented, which demonstrates a complete agreement with the original equations in the limit of small vertical velocity fluctuations. Additionally, the solution primarily consists of gravity waves with an absolute phase error of about 0.1 degrees over a 10-day period. Moreover, the dissipation rate obtained from the numerical solution matches the dissipation rate predicted by the original equations with an absolute error of less than 0.01 dB. Finally, a comparison between the original and modified models reveals that the latter predicts a significantly lower horizontal wavenumber for instability, typically by a factor of 5 to 7, implying a substantially reduced computational cost for numerical simulations based on the modified model. In particular, the dissipation scale of the modified model can be set to a high value, effectively ignoring it, while still accurately reproducing the dissipation predicted by the original equations up to a precision of 10^-4. This value is maintained for all horizontal wavenumbers and accounts for both vertical and horizontal fluctuations of atmospheric perturbations. In the spirit of the Kolmogorov theory of dissipation, the dissipation scale of the modified model can be set to the average scale of turbulent eddies, which typically ranges from 5 to 80 km depending on the altitude and temperature stability. We've also conducted numerical studies to compare these methods in terms of accuracy, false positive rate, and implementation complexity. In particular, we've discovered that neural networks and change detection methods demonstrate potential in learning patterns specific to operating conditions and incidents, while control chart monitoring proves effective in pinpointing anomalies. In contrast to these methods, which require manual data labeling for training and processing, our proposed approach - incident learning - allows for the automatic detection and incorporation of incidents from past event logs, thereby enhancing the system's performance and adaptability over time. We've validated the efficacy of our method through case studies involving distribution grid models with various configurations, including energy storage systems, and log data from a real-world smart distribution system. The results show that incident learning outperforms the alternative methods in terms of accuracy and real-time operation. Moreover, this method has the capability to expand its scope to detect complex incidents in the future. Lastly, we've analyzed the computational efficiency of the methods and found that change detection and control chart monitoring require significantly lower resources than neural networks and our proposed incident learning method. However, we assert that the enhanced performance and scalability of these methods justify any minor increase in computational requirements. To facilitate the replication of our work, we've made the source code and data available for public access. Additionally, we've outlined several future directions for further research and development. A quadric in projective space can be defined by a homogeneous polynomial of degree two over a field. Contrary to common belief, not all such quadrics have a rational parameterization. We determine the conditions under which smooth quadrics admit a rational parameterization, effectively characterizing them within projective space. This characterization yields an explicit formula, revealing that a quadric is rationally parameterized if and only if its dimension is odd or if its dimension is even and its degree is a multiple of the characteristic of the field. This characterization has applications in algebraic coding theory, as it allows us to estimate the distance of quadratic codes. The study of these quadrics also bears a resemblance to the classification of smooth algebraic surfaces in projective space. The main difference lies in the fact that, in the case of surfaces, there are only a finite number of possible types, whereas the classification of quadrics within projective space yields an infinite series for each dimension. The characterization of these quadrics has implications in the study of their tangent defects, which can be expressed in terms of the field's characteristics and the size of the quadric. The classification of these quadrics also enables us to establish a correspondence between rational curves on them and linear subspaces within project space. Furthermore, we demonstrate the availability of quadrics that admit a rational parameterization for any given dimension and degree, provided that the characteristic of the field does not divide the degree. The proof involves selecting a random homogeneous vector, then defining a quadric as the intersection of a hyperplane with the space tangent to it. This method allows us to establish that, for even dimensions, a quadric is rationally parameterized if and only if its degree is a multiple of the characteristic of the field. The correspondence between rational curves on the quadric and linear subspaces within project space enables us to establish a lower bound on the number of such curves for any given degree, including the possibility that the degree is nontrivial and the dimension is odd. The proof involves iterating a transformation that 'pushes' rational curves onto the quadric onto a random homogeneous vector, then shows that such curves cannot 'land' on a quadric that is rationally parameterized for a given degree if they are not rationally parameterized themselves. Past studies have examined how background contributions from top quark pairs will impact the sensitivity of experiments to detect Higgs boson signals, particularly in the context of fermionic pair production. This research extends those findings by analyzing the influence of the top quark pair on a variety of Higgs boson signals, as well as how the inclusion of the W boson pair affects the detection of the Higgs boson in the decay mode $b\bar{b}$. These studies utilize a simulation of the theoretical production processes that is consistent with the standard model, but also includes higher-order corrections based on next-to-leading order results. These predictions are then analyzed against data from a simulated representation of the CMS experiment at a proton-proton collider operating at a center-of-mass energy of 14 TeV. This research considers multiple scenarios of Higgs boson interaction with the top quark pair, as well as the impact of the electromagnetic interaction on the detection of the Higgs boson in the decay mode $\gamma\gamma$. These studies are particularly relevant because they the LHC will soon reach its designed peak luminosity, at which point the sensitivity of the experiment will be largely limited by the efficiency of the detector at dealing with background contributions from the top quark pair. Furthermore, recent advances in theoretical calculations suggest that further progress can be made in the detection of the Higgs boson by accurately accounting for the uncertainty associated with the choice of parton shower model used in simulation. Finally, these studies also examine the detection of the Higgs boson in the decay mode $ ZZ$. In particular, these research findings show that the inclusion of the electromagnetic interaction slightly enhances the detection efficiency of the detector for the $ ZZ$ decay mode of the Higgs boson. A range of factors contributes to public attitudes towards vaccine-related misinformation being widespread and increasingly complex. Existing analyses of this issue often rely on the interpretation of elites rather than understanding the broader public's perspectives. To fill this gap, we've developed a framework for examining how ordinary people perceive vaccine-related misinformation. This approach recognizes attitudes towards vaccine-related misinformation as a nuanced construct with multiple dimensions, rather than a single-point measure. By employing qualitative methods, we identified key areas of public concern related to vaccine-related misinformation, and found that public attitudes are shaped by trust in information sources, perceived motivations behind misinformation, and beliefs about vaccine efficacy. We found that public attitudes towards vaccine-related misinformation are not simply opposition to the concept of misinformation, but rather are influenced by a more intricate set of considerations that are not typically captured in surveys that reduce this issue to simple opinions. These findings can inform public health communications by acknowledging the complex nature of public attitudes towards vaccine-related misinformation. Public health communications may benefit from viewing vaccine-related misinformation as one part of a broader broader set of public concerns that also involve trust in information sources, the potential for being deceived, and the efficacy of vaccines. By acknowledging the multiple dimensions of public attitudes towards vaccine-related misinformation, public health communications may be more effective at addressing this issue by engaging the public on these broader concerns rather than simply opposing misinformation. Attosecond pulses in the extreme ultraviolet (XUV) are generated by focusing a laser pulse to create a high-electron density, then using an adjacent near-infrared field to accelerate these electrons, directing them towards a detector. However, the process is hampered by inconsistencies, particularly in the central wavelength and temporal timing, derived from the inherent uncertainties in the focusing and temporal synchronization of the near-infrared pulse. Our study demonstrates the capability to precisely control both the central wavelength and temporal duration of attosecond pulses through a new technique of co-propagating wavefront manipulation (CPWFM), which modifies the infrared pulse before focusing the electron density. This method reveals significant improvements in attosecond pulse stability, with reductions in central wavelength and temporal fluctuations of nearly threefold and tenfold, respectively. Our findings yield a corresponding enhancement in the quality of the attoseond pulse's spectral coherence, with a coherence time proportional to the temporal fluctuations. This breakthrough holds potential for significant advancements in generating higher-quality XUV attosecond pulses, thereby facilitating precision measurements of atomic inner-shell electronic transitions and ultrafast chemical dynamics. Additionally, the research offers a practical approach for optimizing table-top attosecond pulse generation via a simplified, versatile method. Our study demonstrates the application of this novel CPWFM in two distinct experimental setups, highlighting its versatility and the promise of improved performance in future high-harmonic generation schemes. Deep learning based solution of partial differential equations, particularly ill-posed inverse problems, has become a vibrant research area. Recently, we introduced the Residual-based Adaptive Node Generation (RANG) method which dynamically adjusts the training process by adding nodes to the network based on the prediction error and its derivatives. The conductive band of a ferroelectric field-effect transistor is influenced by the periodic domain pattern within the ferroelectric, creating discrete states in the conduction band that vary according to the domain orientation. As the ferroelectric's polarization changes from one orientation to the opposite, these domain-related states shift energy and eventually reverse order, forming a band structure pattern similar to that of an insulator near a domain boundary. This unique conduction band structure, unique to ferroelectric materials systems with multiple domain states, is a key factor in the electrostatic trapping and 0.1 THz quantum oscillations observed in ferroelectric field-effect transistors. The unique properties of ferroelectric FETs, not seen in ferromagnetic or antiferromagnetic 2D systems, originate from the interplay between the ferroelectric domain wall and the electrostatic potential, giving rise to a new type of electronic state referred to as a Fermi surface "topological pattern." The topological pattern of the Fermi surface in a ferroelectric field-effect transistor is a result of the ferroelectric's ability to switch domains and modify the electrostatic potential, creating a dynamic band structure that can be utilized for the development of advanced electronic devices and the creation of domain-specific quantum states within these devices. The unique domain wall induced electronic states present in ferroelectric materials systems with multiple domains can be utilized for the creation of quantum devices that operate near absolute zero temperature. The ferroelectric field-effect transistor offers a new method for controlling the flow of current at the quantum level by utilizing the ferroelectric's domain wall to modulate the electrostatic potential and thus the band structure of the conductor. A study of Rust's Cargo ecosystem shows that even though upgrades to newer versions of libraries often fix known vulnerabilities, libraries in this ecosystem frequently fail to take advantage of these upgrades. Our research revealed that as of 2020, around 60% of the Cargo ecosystem's libraries have yet to be updated with the latest versions of sensitive dependencies that fix security issues. Additionally, we found that even though 30% of vulnerabilities have resolution variants available for update, these updates remain unreceived by a significant portion of libraries. Our research identifies potential obstacles that hinder libraries in Cargo from being updated, and it sheds light on the role of human decision-making in the maintenance of this software ecosystem. The overall outcome of this study suggests that the community in charge of Rust's Cargo ecosystem lags behind in terms of keeping their dependencies up to date with the latest security fixes, and therefore, there is a need for improved tools that can effectively address security issues and facilitate the maintenance of this software ecosystem. Our research also lays out a potential solution that leverages information retrieval techniques to help libraries in Cargo with updating their dependencies to the latest versions that fix security issues, and the results of our experiments with this solution indicate that a significant portion of libraries can be updated successfully. However, there still remain a substantial number of libraries that cannot be updated due to the absence of replacement variants, and in order to address this issue, we propose the development of an evolutionary algorithm that can help in the creation of library upgrades. Our research shows that the combination of our proposed solution and the new algorithm results in a significant improvement in the effectiveness of the former in the task of updating library dependencies. Our results with this new approach show that a considerable portion of libraries can now be updated successfully, and the outcome of this research indicates that there is a need for the development of advanced tools that can effectively address security issues and facilitate the maintenance of this software ecosystem. Our research also identifies potential future directions in the study of this software ecosystem, and the results obtained from the evaluation of our approach confirm its feasibility and effectiveness. The equations are formulated in a thin diffusion framework that allows the diffusion coefficients to be singular. The research demonstrates that the ergodic property of these equations is influenced by the ergodic property of a related jump-diffusion model. Specifically, it is proven that the ergodic property exists under certain conditions, which include a threshold value for the diffusion coefficient being greater than zero, and a condition on the jump rate. When the ergodic property does not exist, it is possible for the solution to exhibit divergence in its mean square distance from its average long-term value. The research also identifies the parameters that contribute to non-ergodic behavior in both jump-diffusion and thin diffusion models. The key examples highlight the differences in ergodic behavior between pure jump noises and others types of noises. Recently, neural networks focused on image classification have incorporated Gabor filters with landmarks (LGFs) for stable representations across various conditions. Unlike traditional Gabor filters, LGFs use a location-sensitive activation function to maintain representation stability even with small shifts. Although this activation function facilitates robustness to positional changes, it poses challenges for the network when dealing with similar images rotated relative to each other. This study proposes an novel activation function for LGFs to enhance the robustness of image representations to orientation changes. The proposed activation function uses a normalized distance measure that enables stable representations across different positional and rotational conditions. Moreover, this innovation does not necessitate any pre-rotation of training data. Experimental evaluations on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate the benefits of the proposed activation function in making the deep neural network more robust to orientation changes. This study also investigates the properties of the proposed activation function through analytical and numerical assessments. Compared to previous studies using Gabor filters with rotation-invariant properties, the proposed method demonstrates equal or improved performance on the specific task of MNIST classification after the process of data augmentation for robustness. Furthermore, the networks based on the proposed activation function achieved classification accuracy of 96% on CIFAR-10 with applications in robust image classification, feature extraction, and the development of robust neural networks for image processing. The application of the proposed activation function to other datasets remains an area for further research. The code for the proposed method is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/ApoorvInamdar/LGF_activation_function. Additionally, the pre-trained models of the networks used in this study can be found at the same link. Researchers have proposed various forms of Trojan attacks against neural networks. These attacks, which hide backdoors in neural networks through slight modifications to their weights, have been limited to specific classes and inputs. Due to the distinct nature of each attack, they cannot be combined into a single, effective approach that can cover a broad range of scenarios. Our research aims to overcome this challenge by developing a sophisticated Trojan attack, which can be easily executed and hides subtle alterations in neural networks. Additionally, this attack can be used to set multiple backdoors, allowing it to bypass the limitations of previous techniques and attacks from different researchers. To evaluate the effectiveness of our attack, we successfully activated the hidden backdoors using customized images that contained specific text information. Our research also demonstrated the adverse impact of Trojan attacks on reliable neural networks, which are used in various applications such as data classification, semantic segmentation, and image manipulation. Our findings suggest that Trojan attacks can cause significant deterioration in the reliable neural networks' performance on specific tasks, which are within the scope of practice for black-box adversarial attacks. Our code and models are publicly available for reference and testing at the URL: https://github.com/Alea-TT/Trojan-Attack. Our research was conducted on neural networks that were trained using public datasets, which are also available at the same URL for reference and testing purposes. A cutting-edge Imaging Focal Plane Array, ROSIE IFU, has been created using an advanced technology called an Integrate and Switch Detector to revolutionize the field of spectroscopy. This innovative system consists of a 2D detector with 2048 x 2048 pixels that is divided into 4 quadrants, enabling the switch of any quadrant with any other quadrant in a single integration time of 5.6 milliseconds. This unique feature allows for the efficient exploration of the celestial environment by seamlessly integrating multiple fields of view, such as the intricate mapping of nebulae and galaxies. This study highlights the significant advantages of the ROSIE IFU in addressing the common drawbacks of traditional spectroscopy and illustrates its potential in optical and near-infrared spectrographic applications. As part of the IRAC Infrared Array Camera and CIBERS spectrographic project on the James Webb Space Telescope, ROSIE IFU is poised to set a new standard in low-mass flow spectrographic applications. This paper serves as a comprehensive technical introduction to the ROSIE IFU.

The paper explores the use of exothereric states in natural nuclei to investigate the angular distribution of non-resonant astrophysical $S$-factors. The authors apply this framework to the ground-state radiative capture of three targets, analyzing the implications of the mirror exponent $m$ on the shape of $S$-factors and the strength of their non-resonant component. Neural networks have successfully solved intricate inverse and ill-posed problems, outperforming more traditional approaches. However, the specific strategies employed by these neural networks are unclear, rendering them difficult to replicate in other domains. In this research, we establish a method for solving such problems using a combination of convex and non-convex optimization techniques. Our approach involves the optimization of a non-convex energy function, consisting of data fidelity and structural constraint terms, with respect to sparse model parameters. We employ the alternating direction method of multipliers to convexify the constraint term, while the model parameters are represented as a sum of sparse vector and dictionary multiplication, facilitating the incorporation of structural constraints through the incorporation of an explicit sparse prior on the model parameters. We then train the system by minimizing a non-convex energy function over all possible sparse model parameter configurations using a novel meta-algorithm that combines optimization techniques such as the gradient descent, projected gradient descent, and the method of moments. We test our method in 3 very challenging inverse problems - image deconvolution, compressed sensing, and source separation - and demonstrate that it successfully generalizes to new data while producing very good results for these difficult tasks. The source code for the algorithm is available on GitHub. Our results are comparable to the current state-of-the-art methods on these tasks while providing the significant benefit of being easily interpretable. Unlike neural networks, which are difficult to interpret due to their complex and easily generalizable nature, our algorithm's performance is driven by the explicit sparse prior on the model parameters, making it much more easily interpretable. Moreover, we observe that the algorithm's efficacy is closely related to the properties of the dictionary used in the model, with specific dictionaries producing similar performance in image deconvolution and compressed sensing but superior performance in source separation. These findings highlight the potential of our method as a general framework for solving a wide range of inverse and ill-posed problems. Moreover, the algorithm's ability to generalize to new data while producing good results for difficult tasks is reminiscent of the function of regularizers in statistical mechanics and inverse problem solving, suggesting the possibility of a theoretical connection between the two. In this study, we examine weighted oriented graphs, and investigate the situation where the ordinary power of the edge ideal equals the symbolic power of the edge ideal for a given r. We label this condition the 'equivalence property at r' (EQV_r), and aim to provide a characterization of EQV_r through a criterion involving the divisors of the graph. By characterizing EQV_r, we can determine the largest value of r satisfying EQV_r, and derive conditions for the 'equivalence property' (EQV) – the situation where EQV_r holds for all non-negative integers r. We also study the consequences of EQV_r, and provide a lower bound on the values of r satisfying EQV_r. Furthermore, we present examples illustrating the distinct situations described by EQV1, EQV2, and EQV3. Additionally, we extend our findings to weighted oriented bipartite graphs, and investigate the characteristics of EQV_r and EQV. Moreover, we identify a class of weighted oriented graphs, which we term 'EQV-graphs', and which satisfy EQV_r for all non-negative integers r, and provide a characterization of EQV-graphs. We also explore the relationship between the coordinates of the generic initial ideal of the edge ideal and the labels of the graph, and apply these findings to determine the values of r satisfying EQV_r for'staircase' graphs. Moreover, we extend our study to oriented linear suspension graphs and provide a characterization of EQV_r. Furthermore, we extend our study to various classes of weighted oriented graphs, and also provide code for determining EQV_r. In this research, we examine the method of obtaining precise slip conditions on the surfaces of individual fibres in a liquid film that surrounds multiple fibres. Our work extends previous studies by Pezzi and Strano, who investigated this topic using a different approach that involved using the continuity equation for the film's thickness. By contrasting our method with their approach, we demonstrate that the drops formed in the film are unaffected by the method of slip condition determination. Furthermore, we highlight an oversight in their analysis related to mass flow and present a corrected version. Their method is likened to a "black box" approach, which masks the importance of individual fibre properties in the process. On the other hand, by calculating the rate of change in liquid mass, we show that the process is governed by a balance between mass flow and the rate of destruction of the liquid film. Our research was inspired by a study of liquid slip on cotton fibre published by Bonnet, Millman, and Vandenbruck in 2010. Our findings are also connected to a preceding theoretical model developed by the research team, which described the process in a simplified manner. In the theoretical model, the process was controlled by a single parameter, which was not initially identified as the scale factor for mass flow. By presenting both experimental and theoretical results, we examine how the method of slip condition determination affects the maximum liquid throughput and demonstrate that the method used to obtain the slip conditions significantly impacts these outcomes. Our research offers novel methods for determining slip conditions on fibre surfaces and provides a clear understanding of how individual fibre properties contribute to a broader understanding of the process. Additionally, our research provides a stepping stone for future studies focused on how the method of slip condition determination affects other properties of the process. Our research may be applied in industries where fibre slippage occurs due to changes in fibre properties; such industries include the production of rayon fibre, the behaviour of lotus leaves, and the extraction of natural fibre. Our research may also be relevant to future studies on phase transitions and phase oscillations within liquid films. Our research contributes to a broader understanding of phase transitions by providing a phase diagram that shows how individual fibre properties influence a phase known as the "Navy" phase; this phase is distinguished by a rough surface texture and a particular film thickness. The primary objective of UbiSummarize 2021, a challenge introduced at UbiQuitars 2021, is to generate a concise, readable summary of unprocessed raw data from sensor arrays capturing human written activity and contextual information. We define a successful outcome as a summary that accurately captures the duration, location, and contents of written activity alongside contextual details. Given the raw data often includes noise and incomplete data points due to missing timestamps, as well as varied data collection settings, creating a universal dataset to train models is impractical. Therefore, we developed the WrittenActivityDetector, a specialized model capable of identifying written activity and extracting relevant contextual information from sensor data with missing timestamps. Firstly, we utilize an autoencoder to downscale sensor data and extract a compressed feature set suitable for further analysis. Next, a Gaussian Mixture Model is applied to isolate periods of written activity based on the extracted features and a Motion History Descriptor is used to filter out non-written activity. We evaluated the effectiveness of this detection method on two sets of data and successfully demonstrated its ability to accurately identify written activity with varying data rates, ranging from 10 to 50 frames per second, and data completeness levels. Furthermore, we compared this method against alternative approaches and achieved a 90% accuracy rate in a setting where data was collected at 10 frames per second with no contextual information, outperforming the baseline by 5%. Although we found that accurately extracting contextual information from raw data is still a challenging task, our model demonstrated a 75% accuracy rate in this regard, which is a notable improvement over the baseline. These results indicate that WrittenActivityDetector is a viable and effective solution for detecting written activity and extracting contextual information from complex sensor data without relying on a trained dataset. Moreover, this method promotes reproducibility by providing a fully defined, trainable model that can be applied across a wide range of domains with minimal modifications to adapt to different data collection settings. In addition to resolving the UbiSummarize challenge, this model is also capable of standing alone as a written activity recognizer. We intend to extend and enhance the model in the future by incorporating more sophisticated features and improving its performance in scenarios with low data rates and limited contextual information. In this paper, we present the WrittenActivityDetector model and provide a detailed explanation of its design and testing process. We then compare its effectiveness against other approaches and discuss its potential applications and limitations before outlining the planned course for future development. This study introduces the Skincare project's diagnostic tool, an AI-powered system that helps general practitioners and dermatologists differentiate between skin disease types and provide accurate diagnoses. Leveraging an advanced database of 3100 images representing 8 distinct skin conditions, the team trained a deep learning model to prioritize relevant image features, and evaluated its effectiveness against expert human diagnoses on a dataset of 1200 images. Notably, the team discovered that adding patient information to the model enhanced its diagnostic accuracy and proved particularly beneficial for certain disease types. Moreover, they analyzed the effectiveness of limited training data of 200 images and found that the diagnostic output could be improved with subsequent access to more training images. Overall, the results indicate that the Skincare project's diagnostic tool can produce accurate diagnoses while accounting for the uncertainty inherent in limited training data, and offers potential for future improvement with additional training and functionality. Furthermore, the study proposes two approaches for integrating the diagnostic output with dermatological expert rules to produce clinically informed diagnoses, and suggests opportunities for further growth and development. Ultimately, the Skincare project aims to address a critical challenge in healthcare by providing reliable and efficient skin disease diagnosis using image analysis. Although the minimum requirement for the model's training data is quite extensive - comprising 200 images - the team is working on reducing this need through subsequent developments. Conversely, the model can still operate effectively with a much larger set of 3000 images. In conclusion, the Skincare project has successfully implemented an AI-powered diagnostic tool for skin disease diagnosis, and is committed to continuing its development to address the inherent uncertainties in its processes. In the near future, the project aspires to introduce new functionality that will enable diagnostic decisions to be reversed based on subsequent information, and to integrate the model with wider healthcare systems for more seamless interactions. Furthermore, the team is exploring two distinct avenues to expand the project's output: by applying the same approach to other types of diseases, and by adapting its diagnostic tool to mobile apps for increased accessibility and efficiency. In this context, the team is working on a mobile version of the diagnostic tool which will be tested on a large scale with general practitioners in the near future. Deep neural networks are utilized for modeling type Ia supernovae based on photometry data and cosmological parameters, but the results show that the inherent variability in the data cannot be captured solely by minimizing the residual between observations and modeling. By formulating the variability as random field noise in the likelihood function, we modify the traditional maximum likelihood training process to include a penalty term that encourages the variation to be coherent on a specific scale. Through this method, the inherent variability in the data is effectively captured. Our framework, applied to the SDSS dataset, yields a 15% reduction in the variance of distance moduli estimates and a 25% reduction in the variance of H0 estimates compared to the standard ML approach. The introduction of the correlation penalty also facilitates the identification of a scale on which the variation is particularly pronounced, at approximately 0.6 in magnitude of SNe velocity. Furthermore, the method improves the prediction of luminosity variability, with a standard deviation of approximately 0.2 mag in the normal extinction law scenario. The application of our approach to other cosmological probes and problems with multiple parameter variations is also discussed. We propose the term 'aeroink' to describe the peculiar oscillatory feature in the velocity scale of variation for SNe Ia, with the potential to be explored further in depth with more sophisticated modeling. Based on our analysis, the 'aeroink' phenomenon does not appear to be related to known physical processes in SNe Ia but could instead be an indicator of the inherent variability limits of the SN explosion process itself. We outline a future research plan to investigate this issue and improve our understanding of cosmological parameter estimation through the analysis of variability in type Ia supernovae. We also write a brief pedagogical introduction to variational Bayesian methods and their application to the modeling of cosmological parameter estimation based on lightcurve data. The utility of our approach in capturing the Coles-Kitching effect is also briefly mentioned. The behavior of a turbulent plume with variable density properties is analyzed, where the properties of the surrounding fluid change over time. By applying the theory of properties dynamics to this analysis, two distinct regimes of entrainment are identified, where the behavior of the plume is significantly influenced by the interplay between its own density properties and those of the surrounding fluid. It is found that when the plume density properties oppose those of the surrounding fluid, increased entrainment occurs due to an alignment of density gradients, whereas when the plume density properties align with those of the surrounding fluid, decreased entrainment occurs due to obstructed alignment. Moreover, the model reveals that the rate of fluid properties change has a profound effect on the characteristics of the plume. Consequently, considering this effect is essential for accurately estimating particle transport in areas where the properties of the surrounding fluid are changing over time. Ultimately, the model provides a comprehensive framework for analyzing and understanding buoyant and turbulent plumes in dynamic environments. In situations where the properties of the surrounding fluid are not variable, a simplified version of the model is developed, which reduces to the widely accepted model for buoyant plumes first proposed by Gross, 1975. Additionally, the model is applied to a diverse range of examples, including fireballs, lake stratification, and volcanic plumes, where the changes in fluid properties lead to unique behaviors and physical processes not explained by previous models. In one such example, it was observed that when the properties of the surrounding fluid oppose those of the plume, increased entrainment occurs, resulting in a phenomenon known as "self-eradication." Furthermore, when the properties of the surrounding fluid align with those of the plume, a phenomenon known as "focusing," where the plume converges and converges further, is experienced. A graph showing the phase space of the plume, where the behaviors of the plume are mapped in relation to the changes in fluid properties, is also presented. The formation of planetary cores is heavily influenced by the magnetic field generated in the protoplanetary disk. Research has revealed that many exoplanets possess a substantial fraction of their stellar flux in chromospheric and magnetic intensities. This discovery raises the possibility that these magnetic fields originated from the star, specifically through the emission of X-rays and UV radiation generated by the star's magnetic activity, rather than being produced within the disk. To better understand this phenomenon, researchers must develop a predictive model of a cool, rapidly rotating star that exhibits surface convection and turbulence stimulating stellar activity.

A new 3D stellar model is introduced, specifically designed to study the activity of rapidly rotating stars in the mass range of 0.9 to 1.5 solar masses. This model distinguishes itself from existing models by incorporating a unique magnetic field module that uses the Steady-State Mean Field Dynamo theory. Through numerical simulations, researchers have managed to include the impact of rotation on the convection zone's structure, surface convection, and turbulence on the global dynamics and magnetic field behavior in these stars.

To verify the accuracy of the model, researchers have conducted zero-age simulations for different rotation rates and compared the results to observational data on the time it takes for these stars to experience their first magnetic flare. The model predicts that rapidly rotating stars in the mass range of 1.0 to 1.4 solar masses will exhibit their first magnetic flare within the first 6.8 million years.

However, this study has uncovered a limitation of the model: more slowly rotating stars take longer to experience their first magnetic flare. This trend is likely influenced by the absence of turbulence in these stars, which reduces their ability to generate magnetic activity. To address this issue, researchers are planning to incorporate the dynamic generation of magnetic fields through the use of kinematic dynamos in future studies.

Ultimately, the primary goal of this research is to understand the relative importance of planetary core dynamo and stellar activity in the generation of magnetic fields. To achieve this goal, researchers must be able to model the time-dependent evolution of core dynamos within protoplanetary disks, as well as the generation of magnetic fields within the star and the core. By doing so, researchers will be able to determine whether stars contribute significantly to the magnetic fields within planets or if these magnetic fields originate from the protoplanetary disk. The development of multi-task learning models has been enhanced through the creation of incrop, a novel method that successfully applies co-evolutionary techniques to address complex problems with multiple inputs and outputs. By utilizing a dual neural network architecture, incrop enables the separation of tasks through a preliminary input stage and subsequent output transformation, facilitating improved performance and efficiency. Through a comprehensive set of experiments, the effectiveness of incrop has been demonstrated across a range of datasets, including the MNIST, EMNIST, and CharDataset, in both single-task and multi-task scenarios, resulting in notable performance enhancements of up to 2.5% in the latter case. By tackling complex multi-input, multi-output problems and yielding superior results compared to existing approaches, incrop embodies a forward-thinking strategy for multi-task learning. The source code for incrop is freely available on GitHub at https://github.com/tunmith/incrop. The underlying repository also contains a copy of this article.

Efforts to check fairness in concurrent systems have been minimal compared to other properties. FairMC2 is a fair model checker that was implemented as a pedagogical tool to teach McMini, a mini-model checker in C, for validating the McSlippery specification from the Slippery Slope series by Lea. However, FairMC2 proved to be slow due to poor performance, taking about 15 minutes to verify a single fairness criterion on a single thread. To rectify this issue, a new, faster model checker, McMini, was developed in assembly language using GNU Light, resulting in a substantial speed upgrade of at least 65x. Despite being significantly faster, McMini lacks instructions for floating point operations and does not support complex data types, thus rendering it unsuitable for checking the McSlippery specification. To overcome this limitation, a new, fair model checker, FairMcMini, was developed from McMini to enable the efficient checking of fairness in concurrent systems, including those with floating point operations. FairMcMini speed surpasses FairMC2 by at least 65x for single-threaded operations and 25x for multi-threaded scenarios. Moreover, it successfully verified all 26 fairness criteria of the McSlippery specification in under 0.7 seconds. To further emphasize the effectiveness of FairMcMini, it successfully validated the standards-defined SPARC semi-fair fairness specifications for the slipperiness-IV program, completing the process in under 0.2 seconds. In addition to its capabilities, FairMcMini also supports the efficient checking of semi-fair concurrent systems. Spoofing countermeasures are an essential component in the development of automatic speech recognition systems. Recently, the quality of these systems has been enhanced by introducing artifact detection as a pre-processing step. Previous methods were limited to identifying artificial speech cues, but neglected the importance of duration-based cues. This paper addresses this gap by proposing a novel deep neural network architecture that effectively captures duration-based speech artifacts across various speech conditions. The core innovation involves incorporating an attention mechanism within the Bi-LSTM framework, allowing deeper extraction of contextual duration-based features. Experimental results on the ASVspoof 2019 database demonstrate the benefits of this approach, with the introduction of attention leading to a 4.5% EER improvement over the existing state-of-the-art duration-based model. Furthermore, combining this method with existing state-of-the-art spoofing countermeasures results in a 6.4% EER improvement on development and testing datasets. Additionally, the study showcases the effectiveness of attention mechanisms in enhancing deep neural networks, highlighting its potential applications in multiple other natural language processing tasks. The code for this work is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/umaneil/attention-based-lstm-for-spoofing-countermeasures for the benefit of the NLP community.

We investigate nonreciprocal optical coherence properties of photon pairs generated through spontaneous four-wave mixing in a silicon microdisk. The coherence functions are reported to exhibit distinct differences based on the pump's propagation direction. The mode consistency, identified through a novel indicator called the mode consistency index, is found to be more pronounced in the horizontal pump setup. The study also reveals that reversing the pump's direction of propagation yields high mode consistency while demonstrating nonreciprocal coherence effects. The observed mode consistency is attributed to the overlap of orthogonally propagating signal modes and the similar coherence functions of adjacent anti-De Sitter pump modes. This research offers a new perspective on the nonreciprocity in micro/nanophotonic systems, paving the way for advanced development of nonreciprocal optical devices. The findings presented can be applied to a broad range of micro/nanophotonic systems capable of nonreciprocity, including silicon-based microdisk resonators, microtoroids, and nanocavities. Furthermore, the study's observations are expected to have implications in the exploration of new nonreciprocal optical functions at the micro/nanoscale. The meta-learning technique of zero-shot classification has gained significant recognition for its ability to extend a model's capabilities across various classes without the need for extensive training. However, when deployed in a federated learning setting, this approach faces the difficulty of coordinating model updates across disparate devices. Even with centralized management, there are challenges associated with accounting for unique data distributions and knowledge gaps across different clients. To address these issues, we introduce Zeroshot FedRL, a novel framework designed to overcome the limitations of traditional zero-shot and federated learning methods. The core idea involves utilizing a meta-learning framework to develop a bias correction module, enabling a model to accurately classify classes encountered for the first time, even on unfamiliar data distributions. The proposed solution relies on a two-step training process using synthetic data and peer-model information, respectively. The former involves leveraging labeled data to train a general-purpose classifier, while the latter involves training on domain-general or peer-specific data distributions. The results show that Zeroshot FedRL achieves significant improvements over current state-of-the-art techniques, including FedAVG and FedProx, in two distinct benchmark settings. The advantages include reduced knowledge acquisition requirements and better generalizability across unseen data distributions and classes. The framework offers numerous practical benefits, including reduced communication costs, lower communication complexity, and the ability to efficiently extend a model's capabilities to new classes and data distributions. The code for the Zeroshot FedRL framework is publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/adi-abdas/Matlearn/tree/main/zeroshot_fedrl for the purpose of replication. The benchmark experiments were conducted using the MNIST and Fashion-MNIST datasets. The former involves a 28x28 feature extractor, while the latter involves a 7x7 feature extractor both with $3 \times 6$ average pooling layers. The output layers of both models were modified to accommodate the zero-shot taxonomy. The models were trained using PyTorch, with the Adam optimizer and 0.01 learning rate.
