This approach is particularly useful for generating entangled states among photons and can be applied in the preparation of green photons from a parametric down-conversion source. Furthermore, this study proposes a method for efficiently measuring the full connectivity of QFT circuits using a minimum number of projective measurements. The proposed framework aims to facilitate the development of robust and connected QFT circuits for practical one- and multi-qubit quantum computing and communication systems. Moreover, this protocol can be used to enhance the generation of entangled photons for quantum communication by exploiting the connectivity present in the QFT process. Current experiments utilizing the Fourier transform process to create connected states among photons are limited to two-photon systems, and the proposed framework aims to expand this capability to high-dimensional multi-photon systems of up to hundreds of photons, facilitating the connection of multiple photons through the efficient application of QFT gates. The efficiency of the proposed measurement method compares favorably with alternative measurement strategies, and the expected output states of the protocol match those of established quantum algorithms such as the Gaussian boson-sampling model. During the COVID-19 pandemic, local newspapers provided their readers with crucial information about health guidelines, infection rates, hospital admissions, deaths, and related policy debates. To understand the scope of local news coverage, we analyzed articles from 449 German newspapers and discovered significant variations among them. Using data on article volume and content, we created a map of 36 metropolitan areas and evaluated the influence of various factors on local news coverage. Our analysis revealed that the article volume in western Germany was higher than in eastern Germany, likely due to differences in reader engagement metrics measured elsewhere. Our assessment of article content showed that certain topics such as sports and culture were covered more strongly in areas with limited pandemic-related new developments. Conversely, articles focusing on politics and economy prevailed in areas experiencing high pandemic-related activity. Our study addressed the issue of local news scarcity by combining article metadata with national broadcast data and revealing patterns in overlapping coverage. Furthermore, we identified areas with local news coverage that appeared underrepresented, which could indicate a need for enhanced pandemic-related coverage. Our study's findings and maps offer insights that can benefit policymakers striving to increase local news coverage, particularly in areas critically lacking it. Systematic extrapolation in training methods seeks to counter the shortcomings of limited data counts by incorporating an auxiliary task that facilitates predictions beyond the initial training data base. Prior studies on systematic extrapolation have demonstrated its capacity to enlarge the range of predictions, but have also revealed a fundamental constraint - they can only make predictions within the scope of the initial training count. To circumvent this constraint, we present a method called Extrapolated Systematic Intrusion (ESI), effective in enabling predictions that surpass the initial training limit. ES I is an innovative approach to systematic extrapolation that not only expands the scope of predictions but also facilitates predictions within the scope of the initial training base with enhanced accuracy. ES I achieves this breakthrough through the integration of a novel auxiliary task, called intrusion detection, designed to counterdata augmentation and facilitate predictions beyond the initial training limit. ES I's validity has been verified in low-resource settings such as modeling long-range dependencies in character-level language modeling and estimating word usage probabilities in the English language. ES I's results show significant improvements in SMILES string generation and the accuracy of word frequency estimation, outperforming a comparative deep learning model in both scenarios. This paper introduces the xorr filter, a highly efficient variant of the Bloom filter designed to reduce memory consumption and acceleration time. The xorr filter leverages XOR operations to generate a unique output, outperforming traditional Bloom filters in terms of both speed and memory usage, while still maintaining similar error rates. The research presents a detailed analysis of the xorr filter's performance, both in comparison to Bloom filters and across varying metric intervals. Moreover, an optimized algorithm is proposed to efficiently invert the xorr filter, demonstrating a significant speedup of up to 20 times over the original inversion method. The presented ideas are anticipated to be useful in environments where bandwidth is restricted and data retrieval speed is critical. The research was stimulated by the challenges encountered in big data analytics, specifically in accelerating the retrieval of sparse non-zero values in large datasets. The proposed solutions were validated through experiments conducted on single-node and distributed environments. The proposed work was implemented using an open-source system called Spara, which employs xorr filters to expedite data retrieval. The open-source implementation of the algorithm, as well as the detailed code, is available on GitHub for public use. The Alexandrov embedding theorem allows for the construction of a convex polytopal structure on the Neron-Severi group classically or the canonical class in special cases, based on a given smooth projective variety's divisor class group. This decomposition is closely tied to the concept of divisorial Zariski decomposition. This article explores the influence of positive divisor class groups on the convexity structure of the Neron-Severi group's Alexandrov body, offering a new perspective on previous research by Mok- Tongai-Yau. Additionally, it establishes essential conditions for preserving convexity, Riemannian geometry methods, and essential questions regarding the decomposition's influence on the divisor class group's symmetry. Furthermore, this article introduces an innovative approach to examining convexity in the Neron-Severi group's Alexandrov body, allowing for a more precise analysis of specific, high-dimensional examples. Utilizing this decomposition, this article converges a new inequality involving the volume of the Alexandrov body of the Neron-Severi group and the volume of the cone over a canonical model of the variety's canonical class, discovering previously overlooked relationships. Based on this discovery, this article introduces an invariant metric on the variety's Neron-Severi group that depends on the divisor class group. Finally, this article closes with a survey of remaining questions and potential future areas of study. These results are initially applied to a specific example involving a quartic surface, demonstrating the theoretical utility of this convexity and its potential applications in algebraic geometry, particularly in the study of the positivity of the canonical class. Lastly, this article explores potential applications in algebraic geometry, including the classification of varieties with specific properties and the identification of particular exceptional cases. One such case studied is that of a specific quartic surface. This research was partially completed at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, under the sponsorship of the Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics at the University of California, Santa Barbara. Additionally, this article credits inspiration and contributions from multiple researchers, including Campana, Dettmann, Hacon, Hyeon, Morgan, Park, Teipel, and Winckler. This research examines the temporal structure of financial markets using previous transaction data from the period 2007 to 2016, focusing on the S&P 500 index. Analyzing the log-return autocorrelations of this data at various time intervals revealed a two-layer power law distribution, with one time scale standing out at around 2.4 days. To understand the origin of this time scale, both mathematical and statistical methods were applied. The results showed that this time scale is driven by frequent small trades, and its amplitude is influenced by the number of these trades. Additionally, an analytical model based on the random walk hypothesis was developed to support this finding. To validate the methodology's reliability, the study confirmed that the observed time scale does not reflect well-known market cycles or events. Furthermore, the results demonstrated that the observed time scale is unique to the S&P 500 index, and its characteristics differ significantly from those of the US dollar against the euro and the Japanese yen. To investigate the possibility that the observed time scale is caused by market participants' decision-making intervals, the study calculated the average time taken by individual traders to make a decision, yielding a value of around 15 minutes for frequent small trades. Based on these findings, the study proposed a new theory of market dynamics, which attributes the observed time scale to the decision-making intervals of market participants. This new theory offers a novel explanation for the existing premise known as the random walk hypothesis. Moreover, the study's results provide significant insights into understanding market behavior and can potentially offer performance improvements for statistical models operating at the time scale of frequent small trades. Lastly, the study's findings highlight the potential for direct application in portfolio investment, portfolio risk assessment, and the potential impact on market dynamics caused by the decisions of market participants operating at this time scale. This is particularly true for automated trading systems using the methodology of technical analysis, which often analyze market data within a short time period. As a result, the decision-making intervals at which market participants operate can influence the trading strategies of automated systems in ways that are difficult to anticipate in advance. FLVoogd guarantees the integrity of uploaded data by only utilizing benign data sent from the devices. To achieve this, this system combines a novel data filtering mechanism with a specialized efficient clustering algorithm. While other solutions exist that integrate federated learning with machine learning applications such as anomaly detection, there is a notable absence of a solution that implements a federated learning approach for voice-activated systems. Building on the success of this integration, our research demonstrates that FLVoogd is an exceptional solution for developing innovative, federated learning-based applications in the future. In addition to this, our proposed solution has successfully enabled the integration of federated learning technology in voice-activated systems, paving the way for a new generation of secure, distributed AI-powered applications. Current deep learning techniques excel in virtual-to-real (v2r) transitions for autonomous driving tasks. However, the widely accepted definition of sim2real transfer is problematic due to conflicting expectations. In this paper, the sim2real transfer is redefined as the performance boost achieved by models in autonomous vehicle challenges, such as the TrackMCAD, when run on real-world datasets in contrast to purely simulated ones. A case study has been conducted to investigate the transfer of state-of-the-art deep learning methods, specifically PointNet, MNAS, and MFC, on the 3D McAD dataset. The study found that these methods demonstrate notable performance gains on real-world datasets, with MFC and MNAS exhibiting notable success and comparable performance to SAE methods, respectively. Moreover, the study discovered that MFC shows a notable advantage in synthetic-to-real transitions and often matches or surpasses the performance of MNAS, contrary to earlier expectations. The study primarily used the 3D McAD dataset but also explored the sim2real transfer on the TrackMCAD. The findings suggest that MFC and MNAS are well-suited for synthetic-to-real transfers and can be effective alternatives to more complex AE-based methods like MFC. As a result, these methods are recommended for autonomous driving applications that involve real-world to synthetic dataset transitions. This research explores the atmospheric variations among Earth-like planets with different masses and distances from their host stars. We analyzed the atmospheric properties of temperate planets and their potential biogenic and atmospheric processes, considering variations in atmospheric composition, atmospheric retention, and potential biosignatures. We discovered that massive atmospheres on close-in planets have distinct compositions, retaining different gases, which could impact the search for life. Close-in planets with weak magnetic fields and small masses are unable to hold onto their atmospheric escape-prone gases, resulting in an absence of these gases in their atmospheres, whereas massive planets with weak magnetic fields are able to retain their atmospheric escape-prone gases, but have reduced levels of other gases. Conversely, distant planets have similar atmospheric compositions, regardless of their mass. We also find that atmospheric escape and biogenic processes have distinct impacts on different gases, resulting in an overall variation in atmospheric composition among temperate planets. We conclude that considering the mass and distance of a planet is essential for understanding its atmospheric processes and potential biosignatures. As a result, planet mass and atmospheric escape should be prioritized in assessments for exoplanet missions. This paper explores the effectiveness of sparse online nonparametric mean estimation in identifying changes in data streams and isolating their underlying causes. We have developed a dynamic clustering approach based on the Isometric Transformations strategy, combined with a time-varying Online Sortino Esimation algorithm. This method enables the detection of data shifts and their associated patterns without prior knowledge of the number of changes or clusters. To evaluate its performance in restricted environments, we have reduced the available computational resources. This reformulation proves efficient and robust, and we have proven its asymptotic convergence under certain conditions. Through extensive simulations and case studies, we have demonstrated its superior performance compared to existing methods. Furthermore, we have successfully applied this approach to real-world data from smart meters and sports analytics to detect anomalies and extract meaningful patterns. These applications showcase the potential of this dynamic clustering method to improve change point detection and failure mode isolation in resource-constrained settings. The accompanying code is available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/damien-loiseau/Sparse-online-estimation-for-change-point-detection.

We've established the most accurate estimates for the formation and merger times of two massive dwarf galaxies that merged with the Milky Way. By analyzing the motion of stars, we discovered evidence of a 200 million year period of formation activity within these dwarf galaxies, specifically Gaia-Sausage Enceladus and Wukong/LMS-1. A crucial factor in training machine learning models is a large dataset of labeled examples. The time-consuming process of data annotation, which often involves a time-consuming and resource-intensive task of data labeling by human workers, is especially challenging. The method of selective labeling allows for reducing the labeling effort by targeting specific, difficult instances in the data for labeling by human workers, much like a supervisor would. The labeling strategy of selective sampling can be implemented in two different approaches - selective sampling based on uncertainty or density. The approach based on uncertainty involves identifying instances with the highest level of uncertainty in the model, which requires a large amount of computational resources but produces a training dataset with high quality. On the other hand, the approach based on density involves finding instances with the highest density values, which is faster in terms of computational resources but produces a training dataset with lower quality. The method of selective labeling has been successfully tested on different machine learning algorithms and tasks including image classification, medical diagnosis, and text sentiment analysis, showing its effectiveness in producing a high-quality labeled dataset through a reduced number of annotations. The results of the experiments reveal that the method of selective labeling based on uncertainty produces the best results compared to the method of selective labeling based on density and the random labeling approach. The results of the experiments also reveal that the method of selective labeling outperforms the state-of-the-art techniques of active learning and semi-supervised learning. The method of selective labeling has several advantages compared to the active learning technique, including the simplicity of computations, the independence from the complexity of the data, and the independence from the type of model used. The method of selective labeling also outperforms the semi-supervised learning technique, showing its effectiveness in producing a high-quality labeled dataset when the data is not labeled at all. The method of selective labeling can be used for different type of data including image, text, audio, video, tabular data among others. Nevertheless, the unconventional exchange interaction stemming from the interface derived from the experimentally measured values of charges, rather than the typically considered atomic distances. Finally, the study proposes that the EuS/InAs interface may serve as an effective platform for the development of novel spintronics devices and the management of unusual spin textures. We establish Borel Wadge determinacy at two levels of strength within second-order arithmetic, demonstrating that it is not only implied by, but also surpasses, the principles of limited and confined comprehension. Furthermore, the proof technique used is novel and unrelated to the proof style of Novak and Wehrle in their proof of projective determinacy from confined comprehension. Our work also reveals that Borel Wadge determinacy is separate from, yet comparable to, the limited set-muchness property and confined comprehension within the projective levels. The notion of Borel Wadge determinacy being expressed in second-order arithmetic with restricted $\mathcal{0}$ and $\mathcal{1}$ symbols serves as a reliable and accurate axiomatic framework for its entire theory of projective sets through segmentation into confined, limited, and weak second-order parts. In the context of reverse mathematics, the second-order principles of confined, limited, and weak second-order parts play the role of a reliable and accurate axiomatic framework for the projective determinacy axioms of $\mathcal{0}$-choice and harmonic unboundedness. The proof style followed in our paper, however, differs from the proof style in Wehrle's thesis, as the current proof style is more in line with the proof style in Montalbán's thesis. In particular, the proof style in our paper is more in line with the proof style in Montalbán's thesis in that it establishes the relevance of a concept to second-order arithmetic through a process of reduction that starts with the concept itself, as opposed to beginning with a stronger theorem that implies the concept. The proof style in Wehrle's thesis, on the other hand, is more in line with the proof style in Novak and Wehrle's proof of projective determinacy, in that the determinant of a set is defined in terms of the set itself in a circular manner and then shown to be stronger than the set's original determinant. The current proof style, however, is more in line with the proof style in Montalbán's thesis in that the concept itself, as opposed to a theorem that implies it, is expressed in second-order arithmetic and then shown to be reducible to a weaker theorem. To overcome the limitations of existing model pruning techniques, we developed ClickTrain, a novel approach for efficient large-scale transformer pruning within pre-training. This method leverages the diversity of permutation space and unsupervised language modeling tasks to accurately preserve important model parameters, which significantly enhances the accuracy of subsequent task-specific models. Experimental results demonstrate ClickTrain's capability to achieve a remarkable 12 times reduction in model parameters while maintaining the accuracy of state-of-the-art models and surpassing traditional pruning methods. Moreover, the inner mechanism of ClickTrain suggests novel applications in the design of unsupervised language model pruning and efficient large-scale transformer architecture. The code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/umazon/ClickTrain.

By introducing a relation algebra generated from the Kriple frames, we derive a natural equivalence relation for the modal languages in question, thereby defining a relational model structure. Furthermore, we demonstrate that every member of the targeted family of substructural modal logics is characterized as having an algebraic and relational representation, achieved through the association of the logic with a particular relation algebra. In turn, this relation algebra determines a maximal conservative expansion of the original substructural property within the larger framework of distributive lattice theory. In addition, we present a separate derivative system for the original substructural properties themselves, achieved via the application of a novel hyperframe framework. This new approach allows us to derive axioms governing the maximal conservativity property in question. By comparing the algebra-relational and hyperframe frameworks, we are able to establish the equivalence of the two constructions, thereby validating the derived characterizations of the targeted logics through the hyperframe framework. In turn, this equivalence proves useful in facilitating proofs within the hyperframe framework that would otherwise be accomplished using the Kriple frame semantics. In addition to presenting these general results and constructions, we utilize our derived characterizations to solve specific logic-related problems within the particular frameworks of the original substructural properties and substructural modal logics, thereby confirming specific decidability and canonicity properties in question. In particular, we confirm canonicity properties for positive modal logic and the infinitary version of the same logic, as well as the canonicity of the modalities within the infinitary version of the same logic. In addition, we confirm the finite model property and the algebraic and relational maximation property within the positive modal logic and the infinitary version of the same logic. Furthermore, we confirm the finite model property and the algebraic and relational maximation property in the infinitary version of the same logic. The discovery of gravitational waves from merging neutron stars in GW170817 revolutionized the field of astrophysics, offering a singularly accessible opportunity to explore the physics of neutron star mergers across multiple spectrums simultaneously. The electromagnetic radiation observed in the days following the GW170817 detection, which included a kilonova and a host galaxy with accompanying supernova properties, provided a newly formed protostar's direct visual presentation and the elements created within its vast envelope. The analysis of the proton and nuclear processes within this protostar, governed by the r-process, offered a crucial aspect of understanding the astrophysical mechanisms driving neutron star coalescence, although the precise r-process conditions remain unknown. The model of this protostar's structure and the created elements, which dictates the course of the protostar's cooling and the properties of the emitted light, relies heavily on two essential elements: the equation of state of nuclear matter and the nuclear interaction processes, both of which are unknown. The observation of neutron star coalescence, therefore, presents a unique challenge to simultaneously uncover the unknown properties of neutron star mergers, the created elements within their mergers, and the nuclear interactions governing those processes, making GW170817 a landmark event in the progression of astrophysics, poised to open a new frontier in the understanding of r-process nuclei. The nuclear physics community, therefore, stands at the threshold of an exciting opportunity to explore novel approaches in the calculation of r-process nuclei and, by extension, the unknown nuclear interactions that govern them. This presents a compelling case to revisit the traditional views on r-process nuclei and to explore cutting-edge nuclear interactions, with the hope of gaining fresh insights into this complex problem. The present article aims to contribute to this endeavor by collecting and summarizing the current knowledge of the r-process, with a focus on the created elements during neutron star coalescence, as exemplified by the GW170817 event. This review will delve into the latest understandings of the r-process, as expressed through various nuclear interplay conditions, while also highlighting the known uncertainties and current debates in the field. The ultimate goal of this article is to serve as a resource and reference for researchers, with a specific focus on the nuclear physics community, on the current state of knowledge of the r-process. TOI-5542b represents a fascinating subject for examining the composition and formation of planets due to its unique properties. This study provides key insights into the planet's radius, density, and equilibrium temperature following data analysis from the TESS spacecraft and spectroscopic observations with the HIRES and SEMINAL instruments. TOI-5542b orbits a near-solar mass star with a 9.78-day period, possesses a large radius of 1.19 $\pm$ 0.03 R$_{\rm Jupiter}$, and has a temperature of 725 $\pm$ 60 K. We determined that TOI-5542b is most likely a gas giant planet with an atmospheric system containing H$_2$O and/or CH$_4$ clouds. This is deduced from analyzing the system's atmospheric and thermal properties using models that account for atmospheric and thermal components. We found that TOI-5542b undergoes rapid heat loss due to energy exchange with its surrounding atmosphere, resulting in an accelerated cooling rate of 40 $\pm$ 10 K/day upon reaching its current elevation. This study also detects spectral indications of atmospheric activity and gas emission from TOI-5542b, which supports our interpretation that the planet resides within the star interaction zone. As a result, we attribute the detected low-frequency oscillations to this asteroid field rather than the planet itself. This research highlights the value of combining optical and near-infrared spectroscopy in detecting signs of atmospheric activity and gas emission in exoplanets. TOI-5542b is an intriguing subject for further observation and study due to its unique status as a'sub-crown' atmosphere-exoplanet system and potential for shedding light on previously overlooked atmospheric processes. Moreover, TOI-5542b offers an opportune case for examining the effects of radiation on exoplanet atmospheres and the evolution of planetary composition and structure over time. Therefore, we suggest that the planet be targeted in upcoming missions focusing on exoplanet spectroscopy, including the JWST and ARIEL programs. This research offers a groundbreaking discovery of atmospheric activity and gas emission in a near-solar mass star planet system, which expands our understanding of exoplanet characterization and points to new areas for future study and research. Moreover, this study proposes a new detection method for exoplanet atmospheric activity and gas emission that can be applied in upcoming studies using data from spectrographic missions, including the JWST, ARIEL, and Habitable Exoplanet Imaging Mission. Our study focuses on uncovering the underlying mechanisms of one neural network's ability to recognize complex mathematical symbols by substituting its original encoder with a simpler k-neighborhood classifier. This approach retains the original encoder, enabling the existing network to function normally. However, with the substitution, we observe a surprising decrease in performance for challenging symbols, but not for easier ones. Through thorough analysis, we reveal that the kNN classifier is capable of effectively eliminating noise in the image, but often fails to accurately distinguish difficult symbols due to reliance on ambiguous input features. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the existing network's ability to generalize well is closely linked to its capacity to reject sub-optimal input representations provided by the encoder. This research not only offers new insights into the existing network but also introduces a novel and effective technique for assessing the quality of feature representations. At its core, this technique is adaptable to a wide array of feature representation methods and can be utilized as a feature design criterion. Additionally, we employ this technique to develop better feature representations by refining both a ConvNet encoder and a Segmentation Network. In the former case, we utilize a controlled search procedure over a limited set of possible ConvNet designs to discover a top-notch encoder. In the latter case, we replace the original encoder in a two-stage process with a kNN classifier and then optimize the network again from scratch using the new feature representations. As a result, we achieve a considerable improvement in performance for the mathematical symbol recognition task. This research not only provides a new perspective on feature representation but also offers a new method for effective extraction, especially in scenarios where the test set is relatively small compared to the training set. This method can be generalized to other feature representation methods and serves as a valuable design criterion for constructing good feature representations. Moreover, this research provides an innovative approach to existing network design - network refinement. Similar to previous studies, we discovered that replacing a network's original encoder with a kNN classifier enables us to refine the network. However, in contrast to previous studies which primarily focused on understanding the mechanisms of a particular network, we took this approach a step further by utilizing the new feature representations to optimize the network again from scratch using a two-stage process. As a result, we achieved a considerable improvement in performance for the mathematical symbol recognition task. We've developed a rigorous mathematical framework for the BPS spectrum of a one-dimensional supersymmetric black hole, with our method overcoming previous limitations in computational efficiency. We've derived an exact formula for the growth of BPS state degeneracies as the number of points on the Hilbert scheme of C^2 increases exponentially. Our results reveal that an initially rapid growth of BPS state degeneracies eventually plateaus and can be fully accounted for by extremal states with energy increasing exponentially. We've conjugate paired these extremal states, leading to a fully saturated notion of the duality. We've introduced a new functional to describe the BPS spectrum, called the F function, which corresponds to a specific sum of terms representing BPS state degeneracies with specified charges. Utilizing our computational efficiency, we've calculated the growth of the F function for the rank one symplectic group, with our results confirming recent predictions made utilizing an alternative mathematical technique called the holomorphic block decomposition. We've derived explicit formulas for the growth of BPS state degeneracies in the rank one symplectic group, with our results agreeing on a general level with previously made predictions. We've explored applications of our method to various other areas, including non-supersymmetric black holes, which can be studied by introducing a non-supersymmetric 'twist' of the Hilbert scheme of C^2. We've discovered novel states, referred to as pseudo-BPS states, which can be studied both with and without the twist. We've proved that the pseudo-BPS states, when incorporated into the F function, provide the full growth of BPS state degeneracies in the rank one symplectic group up to a specified error. We've calculated the growth of BPS state degeneracies in the rank one symplectic group with specified errors for pseudo-BPS states and real-BPS states. Network predictability in epidemic spreading has been examined, focusing on the correlation between network structure and epidemic magnitude. We found that in certain networks, the predictability of epidemic spreading is high when the network structure is highly determined (or 'bridged'), whereas this predictability drops to near zero in networks with undetermined structures. Notably, we found that the transition from high to low predictability is not influenced by the level of disorder in the network but rather by the emergence of a highly connected component within the network. These findings are supported by numerical results from various models of network disorder, including the Poisson model, the clique model, and a network where random and systematic changes in degree are combined. Furthermore, we found that the intensity of epidemic spreading is highly variable in networks with high predictability, whereas it exhibits little variation in networks with low predictability. These findings are verified through numerical analyses of the complete graph, a graph with random degree variations, and a road network in the Sen city area of Nigeria. To evaluate the practical implications of our findings, we found that the level of network disorder that yields high predictability is comparable to the level of disorder that yields high variability in the intensity of epidemic spreading. These results have significant implications for controlling and managing epidemic outbreaks based on network structure. A practical application of our findings has been implemented in the form of a predictive tool for controlling epidemic outbreaks, which is available at https://github.com/aminer-ufz/NetworkPredictability/tree/master/EpidemicControl. Additionally, all code related to the figures in this study can be accessed at the same repository. Furthermore, discussions on the various models of network disorder used in this study can be found at https://github.com/aminer-ufz/NetworkPredictability/tree/master/Notes-on-network-models. A significant challenge in reinforcement learning (RL) arises from the high likelihood of violating safety protocols, which can result in costly rewards and even damage to physical systems. Safety constraints in RL tasks are often addressed through constrained policy methods but at the cost of increased complexity and only improving the overall reward trajectory marginally. Our method utilizes a two-step approach to learn an initial policy with a focus on maximization, while simultaneously developing a backup policy focused on constraint violation prevention through reinforcement learning. Our method exhibits a new technique for transferring knowledge from the initial policy to the backup policy, which demonstrates notable improvements in constraint violation reduction and even occasional enhancements in the overall reward. Our simulations confirm that the proposed method yields notable improvements in constraint violation reduction and, in some instances, reward enhancement. Moreover, the backup policy developed can function independently and serve as a emergency response mechanism in situations where the primary policy is insufficient. Our method is designed to be self-sustaining and can be applied to various RL tasks with multiple equally acceptable optimal policies. We develop a novel approach to identifying twin primes utilizing elliptic curves and their associated 2-Selmer groups, connecting this method to existing algorithms for random primality testing. This connection leverages the impact of the Brauer-Schmidt criterion on 2-Selmer groups and the link between elliptic curve 2-Selmer groups and $2$-base independence via the Brauer-Parker relation. Furthermore, we introduce a computational technique for generating $2$-base independent pairs of elliptic curves over finite fields, enabling the creation of elliptic curve moduli that contain twin prime generators and, consequently, pseudorandomly generated prime numbers. This methodology serves as a tangible manifestation of a broader, computationally intensive search strategy for such pairs of elliptic curves. Additionally, the developed algorithm and associated data sets are designed to facilitate research in elliptic curve cryptography, constructible curves, and the computational aspects of number theory. All code and data have been made publicly accessible. \bigskip

\noindent \textbf{Keywords}: Elliptic curves, 2-Selmer groups, twin primes, elliptic curve cryptography, constructible curves, random primality testing, algorithmic number theory. \bigskip

This paper proposes a dynamic layered control system for mobile robots equipped with sonet sensors, comprising a sensory layer, a local navigational layer, and a global navigational layer. The sensory layer processes data from the sonar sensors to generate a map of the surroundings. The local navigational layer utilizes ultrasonic range finders to calculate the robot's velocity and target point. The global navigational layer applies the Inertial Measurement Unit and optical flow to determine the robot's position and orientation. In this study, we demonstrate the application of our layered control system to the navigation of a mobile platform through a maze. All computational processes take place in real-time, as evidenced by our experimental results. Additionally, we outline a method for integrating the sensory layer with the global navigational layer to calculate the robot's position and orientation. This approach leverages the estimated global position and rotational coefficients of the robot to improve the sensory layer's perception of the surroundings and generate a topological map of the environment. Furthermore, we explore the application of our layered control system to the navigation of a mobile platform through a maze containing a detectable flat ground. This enables the sensory layer to distinguish between the ground and obstacles in the surroundings. Furthermore, we outline a method for integrating the sensory layer with the global navigational layer to calculate the robot's height and position relative to the flat ground. This approach leverages the estimated global position and rotational coefficients of the robot to improve the sensory layer's perception of the surroundings and generate a topological map of the environment. Moreover, we investigated the performance of our layered control system under various faulty conditions affecting the available sensors. In addition to these performance assessments, we conducted a study on the application of our layered control system to the navigation of a mobile platform equipped with a camera instead of sonar sensors. This entails processing video footage to generate a map of the surroundings and detecting obstacles. This study serves as a foundation for forthcoming work where we will delve into the application of our layered control system to the navigation of mobile platforms equipped with event-driven cameras. This promises significant advancements in processing video footage to generate a map of the surroundings and detecting obstacles. This constitutes a promising area of research that we intend to explore in forthcoming work. This paper’s content is original and has not been published previously. In 1987, Tukey demonstrated the truth of certain implications within model theory by utilizing a single powerful tool: a family of partial orders that can be incorporated into any group of sets. This same family of partial orders has since become known as the Tukey-scale. Recent efforts to expand on Tukey's original result led to the development of a generalized scale that includes cardinal characteristics from set theory, such as $\boxdot$ and $g$. This new scale enables the construction of Tukey-type models, which in turn enable the proof of numerous previously unknown implications between various cardinal characteristics in set theory. Furthermore, using this generalized scale, we are able to derive all of the known Tukey-type model theorems and provide an alternative proof of Tukey's original model. Moreover, we establish a method for creating specific types of ideal pairs and refine and extend several previous results on the conservation of cardinal characteristics, while also resolving two longstanding open problems. Ultimately, the applications of the Tukey-scale with models encompass nearly all of the previously known uses of the family of partial orders, while also providing a unified framework for deriving these uses in set theory. This work may be considered an extended tukey-scale with models, which can be used to prove numerous other theorems. In fact, the authors are only aware of two theorems that cannot be proven using this scale. First, a problem from 2007 asks whether every set in a certain class can be divided into sets that are linearly independent from one another. Second, a problem from 2015 asks whether it is possible for every set in a certain class to have a unique maximal independent subset. These two problems have remained unsolved for over a decade and are presented as a central focus of this research. By utilizing a novel concept known as boundless families of partial orders, we are able to provide a partial answer to both of these questions. A family of partial orders is considered boundless if for any set, an independent set can always be constructed that not only has a unique maximal independent subset but also resides within a specific scale. While we establish that boundless families of partial orders are necessary for the truth of both implications, we prove that the first implication holds in the context of set theory with the continuum hypothesis, and further demonstrate that the second implication holds in the context of set theory with a measurable cardinal. In an effort to simplify and refine our findings, we introduce an alternate characterization of the Tukey-scale, showing that the scale is equivalent to a particular type of ideal

We also establish that these subcategories are independent of higher algebraic K-groups of the ring. Our approach to detecting abusive content on Twitter is centered around a convolutional neural network that processes embeddings from a pre-trained word model, as well as a network of globally connected basic elements. This architecture operates in a semi-supervised environment, capable of handling out-of-vocabulary words. Capable of handling words not in the training data, our model earned a macro F1 score of 0.82 on the Jigsaw Unicyclus abusive language detection challenge, outperforming the benchmark by a 0.04 score point. In addition to our main model, we assessed the effectiveness of various supplementary techniques such as vector pooling methods, domain-specific word models, and ensemble strategies. These explorations aimed to enhance our detection results. Furthermore, we investigated the technical aspects underlying these methods with a particular focus on their applicability to similar semi-supervised tasks. One major discovery made was the development of a domain-specific word model for Twitter, designed to mitigate domain shift, as well as the testing of various vector pooling techniques to combine word and sentence-level embeddings. Ultimately, we found that our initial model proved more effective than these supplementary strategies. A typical challenge in computed tomography imaging arises from noise with varying levels and characteristics across different regions of the image. Current filter-based noise reduction methods are primarily designed to address a single type of noise and often prioritize preserving the image's original edge structure, but fall short in addressing multiple noise types and optimizing the reconstruction of image details. In contrast, we introduce a new model that efficiently removes various noise types during a single training process and also optimizes the reconstruction of image details. The core of this model lies in an image reconstruction residual that utilizes a computationally efficient difference between the predicted and original images, as well as a novel transform-specific prior that enables the removal of different noise types through a single transformation step. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model in accurately removing Poisson and Gaussian noises, outperforming existing methods in terms of image quality and edge preservation. We also show that the proposed model achieves the best results even when the original image is not available, utilizing the predicted image instead. Furthermore, the proposed model proves to be resilient to changes in CT projection data, making it suitable for various applications including low-dose computed tomography imaging and image denoising. The effectiveness of the proposed model is further validated through the analysis of its hyperparameters and the visualization of its predicted images. Previous studies have explored Bayesian Program Learning (BPL) in generating pen trajectories for writing tasks. While BPL produces coherent outputs, the programs it learns are typically defined by a set of fundamental actions such as moving up or down. The quality of these outputs relies on the accuracy of prior assumptions about the programs. The issue with BPL lies in its limitation of learning a comprehensive set of prior assumptions about programs. To overcome this challenge, we developed a novel BPL approach called Hierarchical BPL (H-BPL), which enables the learning of a comprehensive set of prior assumptions. The H-BPL approach is organized into two layers. The first layer is similar to traditional BPL, while the second layer is a knowledge layer that is learned independently, allowing it to be more agile. The outcome of the first layer is then used as input to the second layer, which is similar to how hierarchical models work. The H-BPL approach is tested on a handwriting task and compared to a non-hierarchical BPL approach. The results show that H-BPL converges faster and produces better output quality, especially in situations where there is limited data available. The quality of the output is measured by how closely it matches human-like handwriting. The results show that H-BPL is capable of generating human-like handwriting from minimal data samples, while also reducing the number of data samples required by 25%. The resulting output quality of H-BPL is found to be on par with BPL, while also providing more realistic prior assumptions about programs. I suggest an efficient method to store the potential energy surfaces (PES) of three-nucleon interactions (3NI) in a compact form, enabling faster retrieval of required elements for quantum many-body calculations. This approach involves breaking down the 3NI PES into distinct components based on the angular momentum of the particles involved, then representing each component with reduced computational resources. By doing so, the memory requirements of this scheme are significantly lower than those of standard methods. Furthermore, I outline a straightforward strategy to accomplish this task using existing angular momentum code, as well as the related computational costs. Lastly, I compare the storage efficiency of this scheme with traditional methods. This innovative storage scheme has the potential to greatly simplify the handling of 3NI for extensive many-body calculations, particularly in light of upcoming high-performance computing facilities. Its application may also be adapted for other long-range interactions in physics, encompassing van der Waals forces and the Color-Radiation Pressure force. This technique can be applied to the computation of low-lying energy and charge separation in nuclear and neutron matter via intra-nucleon interactions. Its efficiency makes it suitable for large-scale simulations in astrophysics and nuclear physics, such as neutron stars, nuclear clusters, and certain processes within nuclei. In this research, we investigate the properties of composition operators within the weighted Bergman space of a bounded convex domain with smooth boundaries. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the compactness of these operators when the domain's boundaries feature non-trivial analytic discs. Additionally, we develop criteria for the injectivity and surjectivity of composition operators and examine the essential norms of these operators. Furthermore, we explore specific domains whose composition operator spectra can be precisely determined. Specifically, we consider the following cases: (1) the Poincaré disk, (2) the bidisk, and (3) the 3-dimensional solvable flat Hermitian manifold with the appropriate Euclidean radius. Ultimately, we conclude with a list of unresolved questions and possible directions for further investigation. As a key step in our analysis, we leveraged a boundary estimate of the first author with K. Clank, P. Pflug, and M. Sakhnini to understand the behavior of the composition operator when the boundaries feature non-trivial analytic discs. Additionally, we utilized the big Picard theorem and the characteristics of composition operators within the weighted Bergman spaces to derive our conditions for compactness, injectivity, and surjectivity. Furthermore, we applied the domain's convexity characteristics and the dimension of its boundary analytic discs to derive specific conditions for the compactness of composition operators within the weighted Bergman space. One of the primary findings of this research is that the compactness of a composition operator is solely determined by the boundaries of the domain it operates upon, a characteristic that distinguishes it from the hyperbolic nature of the domain. In a related study, we investigated the properties of the essential norms of composition operators and derived precise formulas for specific domains, including the Poincaré disk, the bidisk, and a flat Hermitian manifold with the appropriate Euclidean radius. Ultimately, we concluded with a list of unresolved questions and possible directions for further investigation in the field of composition operators within the weighted Bergman spaces of bounded convex domains. These questions not only deepen our understanding of the subject at hand but also open the door to possible future research in the field. We have discovered and proved two specific neighbour-transitive code-related hypotheses regarding this pencil of spreads in such quadrangles. Our proof strategy involves establishing the existence of a particular neighbour-transitive code in a specific generalized quadrangle and then demonstrating its relation to existing code theories. Our investigation into the second hypothesis, however, encountered obstacles and was only partially resolved. We have found existing neighbour-transitive codes that violate the conjectured condition in quadrangles W_(2)(3d) and W_(3)(2d), but a complete code for W_(2)(5) remains to be found. Our research also reveals the existence of a specific neighbour-transitive code in the quadrangle W_3(2), known as the Ford-Wolf code, consisting of 65 spreads, which cannot be split into the required two equal sub-spreads. Nonetheless, we managed to find a distinct pencil of spreads with 64 elements, proving the conjecture for this particular quadrangle. Moreover, our research allowed us to develop an efficient algorithm for searching neighbour-transitive codes in generalized quadrangles and a specific neighbour-transitive code in the quadrangle W_4(2) consisting of 65 spreads. We introduced a new approach to examine the two-dimensional structure of the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) using a hierarchical method that evaluates the anisotropy of density patterns across varying scales. To achieve this, we applied a two-dimensional extension of the Reynolds decomposition technique to analyze the 12CO(2-1) velocity field from the Hi-GAL survey. Our findings reveal that the CMZ's density structure exhibits increasing anisotropy on smaller scales, where it shows similarities to the anisotropy of star-forming regions within the inner 10 pc. Additionally, we observed a decrease in anisotropy at larger scales, where it resembles the anisotropy of large-scale molecular clouds. We compared the anisotropy levels in the CMZ with respect to specific scales to that of nearby power-law anisotropy surfaces. We found that the CMZ shows similar anisotropy properties on larger scales (specifically at 220 pc) but displays more pronounced anisotropy on smaller scales (specifically at 8.5 pc) compared to these power-law surfaces. We discussed several factors that may account for the anisotropy properties of the CMZ, including its dynamic history, magnetic field direction, and impact of anisotropic radiation fields. We proposed that the CMZ's anisotropy structure could serve as a key line of inquiry to explore the effects of dynamic processes and evolutionary history on the formation and evolution of molecular cloud complexes. We further suggest that the CMZ's anisotropy properties may reflect its unique star-forming history and the presence of supernova explosions and massive star clusters. We conclude that the CMZ offers a unique and fascinating system to study anisotropy in an HII region and the larger-scale molecular cloud environment. We reserve the name 'R-Reynolds Anisotropy Regions' (R-ARs) for regions or systems that exhibit anisotropy in an HII region environment. We suggest that a comprehensive study of R-ARs could provide valuable insights into the unique star-forming history of these regions and the process of star cluster formation within them. We look forward to exploring and studying anisotropy in other key astrophysical systems such as circumstellar discs, starless cores, and Galactic bulge stars. We reserve the name 'A-Astrophysical Anisotropy Regions' (A-ARs) for regions or systems that exhibit anisotropy in an astrophysical context.

A superconducting temperature sensor was developed using a single cryogenic property gauge and a single-wire resistive temperature detector, serving as a model for a more accurate temperature measurement method. The measurement technique is influenced by two electrical currents flowing through the detector at the same time, resulting in two distinct voltage readings that relate to temperature in different ways. By applying the nonlinear response of the detector in an innovative way, the relationship between the two voltage readings and temperature becomes linear, allowing for accurate temperature measurement within the range of 1 to 4 Kelvin. The response linearity of the sensor was confirmed to be better than 0.25 percent. The resolution and accuracy of the temperature sensor are comparable to those of high-end commercial temperature sensors, with a measured inaccuracy of 0.15 percent at 1 Kelvin and 0.3 percent at 4 Kelvin. The temperature sensor provides stable readings over time, with no noticeable drift within a 24-hour period and an inaccuracy stability of 0.04 percent. The development of this temperature sensor is crucial for the successful operation of quantum devices in circuit model simulations and for achieving high efficiency in quantum information processing. The technique is versatile and can be applied to other temperature detectors with nonlinear properties, as well as those with entirely different responses to temperature changes. Additionally, the principle of this temperature measurement method can be adapted for use in temperature measurement applications at higher temperatures. Furthermore, the idea of employing two electrical currents in parallel to measure temperature has broad applications beyond the described superconducting temperature sensor. Recent research has focused on developing online algorithms for creating spanners, with the goal of reducing the distance between nodes in a graph while also controlling the number of added edges. Specifically, this study investigates the distance between added edges, with the goal of achieving a constant factor closer to the optimal minimum spanning tree distance, and finds that the expected distance of an algorithm given a random set of nodes in a d-dimensional Euclidean graph is within a constant factor of O(log^2 n / \Delta_d) of the optimal, where \Delta_d is the minimum spanning tree edge ratio in dimension d. The previous best distance, \Delta_d = O(log n), was given by a 2019 paper that used a different and more complex algorithm. The new result improves the distance, \Delta_d = O(log^2 n), while still maintaining the same level of computational efficiency, and gives new lower bounds on the distance, \Delta_d, in various dimensions. The same algorithm also provides the best known distance, \Delta_d = O(log n), in 2-dimensional Euclidean spaces. The study further develops and improves existing lower bounds on the distance, \Delta_d, in 3-dimensional Euclidean spaces. The new results show that the distance, \Delta_d, in 3-dimensional Euclidean spaces can be at most 14.35 times worse than the optimal, a significant improvement over the previous best bound, 18.44. The study also investigates and develops new bounds on the competitive ratio of online algorithms for creating spanners in Euclidean spaces, and finds that the competitive ratio of a 2019 algorithm that uses Steiner points is within a constant factor of O(log n / \Delta_d^*) of the optimal, where \Delta_d^* is the minimum steering ratio in dimension d, and nearly achieves this bound in 2-dimensional Euclidean spaces. However, the study finds that increasing the dimension increases the difference between the competitive ratio, \Delta_d, and the optimal steering ratio, \Delta_d^*. This study investigates the pitfalls in cost-based classification approaches that factor in individual device costs but disregard the overall risk. We define risk as the sum of harmful consequences stemming from device misclassification and introduce a realistic cost model for IoT devices. We identify a critical condition under which nearly optimal risk-free classifications are also guaranteed to be optimal in terms of total cost. Furthermore, we demonstrate that in many cases, minimal-risk classifications do not automatically guarantee minimal total costs. We propose a new method to achieve cost-aware classification with minimal risk and confirm its near-optimal status through analysis. Additionally, full extension formulas for our risk and cost metrics are derived, enabling the computation of their values. We compare the efficiency of these formulas with brute-force methods and show that they result in a negligible time complexity difference. We implement and test our approaches using a subset of 101 devices from the Cont containment approach and examine their performance using real-world IoT devices. We also evaluate the impact of device cost precision on the quality of our formulas and the methods proposed in the study. We found that using devices with unique labels but varying costs in their cost structures often results in a complex and computationally demanding classification process; however, reducing the cost precision can significantly and practically improve the classification efficiency while resulting in only a moderately better outcome. We found that our method performs nearly optimally in many scenarios and achieves approximately 70% of the optimal outcome on average. One such application shows that every finite forest can be represented as the free G\^odel algebra on a specific set associated with its topmost branch nodes, which has a dual relationship with the forest itself.  Another application demonstrates that the free distributive lattice on a given set can be represented as the free G\^odel algebra on the same set, which has a dual relationship with the lattice itself.  This in turn provides a generalization of earlier results that established a duality between finite distributive lattices and finite forests, as well as a duality between finite norm algebra and finite trees. The DINO self-supervised method recently gained attention for its impressive performance without any external signals like temperature scheduling or momentum, and achieved comparable results to DREAMER in few-shot classification on ImageNet, outperforming other self-supervised approaches with similar few-shot capabilities while requiring significantly fewer attempts to converge. Notably, DINO's efficiency came at the cost of slightly poorer self-supervised representation quality compared to its counterparts, but demonstrated a clear connection between its training objectives and this reduction in quality. In an effort to improve the representation quality without altering the convergence dynamics, we present a straightforward technique based on regularization that significantly enhances DINO's performance by preventing the collapse of features and improving the discriminability of the method. When evaluated on ImageNet, our approach leads to a 10.1% top-1 accuracy without the need for pre-training on ImageNet, surpassing the previous DINO best few-shot performance by a 8.3% margin. Moreover, our technique proves to be an effective remedy for the weakly-learningable transforms like ViT, even after being fine-tuned on ImageNet. We also show that by combining the DINO self-supervised method with external signals, our approach can achieve state-of-the-art performance in 1-shot and 5-shot tasks on ImageNet, outperforming the DINO best few-shot performance by a 8.6% and 6.3% respectively. Our code will be publicly available at https://github.comfacebookresearchDINO-SELF-SUPervised. Our experiments also show that the self-supervised method can serve as an effective pre-training for the transformers, and the improvement in the representation quality translates to better downstream performance when the self-supervised method is used as a pre-training technique. Our findings also suggest that the self-supervised method can be effectively combined with external signals such as self-guided or pseudo-labels for better convergence dynamics. We present the details of our technique, referred to as DINO-SUP, in a companion paper at ICML 2023. We introduce Stable Artist, an innovative tool that empowers users to deeply manipulate the creation of artificial images. Building upon the strengths of Classless CLAM, Stable Artist streamlines the artistic process, allowing users to produce unique images with just a few intuitive adjustments or by defining preferred characteristics. This breakthrough is possible due to an advanced method of exploring the underlying space of latent variables, enabled by a dynamic sampling of the posterior distribution through conditional generation. This approach detects artistic features at a detailed level and enables users to express preferences regarding the subject's pose, expression, clothing, and more. Consequently, users can create a wide array of artistic pieces with ease. Stable Artist's capabilities are demonstrated through user-created images and comparisons with other state-of-the-art methods. The project is open-sourced at https://github.com/alex1911/stable-artist.

Deep learning predictive models often rely on excessive overconfidence despite straightforward measures available to mitigate this issue. To address this, we introduce a novel approach of quantifying uncertainty in the predictive distribution. This method utilizes heavy-tailed Student's t-distribution to capture the variability in the prediction process, with the goal of understanding the uncertainty as a combination of noise and structural uncertainty. We develop a computationally efficient approach to estimate the uncertainty by incorporating a Bayesian perspective on dropout-based regularization. This method enables accurate quantification of the predictive distribution's uncertainty without necessitating the maintenance of a full posterior, thereby yielding predictions with reduced overconfidence. In various experiments, the proposed method outperforms the existing state-of-the-art approaches in classifying images, detecting objects, and generating text. This method can be applied reliably in the presence of independent and identically distributed data. In the online setting, where data is not iid, we observe improvements but to a lesser extent. This method also offers a versatile framework for general uncertainty quantification in machine learning, with the potential for integration with other methods. Furthermore, this method does not necessitate the use of reinforcement learning or information theoretic approaches to quantify uncertainty. We introduce a new approach for integrating this method with generative adversarial networks, thereby enabling the estimation of the predictive distribution's uncertainty. This method outperforms the existing state-of-the-art approaches in the tasks of generative model evaluation and reinforcement learning, with the prediction of remote objects in simulated autonomous driving being a notable demonstration of its effectiveness. The PPT square conjecture is widely believed to hold true in the realm of finite-dimensional spaces. Assuming its validity, a previously proposed characterization of entanglement-assisted local operations and classical communications (OCC) without cloning (EALO-CNC) in dimension 4+4 using the square channel is demonstrated to be overdefined. Specifically, it is shown that the set of EALO-CNC 4+4 can be generated by only four independent local operations, not ten as previously suggested. Furthermore, it is shown that the set of EALO-CNC in dimension 2+2 using the triangle channel is also overdefined, reducing its defining length from seven to three. These results provide a complete characterization of EALO-CNC in dimensions 2+2 and 4+4 using the triangle and square channels, respectively. The link between the PPT square conjecture and the structure of free independent partial order sets in finite dimensions has also been established. Additionally, it is shown that the minimal generating length of EALO-CNC in dimension 8+8 using the triangle channel is either three or four, and that the set of EALO-CNC in dimension 8+8 using the triangle channel is equivalent to the set of local operations and classical communications (OCC) 8+8 using the triangle channel. These findings build on previous work by Govia and Raeside and provide a complete characterization of OCC 2+2, 4+4, and 8+8 using the triangle channel. Moreover, it is shown that the set of OCC 4+4 using the triangle channel is equivalent to the set of entanglement-assisted local operations and classical communications (EALO-CCC) 4+4 using the triangle channel. Furthermore, it is shown that the set of OCC 8+8 using the triangle channel is equivalent to the set of EALO-CCC 8+8 using the triangle channel. These results demonstrate that OCC is closed under the triangle channel in finite dimensions of at least 8. Discussion and conclusions are presented in the final section. Current learning methods for fraud detection are restricted to specific types of transactions (e.g., credit card, bank account). The typical approach of using a fixed-sized node set in graph learning methods limits the analysis to a single transaction type, making it impossible to generalize to other transactions. To overcome these limitations, we introduce the concept of modular graph learning for transaction-type agnosticism. First, we establish a set of rules for generating valid banking graphs from transaction data. Then, we develop a novel graph generation method that incorporates constraint propagation to ensure generated graphs conform to these rules. The method consists of two parts: a neighborhood explorer for generating the graph structure and a node updater for enhancing the generated graphs. Finally, we obtain the graph labels (normal or fraudulent) through a basic learning algorithm. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated on two large datasets, achieving performance comparable to state-of-the-art techniques on credit card transaction validation and bank account transaction fraud detection. Notably, our method generates valid banking graphs that can facilitate the generalization to multiple transaction types. In the context of novae and other celestial events involving binary systems composed of a white dwarf and a massive companion, a significant portion of the white dwarf's mass is transferred through a process of thermally driven diffusion. This mass transfer contributes substantially to the formation of an accretion disc around the companion star before it is ingested by the black hole, with the rate of mass loss potentially reaching levels important in the evolution of binary systems within the required timescales. To further clarify the phase known as the phase just before the black hole acquires a substantial accretion disc, as well as the process by which a white dwarf accumulates sufficient mass to trigger this phase, we have revisited the relevant stability criteria in the equilibrium of a binary system. This transformation marks the point at which a white dwarf either gains a critical mass to trigger this phase or loses a substantial portion of its mass as part of a mass transfer that facilitates the development of an accretion disc around the black hole. A widely used approach to deblurring images involves restoring them using their sharp version, which is often obtained through a reverse process involving the blurring step. Nonetheless, since blurring is not inversible in general, finding an accurate sharp version remains a challenge. A common technique for addressing this issue involves incorporating additional information from real-world blurring mechanisms, such as motion, but applying an inverse motion to obtain the sharp version remains non-trivial when the blurring mechanism is ambiguous. To overcome this limitation, a novel method is presented in this study, starting with the observation that the commonly employed pre-blurred proxy can be improved by removing the blurring effect that was previously incorporated. To achieve this, the paper introduces a module called reblurring module (RBM) that serves as a direct opposite to blurring, allowing two pathways: a non-parametric path using pre-blurred proxy with reduced blurring and a guided path using edge guidance, both of which lead to a more effective deblurring outcome compared to existing methods. Additionally, the study shows that combining deblurring with defocusing results in a more natural and less over-smoothed result, as well as improved restoration performance. Extensive experiments are conducted to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Code is available at https://github.com/Chen-Esmon/EsmonDeblurring. 

The image deblurring problem has seen significant advancements in recent times, but a major challenge still existing is that existing methods often over-smooth the image when the blurring effect is ambiguous. To address this issue, a novel approach called EsmonDeblurring is presented in this study, starting with the observation that the proxy to the deblurred image, the sharp version, can be accurately obtained by removing the incorporated blurring effect. To achieve this, the proposed method incorporates a module called reblurring module (RBM) that serves as a direct opposite to blurring, allowing two pathways: a non-parametric path using pre-blurred proxy with reduced blurring and a guided path using edge guidance. By accurately removing the incorporated blurring effect, the proposed method achieves a more effective deblurring result compared to existing methods. Furthermore, the study shows that combining deblurring with defocusing results in a more natural and less over-smoothed result, as well as improved restoration performance. Extensive experiments are conducted to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Code is available at https://github.com/Chen-Esmon/EsmonDeblurring.

Recent research applies chemical reaction networks (CRNs) to simulate autonomous systems, drawing parallels with neuronal behavior. Yet, the primary focus centers on the emergence of intelligent behavior, neglecting the computational underlying principles of these biological neurons. This paper explores the fundamental properties of a CRN-based model capable of autonomous learning, similar to neuronal behavior, but with a twist: this model relies on a novel molecular system that facilitates the efficient representation of numerical data, thus addressing the aforementioned gap in the literature. Next, we examine a specific CRN realization of this model and demonstrate how two distinct networks can be derived from it, each capable of supporting two different types of numerical data representations. Furthermore, we investigate the conditions necessary for these networks to exhibit autonomous learning, which involves making predictive decisions based on external signals. Finally, we discuss the prospects for experimental validation and the potential for designing reaction pipelines that make predictive decisions in real-time. Overall, this work highlights the various avenues for research at the intersection of learning theory and reaction chemistry. Moreover, the study showcases the unique challenges and opportunities presented by CRNs that are both intelligent and computationally understudied. As a result, this research takes a novel approach in this domain, offering a fresh perspective on this fascinating field. The recent surge in sequence-to-sequence models has led to considerable enhancements in tree parsing tasks. Nonetheless, existing self-training techniques that fine-tune pre-trained models using tree-structured annotations are hampered by their reliance on accurate gold parsing labels. To address this limitation, we introduce a training algorithm called Deep Contextualized Self-training (DCST) that adapts self-training for these tasks. By utilizing the contextualized representations from pre-trained models, DCST enhances its robustness against noisy tree annotations. DCST arranges the training process into distinct phases - an initial phase of robust feature extraction, followed by fine-tuning the parser using the extracted features. In addition, DCST leverages transfer learning to enhance the robustness of the model. We evaluate DCST on six tree parsing tasks and the results demonstrate its efficacy in overcoming the current self-training limitations, achieving comparable performance to the state-of-the-art unsupervised model without relying on gold parsing labels. Moreover, DCST achieves an average 9.3% relative improvement over the baseline unsupervised model. In some cases, DCST's performance surpasses the unsupervised model by as much as 44.3%. When combined with transfer learning, DCST's improvements total 17.8% relative improvement. We investigate the projective complexity theory (CPT) within a finite field framework. Our work generalizes a fundamental result by Lipton and Reingold, demonstrating that a projective reduction exists between two variables' unordered linear equations over a finite field of prime order p, whenever the size of the equations in question exceeds a p-dependent bound. We establish a similar reduction for equations involving up to k variables, though only under the condition that the field's order p be sufficiently large in relation to k. Additionally, we prove that the class of solvable k-variable unordered linear equations over a prime order p field is CPT-definable within a specific parameter range. An n-tuple is considered nontransitive if there are at least two options, A and B, where using the first element of A and the last element of B in a sequence generates a new, distinct option. We investigate the probability that randomly selected n-tuples exhibit transitivity in both dimensions up to a large, specific c. Notably, recent research by Brightway and Vardi had suggested that the probability of a single nontransitive n-tuple component should approach 1/3 as n approaches infinity, a claim we formally reject by demonstrating that value. We also explore similar probabilities for two-dimensional n-tuples and find that the likelihood of a randomly selected nontransitive n-tuple being transitive in both dimensions should approach 1/2 in the limit as n approaches infinity. We further analyze the probability distribution of the number of transitive components within randomly selected n-tuples and show that this probability distribution should approach a specific, well-defined distribution as n approaches infinity, a distribution which can be solved analytically and which we then use to calculate the probabilities of n-tuples being transitive in both dimensions and also in one dimension. We conclude by investigating the probability distribution of the number of transitive n-tuples and show that this probability distribution should approach a specific, well-defined distribution as n approaches infinity, a distribution which can be solved analytically and which we then use to calculate the probabilities of n-tuples being transitive in both dimensions and also in one dimension.
