The proliferation of software configurations and options has significant implications for a program's performance, with many of these options ultimately being unused in real-world scenarios. A study of the NUPENET project revealed that approximately 30-50% of options are not enabled during run-time, necessitating an uninstalling or removal of them to enhance the system's performance. Unfortunately, the current state of research is characterized by the absence of efficient and effective strategies for detecting and removing inactive options. This paper aims to address this gap by introducing SORPTEA, a approach designed to detect and remove inactive dependencies in a network of software configurations. SORPTEA's key features include a dynamic prediction method that uses past system statistics, a real-time adaptation mechanism to modify system behaviors, and a empirical validation of the approach through the analysis of actual examples from the NUPENET project. The findings reveal that SORPTEA is capable of accurately identifying inactive dependencies in a network of software configurations with high precision and can be applied effectively to various types of system behaviors. Additionally, the results show that removing the detected inactive options using SORPTEA leads to significant performance gains, with an average improvement of 14.5% and up to 80% in some cases for the tested systems. The potential benefits of removing inactive options include enhanced system performance, reduced memory usage, and decreased susceptibility to security vulnerabilities. The approach presented in this study can serve as a foundation for future enhancements in this area, with potential applications including but not limited to, active software systems, data analysis, and other domains. The code underlying SORPTEA is publicly available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/zhenghu1/SORPTEA. The NUPENET project, from which the data used to validate the approach was obtained, can be accessed at https://nupenet.org. A novel approach to quantum teleportation is explored, leveraging entangled anti-polariton qubit states in cavity QED for increased convenience and simplified understanding in quantum information processing. In this methodology, entangled anti-polariton states are generated via strong coupling with a two-level emitter, followed by non-resonant interaction with a quantum memory that preserves excitation in the emitter. In contrast to traditional methods, crystalline optical nonlinearity is not required. Simulations demonstrate that fidelity in this teleportation process surpasses that of the conventional setup utilizing horizontally polarized qubits. Furthermore, quasi-degenerate qubits are shown to be effective in this teleportation process, addressing potential creation challenges of entangled entitites with a large energy gap. Lastly, this method is also shown to be a viable means of generating entangled qubits, offering opportunities for applications such as quantum cryptography and testing Bell's inequality. This work lays the groundwork for the utilization of entangled anti-polariton states in quantum information applications.

In systems where active forces play a significant role, there has been a significant shift towards studying non-equilibrium states and the associated fluctuations. The presentation focuses on the distinct fluctuations exhibited by two types of potentials - harmonic and anharmonic - in a specific active force setting. The analysis also explores the possibility of mimicking the behavior of anharmonic potentials using their harmonic counterpart, with the ultimate goal of better understanding the unique properties of active anharmonic systems and their potential links with phase transitions and stability. Despite presenting a compelling case that fluctuation properties can serve as a key indicator of system dynamics, the findings revealed that fluctuation behavior alone may not be sufficient to establish connections between different configurations of active systems. The presentation concludes by highlighting the need for further investigation into the fluctuation response of active systems, suggesting that exploring this area further could yield valuable insights into their behavior and properties. The underlying ideas were presented in a conference presentation and the associated content is now being shared in this report. In this report, we examine fluctuations in systems with active forces, which exhibit unique characteristics. A novel approach is presented for calculating these fluctuations, which demonstrates that systems with active forces display distinct fluctuations when compared to their passive counterparts. This analysis focuses on the fluctuations of oscillators subjected to an anharmonic or harmonic potential, embedded in a dynamic environment that varies unpredictably. Two notable findings emerge from this investigation. Firstly, the fluctuations associated with anharmonic and harmonic potentials behave differently, despite both potentials exhibiting discrete, stable states. Secondly, the fluctuations of the anharmonic potential can be distinguished from those of the harmonic potential, even within a limited range of excitation levels. Interestingly, the fluctuations associated with the harmonic potential may be induced by adjusting a parameter linked to its anharmonic counterpart. This occurs when the excitation level is adjusted to the point at which the anharmonic potential transitions into its stable state. Notably, this report does not rule out the possibility that the fluctuations of the harmonic potential may be triggered by minor vibrations when the excitation levels are low. In the domain of multi-task reinforcement learning, the development of a unified framework called Multi-task Simulate-and-Train (MaST) has been established. MaST employs a single learned dynamics model to transition between various tasks through context manipulation and simulated trial runs. However, our research reveals a novel issue with MaST: cross-task transfer learning can result in the emergence of task-conflicting policies, which negatively affect performance in a zero-shot setting. To address this challenge, we introduce the Contextual MaST framework, which preserves the benefits of a unified model while mitigating the development of conflicting policies. We achieve this goal by integrating task context with state features and implementing a regulator using a context-invariant value function, thereby successfully preventing the transfer of context across tasks. The results of our experiments confirm the efficacy of our approach in preventing overfitting and promoting transfer learning within tasks. Additionally, the Contextual MaST framework outperforms the baseline MaST model in zero-shot and few-shot settings. The obtained expressions are valid for all values of the system parameters and do not rely on vanishing perturbations, enabling their use in realistic scenarios where the perturbation remains significant. Furthermore, we provide explicit expressions for the efficiency and output power in terms of the system parameters for two specific scaling cases and demonstrate that the expressions for these metrics align with previously published results when the perturbation is small. Additionally, we validate the third law of thermodynamics by analyzing the residual entropy in detail. The derived analytical formulas for the scaling parameter, efficiency, and output power may be useful in studying non-perturbative systems and could have promising applications in micro- and nano-scale energy conversion systems. Lastly, we explore the maximum output power of the system as a function of the scaling parameter and other parameters, including the temperature ratio and mean emittance, and illustrate the distinct behaviors of the system under varying scaling conditions. The obtained results provide a foundation for designing scaling methods to optimize heat engines and enable the exploration of new non-perturbative scaling techniques. We introduce a family of parametric piecewise affine maps with coding theory ties, whose intrinsic coding lattices mirror a subset of the Dyck lattices. We show the topological endomorphisms of these lattices form a parameterized version of the Morita classification, analogous to the de la Harz classification in non-quantum rank one lattices. We explore connections to the study of singularities and other topological features, while also examining the natural embedding of these spaces into the full Dyck lattices. Additionally, we outline potential applications, such as measuring the distance between subshifts, identifying topological properties, and understanding various limits, including the quantum Hall effect and thermodynamic limits. We use the distance formula to study the topology of the space of piecewise affine maps and demonstrate the existence of a scaling limit that corresponds to a recently proposed 'universal theory' of natural coding spaces. This 'universal theory' is shown to be unique and invariant up to a specified equivalence relation, and we also establish the existence of an action by the 'universal theory' group on the space of consistent assignment maps, as well as the existence of a scaling limit that corresponds to a previously studied 'universal theory' of natural coding spaces. Furthermore, we show the distance formula to be invariant under a scaling limit, and demonstrate the existence of a 'universal scheme' that describes the natural coding spaces for a large class of dynamical systems, including subshifts with a local product structure and infinite imprimitivity systems. In particular, we apply the universal scheme to study the natural coding spaces of the works of Rauzy and Arnoux-Cordoba, and we also outline potential applications and future research directions. Finally, we conclude with some open questions and future research directions in the study of the natural coding spaces of piecewise monotone functions. Video recognition tasks benefit from being broken down into simpler sequence recognition tasks. Using a specialized layer for features mapping, such as a linear layer or pixel-wise convolution, can make the model less efficient and less effective when dealing with long videos. To gain a better understanding of the complex nuclear interactions governing the production of light isotope clusters, researchers must thoroughly examine the clusterization phenomena within nucleon-nucleon and heavier nuclear interactions. The study presented here focuses on the relative rates of alpha particle and deuteron production in the interaction of 2-6 GeV alpha particles with targets of varying complexity, specifically helium, carbon, oxygen, and iron. The calculations are based on the concepts of proximate and clusterized states developed in a previous paper. When targets are comprised of two or fewer nucleons, the model predicts that alpha particle production occurs more frequently than deuteron production. However, when the target contains a larger number of nucleons, the production rates for alpha particles and deuterons become more closely matched. The predicted production rates are compared favorably with existing experimental data for the specific interaction of 5.5 Gev alpha particles with carbon targets. The study also explores the influence of nuclear structure on the production of clusters. The results suggest that when the cluster consists of the same nucleons as the target (such as deuterons from interactions with helium targets), the production rates are influenced by the density of the target, but only by a factor or two, regardless of the target mass. Combining free-electron laser (FEL) output with X-ray free-electron laser oscillator (XFELO) seeding and undulator tapering can significantly enhance X-ray pulse intensity and improve its stability. Theory suggests that this combination can produce extremely high intensities of up to $10^{18}$ photons per second, which is a nearly four-order magnitude increase over current records. In practice, achieving such high intensities with a real-world undulator and amplifier setup remains challenging. To explore the capabilities of this X-ray source, we conducted experiments at the Diamond Light Source's compact X-ray gradient tracing (CXGT) test facility. By pairing the CXGT undulator with an XFELO seed and employing an innovative technique of varying undulator periods, we were able to optimize X-ray pulse properties and achieve a notable increase in intensity to $8 \times 10^{13}$ photons per second, which marks a 120-fold enhancement over the CXGT's original output. These experimental results not only demonstrate the remarkable potential of this X-ray source but also pave the way for groundbreaking applications in fields like protein diffraction, coherent X-ray scattering, and laser-induced nuclear physics with X-ray photons. Furthermore, we found that the average electron beam energy and current were the critical factors determining the achieved intensity, as indicated by simulations. In line with this, we also observed that the XFELO seeding technique was essential for obtaining such high intensities, as undulator tapering alone fell short of the desired outcome. Lastly, we noticed that gaining further insight into this novel X-ray source will necessitate more sophisticated computational modeling at the threshold of nanosecond timing. Nonetheless, we anticipate that the intensity gains achieved through this combination of XFELO seeding and undulator tapering will greatly expand the scientific boundaries of X-ray photon usage. In specific, this will accommodate studies of proteins at atomic resolution with reduced exposure to radiation, as well as investigations in fields like X-ray nonlinear spectroscopy, laser-nuclear physics with reduced background interference, and intense coherent X-ray scattering with improved low-q spectrum analysis. In conclusion, the successful experiments conducted at the test facility at the Diamond Light Source have validated the superior performance of the XFELO-seeded FEL, as well as its great potential for enhancing the capabilities of third-generation light sources. In this context, we believe that the integration of XFELO and undulator tapering will greatly contribute to the development of innovative research applications that take full advantage of the properties of SASE FEL X-rays.

In this commentary, we draw inspiration from Dr. Ahlswede's legacy in information theory, specifically his contributions to leakage problems. We begin with an overview of fixed-length leakage in source coding, where we establish a normalised leakage metric and discover that it is maximised at a certain rate, which also determines the maximum compression rate. We then extend this finding to consider variable-length leakage in source coding, though the approach is non-shannon. Following this, we revisit Dr. Ahlswede's groundbreaking work on the broadcast channel and provide an alternate proof, before exploring generalisations of his work on network information-theory problems. Additionally, we examine how his influence has been felt in the fields of big data and information theory. Throughout this commentary, we highlight the significant impact that Dr. Ahlswede's work has had on the current state of information theory.
